We should never finish if we wished to point out all the mistakes of this author concerning American quadrupeds; but to demonstrate still further that the number of seventy species prescribed by him to America is not correct, but quite deficient, and contrary besides to what he himself wrote in the course of his History, we shall give at the end of this dissertation a list of the American quadrupeds drawn from the aforesaid History, to which we shall add the quadrupeds confused by him with others very different, and also those entirely omitted by him, whereby we shall show how far he has strayed from the truth in saying that in America matter has been prodigiously scarce. Besides, to conclude such a scarcity it does not suffice to make known that the species are few, but it would also be necessary to demonstrate that the individuals of such species are few; for if the individuals of the seventy species of American quadrupeds are more than those of the hundred and thirty species of the old continent, nature will indeed be less varied in America, but matter not more scarce. It would likewise be necessary to demonstrate that the species of reptiles and of birds are equally few and scantily numerous, since these no less than those serve to show the scarcity or the abundance of matter; but who is so ignorant of the things of America as not to have knowledge of the

Not content with diminishing the species of American quadrupeds, these authors strive also to shrink their stature. “All the animals of America,” says Count de Buffon, (i) “both those that were transported by men, such as horses, asses, bulls, sheep, goats, hogs, dogs, etc., and those that passed there of themselves, such as wolves, foxes, deer, and elks, are considerably smaller there than in Europe: and this,” he adds, “without any exception.” This stupendous effect he ascribes to the niggardly sky of America, and to the combination of the elements and other physical causes. “There was not,” says M. de P., “under the torrid zone of the new continent any great quadruped. The greatest quadruped (among those proper to those countries) that exists at present in the New World between the tropics is the tapir, which is of the size of a calf.” (k) “The bulkiest beast of the New continent,” says Count de Buffon, “is the tapir, which is as large as a small mule, and after it the Cabiai, which is of the size of a middling hog.”

Ma (e nell’ America, ‘allorchè fu fcoper-

We have already shown in the preceding dissertation that even if we granted these philosophers the alleged smallness of American quadrupeds, nothing would follow against the land or the climate of America; for according to the principles established by Count de Buffon, and cited by us elsewhere, the largest animals are proper to extreme climates, and the less large to temperate and mild ones: and if the advantages of a climate had to be argued from the size of quadrupeds, we should say without more ado that the climate of Africa and of southern Asia is much better than that of Europe. [p. 115] by the Europeans, there were no elephants, rhinoceroses, hippopotamuses, camels, or giraffes, at least there were at one time, if we give credence to Messrs. de P., Sloane, du Pratz, Lignery, and several other authors, who affirm the ancient existence of those great quadrupeds in America, grounded on the finding of fossil bones and of entire carcasses of immeasurable size in various places of that New World; indeed, if we believe what Count de Buffon wrote in volume 18 of his History, there was once in America a quadruped six times bulkier than the elephant, called Mammout by M. Müller; (l) but in Europe there never was, nor can there be, any quadruped of the first size. In America there were no horses, nor asses, nor bulls, (m) before they were transported there from Europe; but neither were they in Europe before they were transported or brought from Asia. All animals draw their origin from Asia, and from there spread to other countries: the nearness of Europe, and the commerce of the Asiatic peoples with the Europeans, facilitated the passage of those quadrupeds into Europe, and with them were also brought some customs and inventions useful to life, of which the Americans were deprived by reason of the distance of the countries and the lack of commerce.

When Count de Buffon asserted that the largest quadruped of the New World was the tapir, and after it the Cabiai, he had entirely forgotten the walruses, the seals, the bisons, the reindeer, the elks, the bears, and the huanachi. He himself

(l) According to what M. Müller says of his Mammout, this quadruped would have been 133 feet long and 105 feet high. Count de Buffon speaks of it thus in volume 16: “The prodigious Mammout, whose enormous bones we have often considered, and which we have judged to be at least six times larger than the largest elephant, exists no more.” In volume 22 he says that he has made sure that those immense bones were once those of elephants seven or eight times larger than that whose carcass he had observed in the Royal Cabinet at Paris; but in his new work entitled The Epochs of Nature he again affirms the ancient existence of that enormous quadruped in America.

(m) When we say that there were no bulls in America, we speak only of the common breed, which is employed in agriculture; for there were bisons, which Count de Buffon sometimes believes to be of the same species as the common bulls, and sometimes doubts. [p. 116] confesses, (n) that the seal seen by Lord Anson and by Rogers in America, and called by them sea lion, was incomparably larger than all the seals of the Old World. Who will dare to compare the Cabiai, which is no larger than a middling hog, with the bisons and the elks? The bisons are for the most part equal to the common bulls of Europe, and often exceed them in size. Let one see the description that M. de Bomare (o) gives of one of these quadrupeds, transported from Louisiana to France, and exactly measured by the same naturalist at Paris in 1769. There is an innumerable multitude of these great animals in the temperate zone of North America. The elks of New Mexico are of the size of a good horse. There was a knight in the city of Zacatecas who used them for his carriage in place of horses, as Vetancurt attests, (p) and at times they have been sent to the court of Spain to be presented to the Catholic King.

> confessa, (n) che la foca veduta da Lord Andson, e da Roggers nell’ America, e da loro chiamato Leone marino, era incomparabilmente più grande di tutte le foche del Mondo antico. Chi oferà paragonare il Cabiai , il qual non è più grande d'un mediocre porco, co' Bisonti , e cogli Alci? I Bisonti son per lo più uguali a' Tori comuni d' Europa, & sovente gli eccedono in grandezza . Vedasi la descrizione, che fa il Sig. de Bomare (o) d’ un di questi quadrupedì, trasportato dalla Luigiana in Francia, ed esattamente misurato dal medefimo Nawralista in Parigi nel 1769. Havvi un innumerabile moltitudine di questi grossi animali nella zona temperata dell’ America fertentrionale, Gli Alci del nuovo Messico fon della grandezza d' un buon Cavallo. Vi fu un Cavaliere nella Cirtà di Zacatecas , che fi servì d' efli per la fua carrozza in vece di cavalli, ficcome ne fa fede il Betancurt , (p) e talvolra sono stati mandati alla Corte di Spagna da presentarsi al Re Cattolico.

The universal proposition in which Count de Buffon affirms that all the quadrupeds common to both continents are smaller in America without any exception has been given the lie by several European authors, who saw those animals with their own eyes, and even by Count de Buffon himself in other places of his History. (q) “The Miztli is either the same as our lion, though by no means maned, or of the same kind; dusky in infancy, and tawny in youth, sometimes reddish or whitish, yet rising to a greater bulk, which may happen because of the difference of region.” Hist. Quadrup. N. Hisp., ch. XI. [p. 117] of Mexico he affirms the same. (r) Neither Count de Buffon nor M. de P. has a just idea of that beast. I saw one, among others, killed a few hours before with nine arquebus shots, much larger than what Count de Buffon would have us believe. These authors, since they do not trust the report of the Spaniards, ought at least to give credence to M. de la Condamine, a learned and truthful Frenchman, who says that the tigers seen by him in the hot countries of the New World did not seem to him different from the African tigers, either in the beautiful colors of the skin or in size, etc. Of the Mexican wolf the aforesaid Hernández says that in figure, color, and inclinations, as in size, it is like the European wolf, except that the latter has a larger head. (s) The same he affirms of the common deer, and Oviedo of the deer and the fallow deer. Count de Buffon himself, in spite of the generality of the principle established by him, without any exception, on the smaller size of American quadrupeds, reasoning afterward in volume 29 on the degeneration of animals, says that the fallow deer and the roe deer are, among the quadrupeds common to both continents, the only ones that are larger and stronger in the New World than in the Old; and discoursing in volume 27 of the otter of Canada he confesses that it is much larger than those of Europe, and says the same of the American beaver: so that he who admitted no exception to his principle admits it after all in fallow deer, roe deer, otters, beavers, and seals. If to these are then added the tigers, the maneless lions, and the deer, according to the testimony of Hernández and of Oviedo, we shall have at least eight species of quadrupeds common to both continents that are larger in the New World than in the Old. To the foregoing must likewise be added those quadrupeds that are equally large in the one and the other continent; since these, as well as

It is therefore false that all the animals of the New World are smaller than those of the Old World without any exception. It is also most false that they are all much smaller, and that Nature has made use in the New World of a different scale of size, as Count de Buffon affirms in another place. (u) In like manner the error of M. de Pauw can be shown in saying that all the quadrupeds of America are a sixth part smaller than their analogues of the old continent. The Tuza of Mexico is the analogue of the European mole, and is larger than it, according to what Count de Buffon says. That Mexican quadruped which Count de Buffon calls Coquallino, and we Tlalmototli, is analogous to the squirrel of Europe, and is, by the same author’s account, twice as large: the shrew of Brazil is analogous to the European shrew, and yet is larger than it, as the aforesaid author confesses. The Cojote, analogue of the jackal, is twice as large. The Llama, or sheep of Peru, analogue of the sheep of Europe, is incomparably larger, etc. But these philosophers, too bent on vilifying America and discrediting its animals, find even

(x) The animals of South America, which are those that properly belong to this new continent, are almost all without tusks, horns, and tails; their figure is bizarre, and their limbs disproportioned and ill put together; and some of them, like the anteaters and the sloths, are of so wretched a nature that they have hardly the power to move and to eat.” (y) “The animals native to the New World,” says M. de Pauw, “are for the most part of an ungainly form, and in some of them so ill arranged that the first draftsmen could make their characters recognizable only with difficulty. It has been observed that most of the species lack a tail, and that they have a certain irregularity in the paws: which is notable in the tapir, the anteater, the Glama of Margraf, the sloth, and the Cabiai. The ostriches, which on our continent have no more than two toes united by a membrane, have all four toes separate in America.” (z)

> Questi discorsi, a dire il vero, sono piuttosto una censura della condotta del Creatore , che del clima dell’ America , non difiunile a quella bestemmia, che da alcuni fi attribuisce al Re Don Alfonso il savio sulla disposizione de' corpì celesti . Se i primi individui di quelle spezie d'’ animali non vennero così ‘dalla mano del Creatore , ma il clima del nuovo Monda è staro , la cagione delle pretese loro irregolarità , qualora tali animali foflero rrasporiati in Europa , fi perfezionerebbe la loro forma , la loro indole , e il loro istinto : alméno dopo dieci, o dodici generazioni quei miserabili animali, ai quali il maligno clima dell'America ha volto la co-

These speeches, to tell the truth, are rather a censure of the conduct of the Creator than of the climate of America, not unlike that blasphemy which some attribute to King Don Alfonso the Wise concerning the arrangement of the heavenly bodies. If the first individuals of those species of animals did not come thus from the hand of the Creator, but the climate of the New World was the cause of their alleged irregularities, then, were such animals transported to Europe, their form, their disposition, and their instinct would be perfected: at least after ten or twelve generations those wretched animals, from which the malignant climate of America has taken away the tail,

Nò , diranno quei Filosofi , perchè non è tanto facile il ricuperar nella natura ciò che fi perde , quanto il pers dere ciò che fi ha: onde ancorchè quegli animali non potesse. ro riavere-nell'antico Contineate la coda, l: corna, o le zan» ne, tuttavia potrebbe dirsi, che il clima dell' America è stato la cagione di tal perdita. Sia pur così , e per tanto non dîscorriamo ora delle irregolarità consistenti in qualche difetto, ma di quelle, che’ son tali per ecceslo della materia. Discorriamo degli truzzi, i quali hanno per vizio della Natura al dir del Sig. de Pavv , (*) due dita più in ciascig piede, o per non lasciare i quadrupedi discorriamo piuttosto dell’ Unau, spezie di Pigro americano, il qual tra le altre irregolarità, ha quella d'aver quarantasei colte . ,, Il nume- » to di quarantasei colte in un animale di sì piccol corpo 9» è, dice il C. de Bufton, una spezie d' errore, o d'eccefla 3 della Natura ; poiché niun animale nè anche dei più gran- » di, © di quelli che hanno il corpo più lungo a proporzion » della lor grofsezza, ne ha tante, L'Elefante non ha più di » quaranta colte , il Cavallo trentasei , il Taflo trenta, il ca» » ne ventisei, e l' Uomo ventiquattro .,, Ora se il primo Unau, che fu al Mondo ebbe dalla mano di Dio quello stesso numero di coste , che hanno presentemente i suoi discendenti , il discorso del C., de, Buffon è una censura del Creatore, e il dire, che quell' eccessivo numero di coste è stato ua errore delda Natura, vorrà dire, che è stato un error di Dio, il qual è la vera Natura effettrice. Son ben sicuro, che una tal bestemmia è troppo aliena dalla sublime mente, e dal cuor cristiano del C. de Buffon ; ma lo spirito filosofico, che regna da pertutto nelle sue opere, l' indufle ralvolta a. far uso di rali espreslioni, che ben disaminate non piaceranno ai buoni Cristiani, a —_ _— Csa" ———— Vr ——— ——— +

(z) Recherch. sur les Américains, pt. 1. [p. 120] the horns, and the tusks, would recover them under a more beneficent climate. No, those philosophers will say, because it is not so easy to recover in nature what one loses as to lose what one has: so that even if those animals could not regain their tail, horns, or tusks on the old continent, it might nevertheless be said that the climate of America was the cause of such a loss. Be it so; and therefore let us not now discuss the irregularities that consist in some defect, but those that are such through an excess of matter. Let us discuss the ostriches, which through a fault of Nature, according to M. de Pauw, (*) have two toes more on each foot; or, so as not to leave the quadrupeds, let us discuss rather the Unau, a species of American sloth, which among its other irregularities has that of having forty-six ribs. “The number of forty-six ribs in an animal of so small a body,” says Count de Buffon, “is a kind of error, or excess, of Nature; for no animal, not even the largest, or those whose body is longest in proportion to their bulk, has so many. The elephant has no more than forty ribs, the horse thirty-six, the badger thirty, the dog twenty-six, and man twenty-four.” Now if the first Unau that existed in the world had from the hand of God the same number of ribs that its descendants have at present, the discourse of Count de Buffon is a censure of the Creator; and to say that that excessive number of ribs was an error of Nature will mean that it was an error of God, who is the true efficient Nature. I am quite sure that such a blasphemy is far removed from the sublime mind and the Christian heart of Count de Buffon; but the philosophical spirit that reigns everywhere in his works has led him at times to make use of such expressions as, when well examined, will not please good Christians.

(A) If, on the contrary, these philosophers believe that the Unau in its first origin had a number of ribs proportioned to the size of its body, and that the malignant climate of America afterwards went on increasing it, we must persuade ourselves that, if that species of quadruped were transported to the old continent and reared under a more favorable climate, it would in the end return to its pristine perfection. Let the experiment be made, then: let two or three males of that ungainly species be transported to the Old World, and as many females, and if after twenty or more generations it is observed that the number of their ribs begins to diminish, we shall at once confess that the land of America is the most unhappy, and its climate the worst, in the world. If it turns out otherwise, we shall say then, as we say from this very moment, that the logic of these gentlemen is more wretched than that quadruped, and that their reasonings are mere paralogisms. For the rest, it is truly a wonder that in a country where matter has been so scarce, Nature should have sinned by an excess of it in the ribs of the sloths and in the toes of the ostriches.

> Ma per dare a divedere, che questi Filosofi impegnati nel far comparir maligno il clima del nuovo Mondo, fì erano affatto dimenticati delle. miserie del proprio lor Continente , addimandiamo loro, qual è l’animale più miserabile dell’ America? Il Pigro, risponderanno incontanente; perchè questo quadrupede è 1l più imperfecro nella sua organizzazione, il più inabile pel moto, il più sprovveduto d'armi per la sua difesa,

But to show that these philosophers, bent on making the climate of the New World appear malignant, had entirely forgotten the miseries of their own continent, let us ask them: which is the most wretched animal of America? The sloth, they will answer at once; because this quadruped is the most imperfect in its organization, the most unfit for motion, the most unprovided with arms for its defense, and above all the one that seems to have less sensation than all other animals: a truly unhappy animal, condemned by Nature to inertia, to hunger, and to weeping, with which it ever arouses in other animals pity and horror. (A) Wishing to give the reason why man resists the influences of climates more than the animals do, Count de Buffon says thus in volume 18: Man is in everything the work of Heaven; the animals are in many respects nothing but productions of the earth. This proposition seems a little too harsh; but far harsher ones are read in his Epochs of Nature. [p. 122] common to both continents. Count de Buffon will not believe it, because it does not suit him, and he says that if any sloth is found in Asia, it was transported there from America; but whatever he may say, it is certain that the Unau, one of the species of sloths, is an Asiatic animal, as Klein, Linnaeus, Brisson, the publisher of Seba’s Cabinet, and above all Vosmaër, a learned and diligent Dutch naturalist, bear witness. (B) The Unau of Bengal, seen, reared, and exactly described by this author, cannot have been transported from America; because there has never been any commerce between South America and Asia by which it could have been transported. Besides, the Unau of Bengal is different from the American one: this has only two toes on its paws, and that five. If Count de Buffon persuades himself that the climate of Asia could increase the number of toes in the American quadruped, we shall say then that the climate of the old continent would also be capable of restoring the tail, the horns, and the tusks to those quadrupeds from which the deadly climate of America had taken them. For the rest, whoever wishes to read and compare the eloquent description that Count de Buffon gives of the American sloths, and that which M. de Vosmaër gives of the pentadactyl sloth of Bengal, will soon recognize that this Asiatic quadruped is as wretched as those American ones.

But let us examine philosophically what these authors say about the alleged irregularity of those quadrupeds. True irregularity in animals is the disproportion in the limbs, or the unsuitability in the form or the disposition of certain individuals with respect to the common run of the species, not that which is observed in a new species compared with another that is known. He would surely be a fool who should deem the Techichi irregular because it does not bark. This is an American quadruped, which, because it resembles the small dogs of Europe, was called a dog by the Spaniards, not because it was of the same species: and hence arose that fable, spread by not a few authors

In fact the argument of M. de Pauw about the American ostriches is of no other caliber. The Touyou (*) is an American bird specifically different from the ostrich; but because it is quite large, and very like that great African bird, it has commonly been called an ostrich. This suffices M. de P. to affirm that there is irregularity in those American birds; but even if we granted him as a favor that the Touyou is a true ostrich, it could never prove what he wishes. He wants us to believe the American ostrich irregular because, instead of having only two toes united by a membrane, like the African, it has four separate ones. But an American could say that the African ostrich is rather the irregular one, because instead of having four separate toes it has only two, and those united by means of a membrane. “No,” M. de P. would reply, all in a rage, “it is not so: the irregularity is certainly in your ostriches, because they do not conform to the ostriches of the Old World, which are the exemplars of the species, nor to the portrait of such birds that the most famous naturalists of Europe have left us.” “Our world,” the American would answer, “which you call new, because three centuries ago it was not yet known to you, is as ancient as your world, and our animals are likewise coeval with yours. Neither are those under any obligation to conform to your animals, nor are we at fault

Our philosophers are in truth no happier in their discourses on the tails of quadrupeds than in what they wrote about the feet of ostriches. They say frankly, and without any regard for truth, that the greater part of the quadrupeds of the new continent are altogether without tails: which, like all the other effects they have observed in those unfortunate countries, they ascribe to the niggardliness of the American sky, to the infancy of Nature in that part of the world, to the bad climate, and to I know not what combination of the elements. Thus reason these celebrated philosophers of the enlightened age. But since, according to Count de Buffon, the species of American quadrupeds number seventy, at least forty would have to be without tails for it to be true that the greater part lack that member, as M. de P. says, and much more would be needed to verify that almost all quadrupeds are destitute of tails, as Count de Buffon affirms. Now such quadrupeds in America are at most six, as we shall see below: therefore their proposition is a monstrous hyperbole, not to say a gross lie.

> Non fono in vero più felici i nostri Filosofi ne' lor discorsi su le code de' quadrupedi , che in ciò che scriffsero intorno a'piedi degli struzzi, Eglino dicono francamente , e senza verun riguardo alla verità, che la maggior parte de’ quadrupedi del nuovo Continente è affatto priva di coda : lo che ficcome tucci gli altri. eff:rri da loro offervari in quegli sventurati paefi, alito ascrivono all' avarizia del Cielo americano, all' infanzia della Natura in quella parte del Mondo, al cattivo clima, ed a non so quale combinazione degli elementi. Così ragionano questi celebri Filosofi del secolo illuminato. Ma eflendo al dir del C. de Buffon settanta le spezie de' quadrupedi americani, bisognerebbe, che almeno quaranta foflero senza coda, acciocchè fofse vero, che la maggior parte è priva di ral membro, come dice il Sig. de P., e molto più per verificare, che quasi rueti i quadrupedì fono sforniti di coda , come afferma il GC. de Buffon . So that in the old continent there are at least fourteen species (D) of quadrupeds unprovided with a tail, and in America only six, from which we might remove the last two, because they are uncertain. (E) In all the thirty small volumes of Count de Buffon’s History of the quadrupeds I have found no other American animal without a tail except the aforesaid. And notwithstanding this, he dares to affirm that in the New World almost all the animals were without a tail. From which one sees that such universal propositions are as easy to utter as they are difficult to prove.

If the climate of America is so pernicious to the tails of animals, why is it that, while four species of apes of the old continent, namely the Pongo, the Piteco, the Gibbon, and the Cynocephalus, are altogether without that member, all the species of monkeys of the New World have it, and some, like the Sakis, have a tail so long that it is sesquiduple their body? Why do squirrels, Coquallins, anteaters, and other such quadrupeds, furnished with an enormous tail in proportion to their bodies, abound so in America? Why has the marmot of Canada, although of the same species as that of the Alps, a larger tail, as Count de Buffon himself confesses? (E) The Pecar is found described by Oviedo, Hernández, and Acosta under the names of Saino and Cojametl, and these authors say nothing of any lack of a tail. Concerning the Tapeto, Count de Buffon believes that it is the Citli of Hernández. Now all Mexicans know that the Citli of Hernández is the hare of Mexico, and we are sure that it has its tail, like the common hare of Europe. (F) If ever there were in America some principle destructive of the tails of animals, those that Columbus transported there from Europe and from the Canary Islands in 1493 would by now have remained entirely tailless, especially the hogs, which brought tails so small; or at least they would have been notably shortened after 288 years; but among so many Europeans who have seen the sheep, horses, oxen, etc. born in America, and those that are at present raised in Europe, there will not be even one who can find any difference between the tails of the one and of the other.

> Questo medesimo argomento vale parimente contra ciò , che dice il C. de Buffon su la mancanza di corna , e di zanne nella maggior parte de' quadrupedi americani, poichè i Buoi , le

This same argument holds equally against what Count de Buffon says about the lack of horns and tusks in the greater part of the American quadrupeds, since the oxen, sheep, and goats preserve their horns unchanged, the dogs and hogs their teeth, and the cats their claws, as all those know who have seen them and compared them with those of Europe. If the American climate were so deadly to the teeth and to the horns of animals, the descendants of those European quadrupeds that were transported there almost three centuries ago would already have lost at least a good part of them, and much more the posterity of the wolves, the bears, and other similar quadrupeds that passed there from Asia perhaps as early as the first century after the universal Flood. If on the contrary the temperate zone of Europe is more propitious to the teeth of animals than the torrid zone of the New World, why did Nature give to the latter, and not to the former, the tapirs and the crocodiles, which in the number, the size, and the ferocity of their teeth exceed all the quadrupeds and reptiles of Europe?

(G) Among all the quadrupeds of the New World there are no others without teeth except the anteaters, just as there are in the old continent the pangolin and the Phatagin, quadrupeds of East India covered with scales instead of hair. All these quadrupeds, since they feed on nothing but ants, have no need of teeth to sustain themselves; but otherwise they are [p. 128] of the climate, or of the niggardly sky of America, or of that imaginary combination of the elements; but because the Creator, whose works are perfect, and whose counsels we must humbly revere, willed to make them so, that such variety might serve the general embellishment of the universe, and make his wisdom and his power shine forth the more. The very thing that makes some animals beautiful would make others deformed. In the horse it is a perfection to have a large tail, in the deer to have a small one, and in the Pongo to be altogether without one.

As to what our philosophers say about the ugliness of the American animals, it is true that among so many there are some whose form does not correspond to the idea that we have of the beauty of beasts. But who has assured us that such an idea is just, rather than imperfect and caused by the limitation of our mind? And how many other animals might we not find in the old continent still worse formed than all the American beasts? (I speak here according to the ideas of those philosophers; for the rest, I respect the hand of the Creator in all his works.) What quadruped is there in America that can be compared in deformity and in disproportion of limbs with the elephant, called a Monster of matter by Count de Buffon himself? (H) “Considering this animal” (says M. de Bomare of the elephant) “in relation to the idea we have of the correctness of proportions, it seems ill proportioned, because of its thick, short body, its stiff and ill-formed legs, its round and crooked feet, its big head, its small eyes, and its large ears: one might also say that the garment in which it is covered is still worse cut and worse made. Its trunk, its tusks, its feet make it as extraordinary as the greatness of its size, [p. 129] feet, shapeless, their toes barely outlined, and finally those minute little eyes and that ridiculous little tail on so immoderate a body, do they not make the elephant the most irregular quadruped? I challenge our philosophers to find me in the New World a quadruped more disproportioned, and whose form is more ungainly. Similar reflections might also be made on the camel, on the giraffe, on the Macaco, of which Count de Buffon says that it is of a frightful deformity, and on other animals of the old continent, and yet we do not dare to blame the climate that rears them, nor even to censure the supreme Artificer who formed them.

Come dunque s'allega la minor ferocia delle bestie americane , come un argomento della lor degenerazione, cagionata dalla malignità di quel clima? Se il clima dell’antico Continente dee reputarlì miglior di quello del nuovo Mando, perchè sorto quello s' allevano le fiere più rerribilì; dovrà credersi per la medesima ragione il clima dell’ Africa incomparabilmzore più eccellente di quello dell' Europa . Questo argomento da noi altrove adoperapo debbe inculcarli per maggior confusione de nostri Filosoh. “ E

What our philosophers say, moreover, about the lesser ferocity of the American wild beasts, instead of helping them to prove the malignity of that climate, serves only to demonstrate its mildness and goodness. “In America,” says Count de Buffon, (I) “where the air and the earth are milder than those of Africa, the tiger, the lion, and the panther are not terrible except in name… They have degenerated, if indeed ferocity added to cruelty made up their nature, or rather, they have done nothing but suffer the influence of the climate: under a gentler sky their disposition has grown gentler.” What more can be desired in favor of the climate of America? How, then, is the lesser ferocity of the American beasts alleged as an argument of their degeneration, caused by the malignity of that climate? If the climate of the old continent must be reckoned better than that of the New World because the most terrible wild beasts are reared under it, then for the same reason the climate of Africa will have to be believed incomparably more excellent than that of Europe. This argument, which we have used elsewhere, ought to be pressed home for the greater confusion of our philosophers.

The Mexican tiger, whether or not it is of the same species as the Royal Tigers of Africa, since that matters not at all to us, is of a surprising strength and ferocity. There is no quadruped, either among the European or among the American, that can withstand it. It boldly assails and tears to pieces men, deer, horses, bulls, and even the most horrible crocodiles, as Acosta attests. (K) This learned author vaunts the intrepidity and the swiftness of that wild beast. Gonzalo de Oviedo, who had traveled through many countries of Europe and was not ignorant of natural history, speaking of those American tigers, says (L) thus: “They are animals very strong in the legs, well armed with claws, and so terrible that in my judgment there is no Royal Lion, even among the largest, that can vie with them in strength and ferocity.” The tiger is the terror of the forests of America: it is not capable of being tamed, nor of letting itself be taken when adult: those that are taken while still small cannot be kept without danger unless shut up in very strong cages of wood or of iron. Such is the character of those beasts which are called cowards by M. de P. and by other authors who did not know how to distinguish the species of quadrupeds with spotted skin.

The American wolves are neither less strong nor less bold than those of the old continent, as all know well who have experience of both. Even the deer, which are, according to Pliny, (P) the most peaceable of animals, are in Mexico so bold that they often attack hunters, as Hernández attests (Q), and it is notorious in that kingdom. I have seen with my own eyes the carnage made in my own house by a deer, become almost domesticated, upon a poor American woman.

M. de P. says of the American crocodiles, whose ferocity is so notorious, that it appears from the observations of M. du Pratz and of some others that they do not have the fury and impetuosity of those of Africa; but Dr. Hernández, who knew well both the one and the other, found no difference between them. (S) Acosta says that the American ones are very ferocious, but slow; but this slowness is not in progressive motion in a straight line, in which they are very swift and agile, but only in turning or bending to one side or the other, as also happens in the African crocodiles, doubtless on account of the inflexibility of their vertebrae. Dr. Hernández affirms that the Acuetzpalin, or Mexican crocodile, flees from those who assail it and pursues those who flee (though the latter happens more commonly than the former). Pliny says the same of the African crocodiles. (T) Finally, if one compares what Pliny relates of the latter with what Hernández says of the former, it will be found that not even in size is there any difference between them. (V)

(R) M. de Buffon might say, as he intimates in volume 18, that no account should be taken of birds as regards the climate; because, being able easily to pass from one continent to the other, it would be almost impossible to distinguish which belong properly to the one or to the other. But since the cause of the journeys that birds make is the cold or the heat of the seasons, which they seek to avoid, the American birds have no need to leave their continent; because they have there countries of every sort of climate in which to defend themselves from the season harmful to them and to seek their food. We are altogether sure that the Mexican birds do not make journeys to the old continent.

(V) Pliny says that the African crocodile often has more than eighteen cubits in length, or twenty-seven Roman feet. Dr. Hernández affirms that the Mexican crocodile is usually more than seven paces long. If he speaks of Castilian paces, they make almost twenty-eight Roman feet; if of Roman paces, they will be thirty-five feet: so that the difference is small, or if there is some excess, it is on the side of the American crocodile. [p. 133] we have seen. He certainly chose to be silent, because he recognized his cause as lost on this side; for whether in the number or the variety of the species, or in intrepidity, or in the beauty of the feathers, or in the excellence of song, the birds of the old continent certainly cannot vie with the American birds. Of their surprising multitude we have spoken elsewhere. The fields, the woods, the rivers, the lakes, and even the inhabited places are full of innumerable species. Gemelli, who had made the circuit of the world and had been in the best countries of Asia, Africa, and Europe, declares that there is no country in the world that can be compared with New Spain in the beauty and variety of its birds. (U) See also what the historians of New France, of Louisiana, of Brazil, and of other countries of the New World say of them.

As regards the beauty of birds, those authors who have otherwise been bent on running down that New World do not dispute its advantages to America. Whoever wishes to form some idea of them should see the works of Oviedo, Hernández, Acosta, Ulloa, and other European authors who have seen the American birds with their own eyes. In New Spain, says Acosta, there is a great abundance of birds adorned with feathers so excellent and so fine that their like is not found in Europe. (ee)

So think two modern Italians, (ff) as learned in certain speculative matters as they are ignorant of the things of America. The testimony of Dr. Hernández, which we copy here below, (gg) would suffice to confound these authors: who, after having heard the best nightingales at the court of Philip II, heard for many years the Centzontli, or polyglots, the cardinals, the Tigretti, the Cuitlaccochi, and other innumerable species of songbirds common in Mexico and not known in Europe, besides the nightingales, the goldfinches, the calandra larks, and others common to both continents. Among all the songbirds the most prized in Europe is the much-renowned nightingale, and yet this is far better in America, according to what M. de Bomare affirms. “The nightingale of Louisiana,” he says, “is the same as that of Europe; but it is more familiar, sings all year, and its song is more varied.” Behold three great advantages of the American over the European. But even if there were in America neither nightingales, nor goldfinches, nor any other bird of those that are esteemed in Europe for their song, the Centzontli or polyglot alone (*) would suffice to leave it nothing to envy any country in the world. I protest to our anti-American philosophers that what Dr. Hernández says about the great excess of merit of the polyglot over the nightingale is quite true, and in agreement with the judgment of the Europeans who have been in Mexico, and with that of the Mexicans who have been in Europe. But since we are on the subject of birds, I wish before putting an end to this article to make an opportune reflection. There is no American animal over which our philosophers make a greater clamor than over the sloth, on account of its stupendous slowness and inability to move. Now what would they say if there were a bird of that kind? This would be without doubt the most irregular animal in the world; since such tardiness or inertia is more unbecoming in a bird than in a quadruped. But where is this bird? In the old continent, and it has been described by Count de Buffon himself, who says that the Dronte, a bird of the East Indies larger than the swan, is among birds what the sloth is among quadrupeds: “It seems

From what we have said up to this point it is evidently concluded that neither is the sky of America niggardly, nor is its climate contrary to the generation of animals: that neither has matter been scarce there, nor has Nature made use of a different scale of size: that it is an error, or rather a heap of errors, all that Count de Buffon and M. de Pauw say about the smallness, the irregularity, and the defects of the American quadrupeds, and even if it were true, nothing of it would help them to demonstrate the malignity of the climate of America; but now let us see whether they do less wrong to the New World in what they say about the alleged degradation of the quadrupeds transported there from Europe.

[p. 138] its discovery, have degenerated, their bodily frame has shrunk, and they have lost a part of their instinct and of their character: the cartilages and the fibers of their flesh have become stiffer and coarser.” Such is M. de Pauw’s general conclusion; let us now see the proofs. 1. Beef is so fibrous that it can hardly be eaten on the island of Hispaniola. 2. The hogs on the island of Cubagua changed their form in a short time to such a degree that they could not be recognized: their hooves grew so much that they were half a palm in length. 3. Sheep suffered a great alteration in Barbados. 4. Dogs brought over from our countries lose their voice and cease to bark in the greater part of the regions of the new continent. 5. The cold of Peru disordered the organs of generation in the camels brought there from Africa. Such are the arguments these philosophers rely on to promote the degradation of the animals of the old continent in America: arguments such that, even if they were true, they would not suffice to prove so universal a conclusion; for what does it matter that beef is so fibrous on the island of Hispaniola, if in almost all the other countries of America it is good, and in many, as in all those of Mexico situated on the coasts of the Pacific Ocean, it is as excellent as the best in Europe, and perhaps even more so? What does it matter that sheep have suffered some alteration in Barbados and in some countries that are too hot, if in the temperate countries of Mexico and of South America they are preserved just as they were when they passed over from Spain? What does it matter that hogs have been disfigured in Cubagua, a wretched little island, without water and without everything necessary to life, if in the rest of America they have acquired, as the same M. de Pauw says, an extraordinary bodily frame, and their flesh has been so greatly perfected that physicians prescribe it to their patients in preference to every other meat? Now, if the disfigurement of the hogs in Cubagua does not prove that the climate of America is not the most suitable for them, why should the damage suffered by the sheep in Barbados, the greater fibrousness of the flesh of oxen in Hispaniola,

[p. 139] and the slight shrinking of some quadrupeds in Canada, prove that the climate of America in general is contrary to the generation of animals, to their bodily frame, and to their instinct?

If such logic were tolerable, we could employ far better arguments against the climate of the old continent, without having to use any other materials than those which Count de Buffon himself furnishes us in his Natural History. Camels, as the same author says, have not been able to multiply in Spain, although that climate, among all those of Europe, is the least contrary to their nature. Oxen have degenerated in Barbary, and in Iceland they have lost their horns. Sheep, says Count de Buffon, have degenerated from their first state in our countries, and in all the hot countries of the old continent they change their wool into hair. Goats have grown smaller in Guinea and in other countries. Dogs in Lapland have become very small and very deformed, and those of temperate climates, when they are carried into cold climes, cease to bark, and after the first generation are born with erect ears. “From the accounts of travelers it is established that mastiffs, greyhounds, and other breeds of European dogs, carried to Madagascar, to Calicut, to Madura, and to Malabar, degenerate after the second or third generation, and that in excessively hot countries, such as Guinea and Senegal, this degeneration is more rapid; for hardly have three or four years passed when they lose their hair and their voice.” Deer in hot, dry, mountainous countries, such as Corsica and Sardinia, have lost half of their bodily frame. If to these and other facts which Count de Buffon gives us we wished to add those furnished by a great many other authors, what an abundance of examples of the degeneration of animals in the old continent we should have, far greater and truer than that of our philosophers! But so that the exaggeration and falsity in their examples may be seen, let us examine one by one all the species of Asiatic and European animals transported into the New World which they say have degenerated.

## OF THE CAMELS

> 14° DISSERTAZIONE IV. DE' CAMMELLI .

“Of all the quadrupeds transported to America,” says M. de P., “those that have succeeded least have undoubtedly been the camels. At the beginning of the sixteenth century some were brought from Africa to Peru, where the cold disordered their organs of reproduction, and they left no posterity.” But, passing over for the moment the chronological error into which he falls, as one that matters little to our purpose, (nn) if it was the cold that destroyed the species of camels in America, the same would happen in Europe, especially in the northern countries, where the cold is beyond comparison greater than in any country of Peru. If the cold was the cause of their extinction, let M. de Pauw blame those who established those quadrupeds in places not suited to their nature, and not America, in which there are hot and dry lands such as are required for the subsistence of camels. The same experiment that was made in Peru with camels was also made in Spain, and proved similarly fruitless; and yet there will be no one to doubt that the climate of that peninsula is among the most temperate and the mildest in Europe. Count de Buffon says that those quadrupeds could be propagated no less in America than in Spain, if all the necessary precautions were taken; and I do not doubt that in the districts of New Galicia they would do quite well. For the rest, it is false that the camels transported to Peru left no posterity; for Father Acosta, who went there some years afterward, testifies that he saw them multiplied, though little. (oo)

But even if in Canada oxen have perhaps lost a part of their bodily frame, as Count de Buffon affirms, and if in Hispaniola their flesh has become more fibrous, as M. de Pauw would have it, at least this is not so in the greater part of the countries of the New World, in which the multitude and the size of those animals and the goodness of their flesh show how favorable those climates are to their generation. Their prodigious multiplication in those countries is attested by a great many European authors, ancient as well as modern. Father Acosta relates (pp) that in the fleet which came from New Spain to Old Spain, and in which he returned to Europe in 1587, that is, about sixty years after the first bulls and cows had been transported to Mexico, 64,360 ox hides were carried from that country, and from Hispaniola alone, which M. de Pauw believes so contrary to the generation of these quadrupeds, 35,444. I do not doubt that if one compared the number of bulls and cows carried from the old continent to the new with the number of hides that America has sent in return to Europe, more than five million hides would be found for each of those animals. Valdecebro, a Spanish Dominican who lived some years in Mexico toward the middle of the last century, relates as a notorious thing that Don Juan Orduña, a Mexican knight, was given thirty-six thousand calves in one year for his cows: (qq) which could not have happened except in a herd of two hundred thousand bulls and cows. Today there are private individuals who own 50,000. But nothing else shows more clearly the stupendous multiplication of such quadrupeds than their selling so cheaply in those countries, where they are necessary for the sustenance of men and for the labors of the field, and where, because of the abundance of

Count de Buffon affirms that cold countries are more suitable to oxen than hot ones; but this is not so in New Spain; for although the oxen of cold and temperate countries are good there, those of the hot countries are nonetheless better. Count de Buffon confesses (uu) that sheep have done very well both in the hot countries and in the cold ones of the new continent; but he adds that although they have multiplied greatly, they are nevertheless leaner, and their flesh is less juicy and less tender, than in Europe: in which he shows that he was badly informed. In the hot countries of the New World sheep for the most part do not do well, and the flesh of wethers is bad: at which there is no cause for wonder, since the hot climate is so contrary to them even in the old continent, as Count de Buffon himself says, that under it they are covered with hair instead of wool. In the cold and temperate climes of New Spain they have multiplied in proportion even more than bulls: their wool is in many places as fine as that of the sheep of Spain, and their flesh as good as the best in Europe, as those Europeans can testify who have been in those countries. The multiplication of sheep in America has been astonishing. Father Acosta testifies (vv) that before he went there there were well-to-do men in America who possessed seventy and even a hundred thousand sheep, and today

Count de Buffon himself, although he commits himself so strongly to disparaging the animals of America, nevertheless confesses that goats have done well in the American climates, and that their multiplication there is much greater than in Europe; (zz) for whereas in Europe they bear in each birth a single kid, or at most two, in America they bear three, four, and sometimes five. M. de P., who worthily gives Count de Buffon the title of Pliny of France, and wants one to defer to his authority in the matter of animals, as to one who has made a review of all the animals of the earth, ought to have weighed these and other confessions of that learned philosopher before setting himself to write about American animals.

[p. 145] degraded in America, M. de P. on the contrary affirms that these are the only animals which have acquired in the New World an extraordinary bodily frame, and whose flesh has been perfected. This contradiction arose undoubtedly from not distinguishing, as they ought, the different countries of America. It may be that there are some, though I do not know of them, in which hogs have lost a part of their size; but it is certain that in New Spain, in the Antilles, in Tierra Firme, and in other countries of America they are as large as those of Europe, and on the island of Cuba there is a breed of hogs twice as large as the European: which is constant and notorious to all those who have been in those countries. Our philosophers can, if they please, get information from several European authors who have seen the hogs of Toluca and of Puebla in New Spain, of Cartagena, of Cuba, etc., about their excessive multiplication and the excellence of their flesh. ## OF THE HORSES AND THE MULES

> DE' CAVALLI, E DELLE MULE.

In nothing else of all that Count de Buffon and M. de Pauw say against the American animals do they do a greater wrong to America and to the truth than in supposing the horses too to be degraded there. Of these Father Acosta says (Bb) “that in many countries of America, or in the greater part, they have turned out, and do turn out, quite well, and there are some breeds as good as the best of Spain, no less for the course and for show than for journeys and toils.”

Such testimony of a European so critical, so impartial, and so familiar with the affairs of America and of Europe is worth far more than all the declamations of those philosophers against the New World. Lieutenant General Don Antonio de Ulloa, a learned Spanish mathematician still living, (Cc) speaks with amazement of the American horses that he saw in Chile and in Peru, and praises highly the Chilean ones for their gait, those that are called Aguilillas for their extraordinary speed, and those called Parameros for their stupendous agility in the running they do in the hunting of deer, with the horsemen on their backs, over the slopes and over the roughest and steepest places of the mountains. He testifies that he made many times, on one of the horses called Aguilillas, which, he adds, was not among the swiftest of its breed, more than fifteen miles in 57 or 58 minutes. In New Spain there is an indescribable quantity of horses and mules. Their multitude may be conjectured from their price, for whereas in the time of the conquest an ordinary horse was worth as much as a thousand scudi, today a good one is acquired for ten or twelve scudi. (Dd) Their size is that of the common horses of Europe; seldom is a horse seen in Mexico as small as the Slavonian ones that we see in Italy, and much less like those of Iceland and of other northern countries according to Anderson, or those of India according to Tavernier and other authors. Their strength is such that it is quite common among the inhabitants of those countries to ride seventy or eighty miles, and sometimes even more, going all the while at a good pace, without ever stopping or changing horses, over roads that are often difficult. Saddle horses, although for the most part geldings, have a stupendous fire. The mules, which in all that kingdom serve for coaches and for the pack, are also, as regards size

(Dd) In New Galicia a middling horse is had for two sequins, a mule for three, or two and a half; and a herd of twenty-four mares with their stallion for twenty-five sequins. In Chile a trotting horse, of those most prized by the countrymen for their strength and their great agility in running, can be had even for half a sequin, that is, for one scudo, and a mare is usually bought for twenty-five baiocchi. [p. 147] such as the common ones of Europe. Those for the pack, which travel in a train, carry about five hundred pounds on their backs; they do not make more than twelve or fourteen miles a day, according to the custom of those carriers; but in this manner they make journeys of eight hundred, a thousand, and even fifteen hundred miles. Those for the coach go at the pace of the posts of Europe, although the coaches carry a much greater weight because of the baggage of the passengers, and the same mules do so on very long journeys, going at least thirty miles each day. Saddle mules are used for the longest journeys. It is common to make on a mule the journey from Mexico to Guatemala, of about a thousand miles, over a road that is largely mountainous and bad, covering thirty or more miles each day. All this that I have adduced to expose the error of our philosophers concerning the alleged degradation of those quadrupeds is public and notorious in that kingdom, and agrees with the report that several European authors give of it. But nothing, in my opinion, shows more clearly the multitude and the excellence of American horses than an observation I have made. Among the many things that the Spaniards settled in America send for from Spain at any cost, out of the love they keep for their native land, I do not know (at least with regard to Mexico) that in the last two hundred years they have ever had horses brought from Spain; and on the contrary I am sure that they have often sent American horses to Spain to be presented to the grandees of the court, and even to the Catholic King himself.

## OF THE DOGS

> ii ai Magnati della Corre, ed anche. allo steflo Re Catto+

Among the great absurdities published by M. de Pauw, which are not few, a very great one is that which he writes about dogs. Dogs, he says (Ee), transported from our countries lose their voice at once, and cease to bark in the greater part of the regions

> DE” CANT.

> Tra" grandi spropositi pubblicati dal Sig. de PawW, i quali non fon pochi , è affai grande quello, che scrive intorno ai Cani. I Cani dice (Ee) trasportati dai noftri: paesi perdono subiro la voce, e cessano. d' abbajare: nella maggior parte delle di pia T € e) Recberch. Philosopb. part. 3. [p. 148] 145 DISSERTAZIONE IV.

(Ee) Recherch. philosoph., pt. 1. [p. 148] of the new continent. Americans have, on other counts, too much to laugh at in M. de Pauw’s work; but on reading this passage about dogs they will laugh uproariously. Even if we conceded to M. de P. that for the most part dogs have degenerated, nothing would be concluded against that new continent that could not equally be concluded against the Old World; since, as Count de Buffon affirms, dogs transported from temperate climates into the cold ones of the old continent lose their voice, and transported into excessively hot countries lose, besides their voice, their hair also. This assertion of Count de Buffon rests on the experiment made with European dogs transported to Asia and to Africa, whose degeneration, the aforesaid philosopher says, is so rapid in Guinea and in other excessively hot countries that after three or four years they remain quite mute and hairless. M. de P. does not dare to say as much of dogs transported to America; but even what he does affirm is entirely false; for which are those countries of America where dogs have lost their voice? On the faith of what authors has he dared to publish such a fable? The greater part of the American countries to which European dogs were transported are subject to the Catholic King, and in none of them has such a misfortune befallen dogs. Neither among the European authors who have noted the particularities of America, nor among the very many Americans who are here at present, come from all the countries of Spanish America, have I found even one who confirms M. de P.’s anecdote. What we do know, however, both from several writers on America and from several persons acquainted with those countries, from whom we have informed ourselves, is that dogs never have rabies in Peru, in Quito, in Chile, and in other districts of that New World. If perhaps in the dominions of England or of France there is some country (which I do not believe) in which dogs have become mute, must it nevertheless be said that they have lost their voice in the greater part of the regions of the new continent? Did M. de P. perchance read that in some countries of America there were dogs that did not bark, and was that enough for him to publish

Il C. de Buffon per l’opposto afferma, (Ff) che i Cani europei sono ben riusciti tanto nei paesi caldi , quanto nei freddi del nuovo Mondo : nel che accorda senz' altro un gran vantaggio al clima dell’ America sopra quello dell' antico Continente .

that European dogs transported to America promptly lost their voice. He might similarly say that figs transported from Europe to America at once become thorny, because the Nochtli, or prickly pear (Tuna), which by some resemblance to the fig was called by the Spaniards fig of the Indies, has thorns, just as the Techichi was called by them little dog of Mexico because it resembles little dogs; but neither is this quadruped a true dog, nor is that fruit a true fig. It is far too easy to fall into such errors when ideas are not regulated, nor passions moderated. Count de Buffon on the contrary affirms (Ff) that European dogs have done well both in the hot countries and in the cold ones of the New World: in which he undoubtedly grants a great advantage to the climate of America over that of the old continent.

> Niente dicono in particolare i nostri Filosofi ‘su la degenerazione dei Gatti nell’ America; ma debbono intendersi compe nelle loro afferzioni universali . Contuttociò il C. de Bufon , il quale nel pafso sopra citato non ammette alcuna eccezione in ciò, che dice intorno alla degenerazione degli animali in America , ragionando poi in particolar dei Gatti, dopo aver vantati quelli di Spagna, come i migliori di tutti , afferma , che questi Gatti spagnuoli trasportati in America banno conservari i loro bei colori, e non banno punro degenerato (Gg).

Our philosophers say nothing in particular about the degeneration of cats in America; but they must be understood as included in their universal assertions. Nevertheless Count de Buffon, who in the passage cited above admits no exception to what he says about the degeneration of animals in America, speaking afterward of cats in particular, after having praised those of Spain as the best of all, affirms that these Spanish cats transported to America have kept their fine colors, and have not degenerated at all (Gg).

We do not doubt that impartial readers will recognize, from what we have sincerely set forth thus far, the errors and contradictions of our philosophers, caused by the ridiculous determination to defame the New World, the falsity of their observations, the groundlessness of their reasonings, and the rashness of their censure.

(e) The anteater is called by the Spaniards Oso ormiguero, that is, ant-bear, although it is perhaps more different from the bear than the dog is from the cat. Count de Buffon distinguishes three species of it in America: the first is called by him simply Fourmillier, or anteater; the 2nd Tamanoir, and the 3rd Tamandua. The Peruvians call them Hucumari, the people of Quito Huauniri and Cuckichi, the Tamanacs on the Orinoco Uaracà. In Brazil they call the large anteaters Tamanduà-guazu, and the small ones Irara and Guatimondè.

Thus Count de Buffon, who found in all America no more than seventy species of quadrupeds, in the course of his Natural History recognizes and distinguishes at least ninety-four. I said at least; for to the aforesaid there ought to be added those of the common hog, of the ermine, and others, which, although denied to America by Count de Buffon in one place of his History, have nevertheless been granted to it in other places.

§ II.

> VOLPE comune. ‘14.

Species Confused by Count de Buffon with Other, Different Ones.

> URSON, quadr. de’ paesi freddi simile al Castore, ma diverso. 25.

The Guanaco with the Llama, or Gliama. (t) The Vicugna with the Paco. The Citli with the Tapet, or Tapiitì. (u) The Huitztlacuatzin, or Mexican porcupine, with the Cuandù, or porcupine of Guiana. (x) The Tlacocelotl with the Ocelotl. (y)

> ZORRILLO, o sia Zorriglio , spezie di Puzzola. (/) 27.

The

> Sicchè il C. de Buffon, 1l quale non trovava in tutta l’ America più di settanta spezie di quadrupedì, ne! decorso della sua Storia Naturale ne riconosce e distingue almeno novantaquattro . Disfi almeno; xRa alle sopradette doveano aggiungersi quelle del Parco comune ell'Ermellino, ed altre, le quali benchè negate dal C. de Buffon all’ America in un luogo della sua Storia, le sono pure state accor» date in altri luoghi,

(r) Count de Buffon rightly distinguishes two species of sloths, the one furnished with a tail, and the other without it; for besides this they have other different characters. In Quito they call sloths Quillac, or Quiglac, and on the Orinoco Proto. The Spaniards call them Pereza, that is, Sloth, and Perico ligero, that is, Swift Dog, by antiphrasis.

> & I ) > Spezie confuse dal C. de Buffon con altre diverse.

(s) Zorrillo, that is, Little Fox, is the generic name which the Spaniards, and other countries, give to polecats. The Mexicans call them Epatl. In Chile Chinghe, and in other countries of South America Mapurito, Agnatuja, etc.

> Il Guanaco colla Llama, o Gliama (*) La Ficugna col Paco. Il Cîrli col) Tapet, o sia Tapiiti. (#*) L'Huitetlacuatzîn o Istrice messicano col Cuandù , o Iftrice della Gujana . (x} Il Tlacocelott coll' Oceloti. (y) , HH

(t) Besides other grounds of difference among the Gliama, the Guanaco, the Vicugna, and the Paco, they have never been seen to couple with one another, even when put together in one place. Now if this suffices to conclude the specific difference between the dog and the wolf, quadrupeds otherwise very similar both in their external features and in their internal organization, what shall we say of these four quadrupeds, which differ from one another more than the dog does from the wolf?

> (r)J1l C. de Buffon distingue a ragione due spezie di Pigri, l'una fornîta coda , e l'altra priva d'elsa; poichè oltre a questo hanno altri caratterî di. versi, Nel Quito appellano i Pigri Quillac, o sia Quiglac,e nell’ Orinoco Proto. Gli Spagnuoli gli chiamano Pereza, cioè Pigrizia, e Perico ligero, cioè Can veloce, per antifrafi. ri

These forty species added to the hundred and two mentioned above make a hundred and forty-two species of American quadrupeds. If to these, then, are added those of the horses, asses, bulls, sheep, goats, common hogs, Guinea hogs, dogs, cats, and domestic rats, brought there after the conquest, we shall have at present in America as many as a hundred and fifty-two species. Count de Buffon, who in all his Natural History never counts more than two hundred species of quadrupeds in the countries of the world discovered up to now, enumerates three hundred in his new work on the Epochs of Nature. So much did that number grow in a few years! But let them be three hundred: behold, America, although it makes up no more than a third of our globe, has nonetheless at least half the species of quadrupeds. I say again, at least; for I have left out all those of which I doubt whether they are different from those described by Count de Buffon. The principal aim I set myself in the compiling of this Catalogue was not to demonstrate the error of Count de Buffon in his enumeration of American quadrupeds, and the falsity of what he wrote about the imaginary scarcity of matter in the New World; but rather to serve European naturalists, by pointing out to them some quadrupeds hitherto unknown, and by smoothing somewhat the difficulties that a misunderstood nomenclature has caused. These gentlemen would wish that the names of those quadrupeds were accompanied by an exact description, and I would gladly oblige them as far as possible, were it not foreign to my purpose. In making this catalogue, besides the great study I have devoted to it, I have obtained written information from learned, accurate, and experienced persons of various countries of America, to whose singular kindness I confess myself exceedingly obliged.

## D I S S E RTAT I O N V

## ON THE PHYSICAL AND MORAL

## CONSTITUTION OF THE MEXICANS

> DISSERTAZIONE YV.

Four classes of men may be distinguished in Mexico and in other countries of America. 1. The Americans proper, commonly called Indians, that is, those who descend from the ancient settlers of that New World and have not mixed their blood with that of the peoples of the old continent. 2. The Europeans, Asiatics, and Africans established in those countries. 3. The children or descendants of these, who are called by the Spaniards Criollos, and whom we shall call Creoles, although that name is given chiefly to those children or descendants of Europeans whose blood has not been mixed with that of Americans, Asiatics, or Africans. 4. The mixed races, called castas by the Spaniards, that is, those who are born of, or descend from, a European man and an American woman, or a European and an African woman, or an African and an American woman, etc. All these classes of men are defamed and abused by M. de P. He supposes, or feigns, the climate of the New World to be so malign that it causes to degenerate not only the Creoles and the Americans proper born there, but even the Europeans who inhabit those countries, although they were born under a milder sky and a climate more favorable, as he believes, to all animals. If M. de P. had written his Recherches philosophiques in America, we might rightly suspect the degeneration of the human species under the American climate; but since we see that this work, and very many others of the same caliber, are produced in Europe, we are the more confirmed in the truth of that Italian proverb taken from the Greeks, All the world is one country. But leaving aside now the absurdities of that philosopher and of his partisans against the other classes of men, we shall argue only about those that he wrote against the Americans proper, since these people

> SU LA COSTITUZIONE FISICA E MORALE j DEI MESSICANI.

> Uattro classi d' Uomini posfono distinguersi nel Messico, e Qi altri pack dell' America. 1, gli Americani propri, volgarmente appellati Indiani, cioè coloro, che discendono dagli antichi popolatori di quel nuovo Mondo, e noa hanno mischiato il lor sangue con quello dei popoli dell’ antico Continente, 2. Gli Europei, gli Asiatici, e gli Africani - Rabilitifi in quei paesi. 3. I figli, o discendenti di costoro, i quali sono appellati dagli Spagnuoli Crio/los, e voi diremo Creogli, benchè tal nome fi dia principalments a quei figli, o discendenti d’ Europei , il cui sangue non fiasi milchiato con quello degli Americani, degli Afiatici, o degli Africani. 4. Le razze mischiate, appellate caftas dagli Spagnuoli, cioè quelli , che son nati, o discendono da Europeo, ed Americana , o da Europeo ed Africana, o da Africano ed Americana ec. T utte i classi d' uomini vengono infamate e strapazzate dal Sig. e P. Egli suppone, o finge tanto maligno il clima del nuovo Mondo , che fa degenerare non solo i Creogli, e gli Americapi propri quivi nati, ma eziandio gli Europei abiratori di quei paesi, contuttochè fieno nati sotto un cielo più mite, e fotto . un clima più favorevole, come egli crede , a tutti gli animali. Se il Sig. de P. avesse scritto le sue Ricerche Filosofiche in America, potremmo a ragion sospettare la degenerazione della spezie umana sorro il clima americano; ma siccome vediamo, che tal opera, e moltissime altre dello stesso calibro fi fanno in Europa, ci confermiamo vieppiù nella verità di quel roverbio italiano preso dai Greci, Turro il mondo è paese. Ma Jasciando ora gli spropositi di quel Filosofo, e dei suoi parti- giani contra le altre classi d' uomini, ragioneremo soltanto. di quelli, che egli scrifle contro gli Americani propri , gina co» 7 ore [p. 161] storo sono e i più ingiuriati, e i più indifesi , Se nello scrivere questa dissertazione fossimo indotti da qualche passione o interefle , avremmo piuttosto intrapresa la difesa dei Creogli, come quella, che oltre all'eflere aflai più facile, dovrebbe intereflarci più. Noi fiamo nati da genitori Spagnuoli , e nona abbiamo veruna affinità o consanguinità cogl' Iodiani nè possiamo sperar veruna ricompensa dalla loro miseria. Sicché niun altro motivo, che l'amor della verità , e lo zelo per l’ umanità , ci fa abbandonar la propria causa per difender l'altrui con manco perìcolo d' errare,

[p. 161] are both the most abused and the most defenseless. If in writing this dissertation we were moved by any passion or interest, we should rather have undertaken the defense of the Creoles, as that which, besides being far easier, ought to concern us more. We are born of Spanish parents, and have no affinity or consanguinity with the Indians, nor can we hope for any reward from their misery. So that no other motive than the love of truth and zeal for humanity makes us abandon our own cause to defend another’s with less danger of erring.

> 6. I. Su le qualieà corporali dei Messicani,

§ I.

> Il Sig. de P., il quale biasima la statura, la forma, e le pretese irregolarità degli animali americani , non è stato più indulgente verso gli Uomini. Se gli animali gli parvero una festa parte più piccoli di quelli d' Europa , gli uomini sono ancora, al dir di lui , più piccoli dei Calstigliani. Se negli animali notò la mancanza di coda, negli uomini pur ceniura la mancanza di pelo. Se negli animali trovò delle deformità notabili, neg li uomini vitupera il colore ec le fattezze. Se credette , che gli animali v' erano men forti di quelli dell’ antico Continente, afferma parimente , che gli uomini vi sono debolislimi, e che soggiacciono a mille malattie cagionate dalla corruzione di quell’ aria, e di quel terreno puzzolente.

On the Bodily Qualities of the Mexicans.

> Intorno alla statura degli Americani dice in generale, che benchè efla non fia uguale a quella dei Castigliani , v' è poco di. vario. Ma noi fiamo affatto sicuri , ed è notorio in tutta la nuova Spagna, che gl’ Indiani abitatori di quei ‘paesi , cioè di quelli, che sono dai gradi nove fino ai quaranta di latitudine settentrionale, fin dove son giunte le scoperte degli Spagnuoli, hanno d'altezza più di cinque piedi parigini, e che quelli, che non oltrepassano quella misura, sono afsai più rari } gl Iadiani, che fra gli Spagnuoli, Siamo inoltre certi, che molte

M. de P., who censures the stature, the form, and the alleged irregularities of the American animals, has not been more indulgent toward men. If the animals seemed to him a sixth part smaller than those of Europe, men are still, by his account, smaller than the Castilians. If in the animals he noted the lack of a tail, in men he likewise censures the lack of hair. If in the animals he found notable deformities, in men he reviles the color and the features. If he believed that the animals there were less strong than those of the old continent, he likewise affirms that the men there are extremely weak, and that they are subject to a thousand maladies caused by the corruption of that air and of that stinking soil.

> Storia Anrica del Messico Tomo IV. Xx di [p. 162] di quelle Nazioni, siccome gli Apaches, (*) gli Hiaquesi, i Più meli, ed i Cochim), sono almeno tanto alti , quanto i più alti Europei, e non sappiamo, che in rutta la valta estensione del Buovo Mondo fi trovi alcun popolo, fuorchè quello degli Eski. maux» che fia d'una statura ranto piccola, quanto quella - dei Lapponeli , dei Samoyjedi, e dei Tartari settentrionali nell’ an tico Continente. Onde da questa parte sono uguali gli abitatori d'ambidue i Continenti.

Concerning the stature of the Americans he says in general that, although it is not equal to that of the Castilians, there is little difference. But we are entirely sure, and it is notorious throughout New Spain, that the Indians who inhabit those countries, that is, those that lie from the ninth degree to the fortieth of north latitude, as far as the discoveries of the Spaniards have reached, are more than five Paris feet in height, and that those who do not exceed that measure are far rarer among the Indians than among the Spaniards. We are moreover certain that many [p. 162] of those nations, such as the Apaches, (*) the Yaquis, the Pimas, and the Cochimís, are at least as tall as the tallest Europeans, and we do not know that in all the vast extent of the New World there is any people, except the Eskimos, whose stature is as small as that of the Laplanders, the Samoyeds, and the northern Tartars in the old continent. Hence in this respect the inhabitants of both continents are equal.

As to the regularity and proportion of the limbs of the Mexicans, there is no need to say more than we have said in bk. I of our History. We are persuaded that among those who will read this work of ours in America, there will be none to contradict the description of the form and character of the Indians, unless he has his eyes in the back of his head or his wits turned. It is true that Don Antonio de Ulloa says (a), speaking of the Indians of Quito, that it has been observed “that among them the imperfect abound, either because they have bodies irregular and monstrous by reason of their smallness, or because they become witless, mute, or blind, or because some limb is lacking to them;” but having made inquiries into this singularity of the people of Quito, I have learned, from information given me by trustworthy persons well acquainted with those countries, that such defects are caused neither by bad humors nor by the climate, but by the misguided and cruel humanity of their parents, who, in order to spare their children the burdens and labors to which the healthy Indians are subjected by the Spaniards, deliberately make them useless or imperfect: which does not happen in other countries of America, nor even in those places of the same kingdom of Quito where the Indians are free from those labors. M. de P., and after him Dr. Robertson, say that among the savages of America no deformed are to be found; because they put to death, as the Lacedaemonians once did, those infants

E' dunque affai diversa’ da quella, che s' immaginano i suddetti Autori , la ca» gione di quel fenomeno offeryato da tanti Scrittori negli Americani.

(a) A Voyage to South America, etc. [p. 163] who are born hunchbacked, blind, or lacking some limb; but that in those countries in which they have been brought into society, and where the vigilance of those who govern them does not permit such infanticides, the number of irregular individuals is greater than in any country of Europe. This would be a fine way out of the difficulty, if it were true; but if by chance there has been in America some tribe of savages that imitated the barbarous example (**) of the much-renowned Lacedaemonians, it is certain that those authors have no right to impute such inhumanity to the rest of the Americans; since it has not been in use, at least among the greater part of those nations, as can be demonstrated by the testimony of the writers best instructed in their customs. Moreover, in all the countries of Mexico, or New Spain, which make up at least a fourth part of the new continent, the Indians live united in society, and gathered in cities, towns, and villages, under the care of Spanish or Creole magistrates and parish priests: no examples of cruelty toward tender children are ever seen or heard of there, and notwithstanding this, the deformed are so rare there that all those Spaniards and Creoles who came from Mexico to Italy in 1768 were then, and are still today, amazed to observe in the cities of this most civilized peninsula so great a number of blind, hunchbacked, lame, crippled, etc. The cause, then, of that phenomenon observed by so many writers among the Americans is quite different from what the aforesaid authors imagine.

As for the color of the American peoples, no argument can be drawn from it against the New World; because that color is less distant from the white of the Europeans than from the black of the Africans and of a great part of the Asiatics. This is one of those many passages of the Recherches philosophiques at which the Mexicans and other American nations will not be able to restrain their laughter, on seeing a European philosopher so intent on stripping them of what they have received from nature. He no doubt read that ignominious description which Señor Ulloa gives of some peoples of South America, (c) and from this particular premise drew, according to his logic, that universal conclusion.
