Consta per la deposizione di tutti gli Storici del Messico, che l’esercito di Cortès , composto di sei mila, e più di quattrocento tra Spagnuoli , Tilascalleli , e Cempoallesi , s' alloggiò tutta nel palazzo, che era [tato del Re Axacajatl, e ve ne avanzò ancora per l'abirazione del Re Motezuma, e de’ suoi familiari , oltre a' magazzini , ne' quali fi guardava il tesoro del Re Axajacarl, Consta pe la deposizione de' medesimi Storici della magnificenza , e llilima disposizione del palazzo degli uccelli, e Cortès aggiunge , che negli appartamenti, che v' erano poteano albergarfi agiaramente due gran Principi con tutta la loro Corte, e descrive minutamente i suoi porrici, le loggie, e i giardini , Lo stesso Cortés dice a Carlo V., che nel palazzo del Re Nezahualpilli in Tezcuco alloggiò con seicento ‘Spagnuoli, e quaranta cavalli , e che era tanto ‘grande, che ve ne potrebbono ancora stare agiatamente altri seicento. Similmente parla del lazzo del. Signor d’Iztapalapan, e d'altre Città, lodandone struttura, la bellezza, e la magnificenza. Tali erano le capanne de’ Re, e de' Signori Melslicani .

[p. 229] themselves before their eyes the Mexican palaces. The Anonymous Conqueror, in his curious and truthful Relation, speaking of the buildings of Mexico, says thus: “There were fine houses of lords, so large, and with so many apartments and gardens, upper and lower, that they filled us with amazement and admiration. Out of curiosity I entered four times a palace of Moctezuma, and after wandering through it until I was tired, I never saw it all. They were accustomed to have around a great courtyard very large chambers and halls; but above all there was one so large that more than three thousand persons could stand inside it without discomfort: it was such that in the gallery above it there was formed a little square in which thirty men on horseback could have played at canes.” Similar expressions are read in the History of Bernal Díaz. It is established by the deposition of all the historians of Mexico that the army of Cortés, composed of six thousand, and more than four hundred, among Spaniards, Tlaxcalans, and Cempoalans, was lodged entirely in the palace which had been King Axayacatl’s, and there was room left over for the lodging of King Moctezuma and his household, besides the storehouses in which the treasure of King Axayacatl was kept. The magnificence and very beautiful arrangement of the palace of the birds is likewise established by the deposition of the same historians, and Cortés adds that in the apartments there two great princes could lodge comfortably with all their court, and he describes minutely its porticoes, its loggias, and its gardens. The same Cortés tells Charles V that in the palace of King Nezahualpilli in Texcoco he lodged with six hundred Spaniards and forty horses, and that it was so large that another six hundred could still have been lodged there comfortably. Similarly he speaks of the palace of the lord of Iztapalapa, and of those of other cities, praising their structure, their beauty, and their magnificence. Such were the huts of the Mexican kings and lords.

M. de P.’s statement that Cortés had that palace built in haste because he could find no suitable dwelling in that whole capital is an error, or rather, to speak with greater propriety, a great lie. It is

> IL dire; che fa il Sig. de P., che Cortès fecevi ‘costruire in fretta quel palazzo, perchè non trovava abitazione proporzionata in tutta. quella Capitale, è un ertore, © per dir meglio, e: parlar con ‘maggior proprietà, è una gran: bugla. E' [p. 230] vero ,. che Cortès durante l'assedio di M:ssizo, bruciò, e ro. vinò la maggior parte di quella gran Città: come egli medesimo ne fa fede, e a tal fine dimandò, ed ottenne da’ suoi Alleati alcune migliaja di Contadini, che non aveano altro impiego, che quello d’andar rovinando gli edifizi secondoché gli Spagnuoli vi fi avanzavano , acciocché non restasse alle loro spalle veruna casa, da cui potessero danneggiarli i Messicani . Non farebbe dun. que da maravigliare , se Cortés non avelle trovato alcuna abirazione proporzionata in una Città, che egli medesimo avea distrutta; ma non fu la rovina tanto generale, che non restas. se un gran numero di buone calè nel quartiere di Tlacelolco, pelle quali avrebbono potuto comodamente alloggiarfi rutti gli Spagnuoli con buon numera dei loro Alleati . Dappoichè piacque a Nostro Signore , dice Cortès nella sua ultima lettera a Car» lo V., che questa gran Cirià di Temixritan fosse conquistare , non mi parve bene di risedere in essa per cagione di molti inconvenienti » sicchè me ne andai con tutta la mia Genee a flare în Cuyoacan. Se fofle vero ciò, che dice il Sig. de PaWw , ba. stava dire, che non restò in Messico, perchè non ‘v' erano ca» se dove stare. Il palazzo di Corrès fi fabbricò nel medesima sito dove era già quello di Morezuma . Se Cortès non avesle rovinato questo palazzo , avrebbe potuto abitar comodamente in eflo, come vi abitava quel Monarca con tutta la sua Corte. E' poi falso, che sussista presentemente il palazzo fabbrica. to da Cortès ; poichè questo fu bruciato nel 1692, in una fedizione popolare . Ma soprattutto è falfislimo, che le mura degli edifizi messicani non foflero altro, che sassi grandi posti gli uni sopra gli altri fenza veruna unione, siccome fi convince per la testimonianza di tutti gli Storici, e per gli avanzi degli edifizi antichi, di cui a suo luogo ragioneremo . Sicché non evvi in tutto il passo più citato del Sig. de P. neppur una proposizione , che non sia un errore ,

[p. 230] true that Cortés, during the siege of Mexico, burned and ruined the greater part of that great city: as he himself bears witness, and to that end he asked for and obtained from his allies some thousands of peasants, who had no other employment than that of going about ruining the buildings as the Spaniards advanced, so that no house should be left at their backs from which the Mexicans could harm them. It would not be surprising, therefore, if Cortés had found no suitable dwelling in a city which he himself had destroyed; but the ruin was not so general that there did not remain a great number of good houses in the quarter of Tlatelolco, in which all the Spaniards, with a good number of their allies, could have lodged comfortably. Since it pleased Our Lord, says Cortés in his last letter to Charles V, that this great city of Tenochtitlan should be conquered, it did not seem good to me to reside in it, on account of many inconveniences; so that I went with all my people to stay in Coyoacán. If what M. de Pauw says were true, it would have sufficed to say that he did not remain in Mexico because there were no houses in which to stay. The palace of Cortés was built on the same site where that of Moctezuma had formerly stood. If Cortés had not ruined this palace, he could have lived in it comfortably, as that monarch lived in it with all his court. It is, moreover, false that the palace built by Cortés exists at present; for it was burned in 1692 in a popular sedition. But above all it is most false that the walls of the Mexican buildings were nothing but large stones laid one upon another without any binding, as is proved by the testimony of all the historians, and by the remains of the ancient buildings, of which we shall speak in their place. So that there is not, in the whole passage of M. de P. already cited, a single proposition that is not an error.

[p. 231] ever been so great a number of public buildings in any city from Rome to Peking: wherefore Gómara, less rash or wiser than Solís, says that, counting seven little chapels, there were not found more than eight places destined for placing the idols of Mexico.” (t) That it may be seen how great is M. de P.’s infidelity in citing authors, I wish to give here the passage of Gómara which he alleges: “There were,” says this author in ch. 80 of his Crónica de la Nueva España, “many temples in the city of Mexico, scattered through the parishes or districts, with their towers, in which were the chapels and the altars for placing the idols… Almost all had the same form: so that what we shall say of the principal temple will suffice to make all the others known,” and after making a minute description of that great temple, in which he extols its height, its breadth, and its beauty, he adds: “Besides these towers, which were formed with their chapels above the pyramid, there were forty and more other towers, small and large, on other lesser Teocalli, (u) which were within the precinct of that principal temple, all of which were of the same form as that… Other Teocalli or Cues there were in other places of the city… All these temples had their own houses, their own priests, and their own gods, with everything necessary for their worship and service.” So that the same Gómara who, according to M. de P., numbers in Mexico no more than eight places destined for placing the idols, including seven little chapels, clearly reckons more than forty temples within the precinct of the principal temple, besides many others scattered through the parishes or districts. Who can ever trust M. de P. after so manifest a falsification?

(u) Teocalli, that is, House of God, was the name which the Mexicans gave to their temples. Among the Spaniards some called them temples, others Adoratories, others Mosques, as men accustomed to the language of the Saracens, and others Cues, a word taken from the Haitian language. Besides these names, they also gave to the small temples those of Sacrificaderos and Humilladeros, that is, places of sacrifice and of adoration.

[p. 232]

> 233 DISSERTAZIONE VI.

It is true that Solís showed himself rather imprudent in putting down as certain that number of temples which the first historians expressed only by conjecture; but M. de P. also shows himself rather injudicious in including among the public buildings even those little chapels which the Spaniards called temples. Of these there were innumerable: all those who saw that country before the Conquest testify unanimously that both in inhabited places and on the roads and on the mountains such buildings were to be seen everywhere; which, though small and quite different from our churches, were nevertheless called temples, because they were consecrated to the worship of the idols. Thus from the letters of Cortés, as from the History of Bernal Díaz, we learn that the conquerors scarcely took a step in their expeditions without coming upon some temple or chapel. Cortés says that he himself counted more than four hundred temples in the city of Cholula alone. But there was a great difference in size between the one and the other temples. Some were nothing but little mounds of no great height, on which there was a little chapel for the titular idol. Others again were of a stupendous size and breadth. Cortés, where he speaks of the greatest temple of Mexico, protests to Charles V that it is not easy to describe its parts, its size, and the things contained in it, that it was so large that within the precinct of the strong wall which surrounded it a town of five hundred houses could be contained. Not otherwise do Bernal Díaz, the Anonymous Conqueror, Sahagún, and Tovar, who saw them, speak of this and of other temples of Mexico, of Texcoco, of Cholula, and of other cities, and the Mexican and Spanish historians who wrote afterwards and informed themselves well, such as Acosta, Gómara, Herrera, Torquemada, Sigüenza, Vetancurt, etc., etc. Hernández described one by one the seventy-eight parts of which the greatest temple was composed; Cortés adds that among the lofty towers of the temples that adorned that great capital there were forty so elevated that the smallest of them was not inferior in height to the famous Giralda

> E' vero, che Sol\ìs fi mostrò poco avveduro nel mettef come certo quel numero di- tempj, che i primi Storici espres. fero soltanto per congettura; ma il Sig. de P. fì dà ancora’ a divedere poco accorto nel comprendere tra gli edifizi pubblici anche quelle cappelline, che gli Spagnuoli appellarono Tempj. Di questi ve n' erano innumerabili : Tutti coloro, che videro quel paese prima della Conquista , testificano concordemente, che tanto nei luoghi abitati, quanto nelle strade, e nelle montagne fi vedevano dappertutto sì farti edifizi*, i“ quali, benchè piccoli, ed affatto diversi dalle nostre Chiese ,furono pure chia mati tempj , perchè erano consacrati al culto degl'Idoli . Sì è veduto talora nella N. Spagna fabbricare in una sola notte un villaggio intero ( benchè composto di capanne di legno coperte di fieno ) e condurvi i nuovi co» loni le loro famiglie, i loro animali, e tutta‘ la lor roba . (x)

All this cloud of witnesses testifies against M. de P. Nevertheless he will not believe that great multitude of temples in Mexico; because Moctezuma I, he says, was the one who gave that village the form of a city: from the reign of this monarch to the arrival of the Spaniards no more than forty-two years had elapsed: which space of time certainly does not suffice to build two thousand temples. Here are three assertions, which are so many errors. 1. It is false that Moctezuma I gave Mexico the form of a city; for we know from history that that court had the form of a city from the times of the first king, Acamapichtli. 2. It is also false that from the reign of Moctezuma I to the arrival of the Spaniards no more than forty-two years had elapsed. Moctezuma began to reign, as we have shown in the second Dissertation, in the year 1436, and ceased to live in 1464, and the Spaniards did not arrive at Mexico before 1519: from the beginning of that reign, therefore, to the arrival of the Spaniards eighty-three years elapsed, and from the death of that king fifty-five. 3. M. de Pauw shows himself wholly ignorant of the construction of the Mexican temples, and does not know how great was the multitude of workmen who concurred in the building of the public edifices, and how great their speed in building them. There has sometimes been seen in New Spain an entire village (though composed of wooden huts covered with hay) built in a single night, and the new colonists conducting into it their families, their animals, and all their goods. (x) See what Torquemada relates in bk. 3, ch. 33 of the Monarquía indiana. [p. 234] indubitable from the testimony of Cortés and of all those who saw the ancient cities of that empire, (y) that the Mexicans and all the other nations living in society used walls, bulwarks, palisades, ditches, and entrenchments. But even if none of so many eyewitnesses bore witness to it, the ancient fortifications that still stand today at Cuauhtochco, otherwise Guatusco, and near Molcaxac, of which we have spoken elsewhere, would suffice to demonstrate the error of M. de Pauw. It is true that such fortifications were not comparable with those of Europe; for neither had their military architecture been so far perfected, nor had they any need to put themselves under cover from artillery, of which they had no knowledge; but they gave sufficient proof of their industry in devising so many kinds of defenses with which to protect themselves from their ordinary enemies. Whoever, moreover, reads the unanimous testimony of the conquerors will not doubt the great toil they had in storming the ditches and entrenchments of the Mexicans at the siege of the capital, although they had so excessive a number of allied troops, and the advantages of firearms and of the brigantines. The terrible defeat which the Spaniards suffered when they wished to withdraw from Mexico will never allow one to doubt the fortifications of that capital. It was not surrounded by walls, because its situation rendered it secure enough by means of those ditches which were on the three causeways by which enemies could assail it; but other cities, which were not placed in so advantageous a situation, had walls and other defenses for their protection. Cortés himself gives an exact description of the walls of Cuauhquechollan.

Furono molti gli Europei, che videro sì fatti Javori , e fi maravigliarono dell’ abilivà degli artefici ame» ricani. 1 loro lavori di getto furono ammirati dagli Orefici di Europa , secondochè affermano parecch} Autori Europei allor viventi , e tra gli altri lo Storico Gomara, il qual ebbe quelle opere nelle sue mani, e sentì il parere degli Orefici Sivi» gliani, che non fi credevano capaci d imitarle .(z) E dove trovar mai , chi fia capace di far que' lavori maraviglioli da noi accennati nel lib. VII.& 51. della nostra Storia, e da moltifli» mi Scrittori concordemente testificati , siccome quello per esem+ pio di far di petto un pesce, che abbia le squame alternatamente l'una d'oro, e l'altra d’argento? Corràs dice nella fe. conda sua lettera a Carla V. che le immagini d’oro, e di piuma erano così ben lavorate da’ Messicani , che niun Artefice d' Europa potrebbe farle migliori : che quanto alle gioje non fi potea comprendere, con quali strumenti fatte fossero opere tan» to perfette: e che i lavori di penne erano vali, che nè in cera, nè in sera si potevano imitare. Nella sua terza lettera al , mede» fimo Carlo V. laddove parla del bottino di Messico , gli dice, che tra le spoglie de' Messicani vi trovò certe rotelle d’ oro, e di penne , ed altri lavori della stetfla materia così maraviglioli , che non eflendogli possibile di darne una giusta idea per iscritto, gli manda a Sua Muestà, acciocchè co' suoi propri occhi possa rendersi ficura della ‘loro eccellenza e perfezione . Io son certo , che Cortès non avrebbe parlato così al suo Re di que'lavori , che gli mandava , affinchè co' suoi occhj ‘gli vedessz: , {e non fosffero _ rali, quali egli gli rappresentava . Quali negli steli termini, che Cortés ne parlano tutti quegli Autori, che videro sì fatte opere come Bernal Diaz, il Conquistatore Anonimo , Gomara , Hernan-

The same authors who bear witness to the architecture of the Mexicans testify also to the excellence of their goldsmiths, their weavers, their gem-engravers, and their workers in feather. Many Europeans saw such works, and marveled at the skill of the American artisans. Their cast-metal work was admired by the goldsmiths of Europe, as several European authors then living affirm, and among others the historian Gómara, who had those works in his hands and heard the opinion of the goldsmiths of Seville, who did not think themselves capable of imitating them. (z) And where shall one ever find a man capable of making those marvelous works that we mentioned in bk. VII, § 51 of our History, and that are attested in agreement by very many writers, such as that, for example, of casting a fish whose scales are alternately one of gold and the other of silver? Cortés says in his second letter to Charles V that the images of gold and of feather were so well made by the Mexicans that no artisan of Europe could make them better; that as for the jewels, it could not be understood with what instruments works so perfect had been made; and that the works of feathers were such that they could not be imitated either in wax or in silk. In his third letter to the same Charles V, where he speaks of the booty of Mexico, he tells him that among the spoils of the Mexicans he found certain shields of gold and of feathers, and other works of the same material so marvelous that, since it was not possible for him to give a just idea of them in writing, he sends them to His Majesty, so that with his own eyes he may assure himself of their excellence and perfection. I am certain that Cortés would not have spoken thus to his king of those works which he sent him, so that with his own eyes he might see them, if they had not been such as he represented them. Almost in the same terms as Cortés all those authors speak of them who saw such works, such as Bernal Díaz, the Anonymous Conqueror, Gómara, Hernández,

Dr. Robertson (A) indeed acknowledges the unanimous testimony of the ancient Spanish historians, and believes that they had no intention of deceiving us; but he affirms that all were induced to exaggerate by the illusion of their own minds, caused by the heat of their imagination. Here is a fine solution, of which anyone might avail himself to deny credence to all human histories. All, then, were deceived, not excepting even the most illustrious Acosta, nor the learned Hernández, nor the goldsmiths of Seville, nor King Philip II, nor the Supreme Pontiff Sixtus V, all of them admirers and praisers of those Mexican works? (B) All had a heated imagination, even those who wrote a few years after the discovery of Mexico? Yes, all; only the Scot Robertson and the Prussian de Pauw have, after two centuries and a half, that temperament in the fancy which is required for forming a just idea of things, perhaps because the cold of their countries will have slackened the heat of their imagination. “It is not from those descriptions, but from considering such specimens of their arts as are still preserved, that we must decide,” adds Robertson, “concerning their degree of merit (of the Mexican works)… Many of their ornaments in gold and silver, as well as various utensils employed in common life, are deposited in the magnificent cabinet of natural and artificial productions, lately opened by the king of Spain; and I am informed by persons on whose judgment and taste I can rely, that these boasted efforts of their art are uncouth representations of common objects, or very coarse images of the human and some animal forms, destitute of grace and propriety.” And in the note he says thus: “In the armoury of the royal palace of Madrid, are shewn suits of armour, which are called Montezuma’s. They are composed of thin lacquered copper-plates. In the opinion of very intelligent judges

(B) Let one reread on this what we have written in bk. VII, § 51 of our History. [p. 237] they are evidently eastern. The forms of the silver ornaments upon them, representing dragons, &c. may be considered as a confirmation of this. They are infinitely superior in point of workmanship to any effort of American art… The only unquestionable specimen of Mexican art that I know of in Great Britain, is a cup of very fine gold, which is said to have belonged to Montezuma… A man’s head is represented on this cup. On one side the full face, on the other the profile, on the third the back parts of the head… The features are rude, but very tolerable, and certainly too rude for Spanish workmanship. This cup was purchased by Edward earl of Orford, while he lay in the harbour of Cadiz.” Thus far Robertson, to whose arguments we reply: 1. That there is no reason to believe that those rude works are truly Mexican. 2. That we do not even know whether those persons on whose judgment Robertson thought he could rely were such as to deserve our faith; for we have observed that Robertson often relies on the testimony of Gage, of Corral, of Ibagnez, and of other such authors, wholly unworthy of being believed. It might also be that those persons who judged of such works had a heated imagination; since it is far easier, according to the condition of our fallen nature, to heat the imagination against a nation than in its favor. 3. That it is far more probable that those copper arms, believed by intelligent judges to be evidently eastern, are truly Mexican; for we are certain from the testimony of all the writers on Mexico that those nations used such plates of copper in war, and that with them they sought to cover the breast, the arms, and the thighs to defend themselves from arrows, whereas we do not know that they were ever in use among the inhabitants of the Philippine Islands, (C) or among any other people,

(C) Dr. Robertson says that the Spaniards probably had those arms from the Philippine Islands. [p. 238] that traded with them. The dragons represented on those arms, instead of confirming, as Robertson believes, the opinion of those who think them eastern, rather confirm our own; for there never was any nation in the world among whom the images of terrible animals were so much in use on their arms as among the Mexicans. Nor should it cause wonder that these people had an idea of dragons, since they had also that of griffins, as Gómara bears witness. (D) 5. That although the images formed in the works of gold and silver are clumsy, these might nevertheless be excellent, marvelous, and inimitable; because in those works two wholly distinct and unconnected arts must be considered, that of design and that of casting: so that the fish of which we spoke above might be badly formed as to its figure, and yet that alternation of scales of gold and silver, made by casting, be marvelous and astonishing. 6. Finally, the judgment of some wholly unknown persons upon those few doubtful works which are in the royal cabinet of Madrid cannot prevail against the unanimous testimony of all the ancient writers, who saw innumerable works that were certainly Mexican.

From all that we have set forth so far, the great wrong that M. de Pauw has done the Mexicans is made manifest, in believing them inferior in industry and sagacity to the crudest peoples of the old continent. Father Acosta, where he discusses the industry of the Peruvians, says thus: “If these men are beasts, let him judge who will; for I am sure that in that to which they apply themselves, they surpass us by far.” (E) Is not this candid confession of a European of so much critical sense, so much experience, and so much impartiality worth far more than all the invectives of a Prussian philosopher, than all the reasonings of a Scottish historian, both of them either ill informed about the things

(E) Natural and Moral History, bk. 6, ch. 8. [p. 239] of America, or prejudiced against the Americans? But even if we conceded to M. de Pauw that the industry of the Americans in the arts is inferior to that of the other peoples of the world, nothing should be concluded from it against the souls of the Americans, or against the climate of America; since it is certain and indubitable that the inventions and the progress of the arts are for the most part due rather to chance, to necessity, and to greed than to talent. The men most industrious in the arts are not always the most talented, but often the neediest, or those most drawn to gold. “The sterility of the land,” says Montesquieu well, (F) “makes men industrious… it is necessary that they procure for themselves what the earth does not yield them. The fertility of a country brings with it, together with the ease of sustaining oneself, idleness.” “Necessity,” says Robertson, “is the great prompter and guide of mankind in their inventions.” The Chinese would certainly not be so industrious if the excessive population of their country did not make their own support difficult for them; nor would so much progress have been made in the arts in Europe, if the enticement of rewards, or the hope in the artisans of bettering their fortune, had been lacking. Nevertheless the Mexicans can boast many inventions of their own capable of immortalizing their name, such as, besides those of their famous cast-metal works and of the mosaics of feathers and shells, that of paper; (G) that of dyeing in indelible colors, of spinning and weaving the finest fur of rabbits and hares; that of making razors of Itztli; (H) that of raising cochineal so industriously for use in dyes; that of enamel in the floors of their houses, and a thousand others no less estimable, that can

(G) See what we say in bk. 7 of the History about the different kinds of Mexican paper, namely of cotton, of maguey, of mountain palm, and of silk. The invention of paper is without doubt older in America than in Egypt, whence it was communicated to Europe. It is true that the paper of the Mexicans was not comparable in fineness with that of the Europeans; but it should be noted that they did not make it for writing, but for painting.

Che invenzione per esempio più fingolare e maravigliosa, che quella d' addimesticare i pesci marini, e servirsene per dar la caccia ad altri pesci grandi, come faceano gli abitatori delle Isole Antille ? Questa sola arte, di cui fanno menzione Oviedo, (1) Gomara, ed alrri Autori non basterebbe a smentire l’ingiuriole invettive del Sig, de PawW contra l'in. dultria degli Americani?

(H) See what we say in bk. 7, § 56 of the History about that art. [p. 240] can be seen in our History and in the works of the other historians of Mexico, just as the arts of the Peruvians can in the works of Acosta and of the Inca Garcilaso, and in the Lettere americane of the learned Count Carli. But what wonder is it that such inventions were found among those civilized nations, when even among other American peoples not yet polished some very singular arts were found? What invention, for example, is more singular and marvelous than that of taming sea fish and using them to hunt other, larger fish, as the inhabitants of the Antilles used to do? Would not this art alone, of which Oviedo, (I) Gómara, and other authors make mention, suffice to give the lie to the insulting invectives of M. de Pauw against the industry of the Americans?

“The languages of America,” says M. de P., “are so restricted, and so scant of words, that it is not possible to express in them any metaphysical concept. There is not one of these languages in which one can count beyond three. (L) It is not possible to translate a book, not only into the languages of the Algonquins and of the Guaranís or Paraguayans, but not even into those of Mexico or Peru, because they do not have a sufficient abundance of proper terms to enunciate general notions.” Whoever reads these magisterial decisions of M. de P. will doubtless be persuaded that he decides so

> (LI) Ne!la Resa sezione 1. della parte 5. delle Ricerche Filosofiche, nella qua» le afferma , che non v' è niuna lingua Americana, nella quale fi possa nume» zare oltre a tre, dice cite i Messicani contavano fino a dieci, [p. 241] DISSERTAZIONE VI. 24î sì dopo d'aver viaggiato per tutta Ì' America , d'aver trattato con tutte quelle Nazioni, e d'avere esaminate tutte le loro lingue; ma non è così. Il Sig, de P. seoza uscir dal suo ga. binetto in Berlino, sa meglio le cose d' America, che gli stesi Americani, e nella cognizione di quelle lingue fupera coloro , che le parlano. Io imparai la lingua meslicana, e la sentii para lar dai Messicani molti anni ; eppur non sapeva, che essa folle così scarsa di voci numerali , e di termini significanti le idee universali, finattantochè aon venne a illuminarmi il Sig. de P. Io sapeva, che i Messicani imposero il nome Cenzzonrzli, ( 400.) o piuttosto quello di Cenrzonzlarale ( colui, che ha voci quattrocento ) a quell' uccello tanto rinomato per la singolar dolcezza, € per l'incomparabile varierà del suo canto. lo sapeva altresì, come i Messicani contavano anticamente per «iquipilli e le mandorle di caccao nel loro commercio, e le loro truppe nella guerra : che «iquipilli valeva otto mila: ficchè per dire, che un esercito fi componeva, per esempio di quaranta mila uomini, dicevano, che aveva cinque siquipilli. Io sapeva finalmente , che i Messicani aveano voci numerali per esprimere quante migliaja, e milioni volevano ; ma il Sig. de P. sa rutto il contrario, e non vi è dubbio, che il saprà meglio di me ; perchè io ebbi la disgrazia di nascere sotto un clima meno favorevole alle operazioni intelletcuali . Nulladimeno io voglio per compiacere alla curiosità dei miei Lettori metter quì forro la ferie dei nomi numerali , di cui fi son serviti sempre mai i Messicani , (*) Nella quale fi vede, che coloro, che al dir del Sig. de P. non aveano voci per numerare oltre a tre, ne aveano pure a dispetto di lui per contare almeno fino a quarantotto milioni, Similmente potremmo convincere l' errore de’ Signori de la Condamine, e de P. in molte altre lingue Storia Antica del Messico Tom. IP. H h d' Auni

(L) In the same section 1 of part 5 of the Recherches philosophiques, in which he affirms that there is no American language in which one can count beyond three, he says that the Mexicans counted up to ten. [p. 241] after having traveled through all America, having dealt with all those nations, and having examined all their languages; but it is not so. M. de P., without leaving his study in Berlin, knows the things of America better than the Americans themselves, and in his knowledge of those languages surpasses those who speak them. I learned the Mexican language, and heard it spoken by Mexicans for many years; and yet I did not know that it was so scant of numeral words, and of terms signifying universal ideas, until M. de P. came to enlighten me. I knew that the Mexicans gave the name Centzontli (400), or rather that of Centzontlatole (he who has four hundred voices), to that bird so renowned for the singular sweetness and the incomparable variety of its song. I knew also how the Mexicans anciently counted by xiquipilli both the almonds of cacao in their commerce and their troops in war: that a xiquipilli was worth eight thousand; so that to say that an army was composed, for example, of forty thousand men, they said that it had five xiquipilli. I knew, finally, that the Mexicans had numeral words with which to express as many thousands and millions as they wished; but M. de P. knows quite the contrary, and there is no doubt that he will know it better than I, for I had the misfortune to be born under a climate less favorable to intellectual operations. Nevertheless, to gratify the curiosity of my readers, I wish to set down here below the series of numeral names which the Mexicans have always used. (*) From it one sees that those who, according to M. de P., had no words for counting beyond three, had them nevertheless, in spite of him, for counting at least up to forty-eight million. In the same way we could convict Messrs. de la Condamine and de P. of error in many other languages

Quantunzue questa lingua fia stimata una delle più rozze del Melli * co, ha tuttavia delle voci per esprimere quante migliaja fi vogliono» [p. 243] sono tanto scarse le lingue Americane, che non fono capaci d esprimere un concetto metafisico; la qual lezione egli imparò dal Sig. de la Condamine., ,, Tempo, dice questo Filosofo. » ragionando delle lingue degli Americani, Durazione , Spazio, Essere , Sostanza , Materia , Corpo , tutre queste parole, e mol» » te altre non hanno vocl equivalenti nelle lor lingue: e non » solo i nomi degli esseri mecafisici, ma nè pure quelli degli » esseri morali, possono da loro esprimersi, se non impropria» 9 mente, e per lunghe circonlocuzioni. ,, Ma il Sig, de la/Ccondamine sapeva tanto delle lingue Americane , quanto il Sig. de P., ed egli prese fenz'altro informazione da qualche uomo ignorante , siccome accade speslo a” Viaggiatori». Noi siamo affarto sicuri, che molte lingue Americane non hanno quella scarsezza di voci, che pensa il Sig. da la Condamine; ma tralasciando ora ciò, che riguarda le altre, discorriamo soltanto della messicana , la qual è il principal soggetto della nostra contesa . E' ben vero, che i Messicani non aveano voci per esprimere i concetti della materia , della sostanza, dell’ accidente e simili; ma egli è parimente certo, che niuna lingua, o dell Alfa, o dell’ Europa avea tali voci , prima che i Greci comin» ciafsero ad assottigliare , ad astraere le loro idee, ed a crear nuo» vi termini per esprimerlo, Il gran Cicerone , il qual sapeva tanto bene la lingua latina , e fiorì a que’ tempi , in cui efla era nella sua maggior perfezione , contutrochè la stimaffe più iosa della greca , egli nondimeno stenta spesso nelle sue opere filosofiche a trovar voci corrispondenti alle idee metafisiche de’ Greci. Quante volte non su egli costretto a crear nuove vo» ci equivalenti in qualche modo alle greche, perchè non le trovava tra le voci usate da' Romani ? Ma ancor oggid\, dappoichè quella lingua fu arricchita di molte parole inventate e da Cicerone, e da altrì dotti Romani, che ad esempio di Juî si diedero allo studio della Filosofia, le mancano pur termini da esprimere molri concetti metafisici , se non fi ricorso al barbaro linguaggio delle scuole. Niuna di quelle lingue , che parlano i Filosofi dell’ Europa, avea parole fignificative della materia, della sustanza , dell'accidente, e d'alui fimili concerti; Huha € pe [p. 244] e però fu necessario, che i Filosofanti adottaffero le voci” latîne, oppur le greche . ] Messicani antichi , perchè non s' impiegavano nello itudio della Metafisica, sono scusabili di non avere inventate voci da esprimere quelle idee; non è però tanto scarsa la loro liogua di termini fignificarivi di cose metafisiche , -e morali , quanto afferma il Sig. de la Condamine, che son quelle dell’ America Meridionale: -anzi affermo, che non è facile di trovare una lingua più atta della Messicana a trattar le matezie metafisiche ; poichè è difficile di trovarne un' altra, chetanto abbondi , quanto quella di nomi astratti ; mentre pochi sono in effa: i verbi, da' quali non fi formino verbali corrispoadenti a quelli in jo de' Latini, € pochi sono ancora i nomi sustantivi, o addiettivi , da' quali nooa f formino nomi astratti elsprimenti l'essere, o come fi dice nelle scuole, la quidditd delle cose: i cui equivalenti non posso trovar nell' Ebraico, nel Greco, nel Latino, nel Francese, nell" Iraliano, nell’ Ioglese nello: Spagnuolo, o Portoghese: delle quali lingue mi pare d'a— ver quella cogaizione , che fì richiede per farne il paragone - Or per dare qualche saggio di questa lingua, e per compiacere. alla curiosità de' Lettori, metterò quì fotto i lor occhj ‘alcune voci significanti concetti mertafilici , e morali, e intese anche: dagl' Indiani più rozzi. (M) Mari in the Araucanian language means ten, Pataca a hundred, Huaranca a thousand, Patachuaranca a hundred thousand, Maripatacahuaranca a million. After finishing this Dissertation I acquired also the series of the numeral names in the Otomi language. Although this language is esteemed one of the rudest of Mexico, it has nevertheless words to express as many thousands as one wishes. [p. 243] the American languages are so scant that they are not capable of expressing a metaphysical concept; a lesson which he learned from M. de la Condamine. “Time,” says this philosopher, reasoning about the languages of the Americans, “Duration, Space, Being, Substance, Matter, Body, all these words, and many others, have no equivalent words in their languages: and not only the names of metaphysical beings, but not even those of moral beings, can be expressed by them, except improperly and by long circumlocutions.” But M. de la Condamine knew as much about the American languages as M. de P., and he took his information, no doubt, from some ignorant man, as often happens to travelers. We are quite sure that many American languages do not have that scantiness of words which M. de la Condamine imagines; but leaving aside now what concerns the others, let us discourse only of the Mexican, which is the principal subject of our dispute.

> (*) SAGGIO DI YOCI MESSICANE SIGNIFICANTI CONCETTI METAFISICI E MORALI.

It is quite true that the Mexicans had no words to express the concepts of matter, of substance, of accident, and the like; but it is likewise certain that no language, either of Asia or of Europe, had such words before the Greeks began to subtilize, to abstract their ideas, and to create new terms to express them. The great Cicero, who knew the Latin language so well, and flourished in those times in which it was at its greatest perfection, although he esteemed it more copious than the Greek, nevertheless often struggles in his philosophical works to find words corresponding to the metaphysical ideas of the Greeks. How many times was he not compelled to create new words equivalent in some way to the Greek, because he did not find them among the words used by the Romans? But even today, since that language was enriched with many words invented both by Cicero and by other learned Romans who, following his example, gave themselves to the study of philosophy, it still lacks terms to express many metaphysical concepts, unless one has recourse to the barbarous language of the schools. None of those languages which the philosophers of Europe speak had words signifying matter, substance, accident, and other similar concepts;

Hh2 [p. 244] and so it was necessary that those who philosophized should adopt the Latin words, or else the Greek. The ancient Mexicans, because they did not engage in the study of metaphysics, are excusable for not having invented words to express those ideas; yet their language is not so scant of terms signifying metaphysical and moral things as M. de la Condamine affirms of those of South America; indeed I affirm that it is not easy to find a language more apt than the Mexican for treating metaphysical matters, since it is difficult to find another that abounds so much as that does in abstract nouns; for there are few verbs in it from which verbals corresponding to those in -io of the Latins are not formed, and few also are the substantives or adjectives from which abstract nouns are not formed, expressing the being, or as it is called in the schools the quiddity of things: the equivalents of which I cannot find in Hebrew, Greek, Latin, French, Italian, English, Spanish, or Portuguese; of which languages I seem to have that knowledge which is required for making the comparison. Now, to give some specimen of this language, and to gratify the curiosity of the readers, I shall set below before their eyes some words signifying metaphysical and moral concepts, and understood even by the rudest Indians. (*)

The excessive abundance of such words has been the cause that the highest mysteries of the Christian religion have been set forth without great difficulty in the Mexican language, and that there have been well translated into

So many are the books published in Mexican on religion and on Christian morals that of them alone a good library could be formed. After this Dissertation we shall give a brief Catalogue of the principal authors whom we remember, no less to confirm what we say than to show our gratitude for their labors. Some of them have published a great number of works that I have seen. Others, to ease for the Spaniards the understanding of the Mexican language, have composed grammars and dictionaries of it.

Those Europeans who have learned Mexican, among whom there are Italians, French, Flemings, Germans, and Spaniards, have celebrated that language with great praises, and have extolled it to such a degree that by some it has been esteemed superior to the Latin and the Greek, as we have said elsewhere. The Chevalier Boturini affirms that in urbanity, in polish, and in the sublimity of its expressions there is no language that can be compared with the Mexican. This author was not a Spaniard, but a Milanese; he was not a common man, but erudite and critical; he knew at least Latin, Italian, French, and Spanish quite well, and of Mexican he knew enough to be able to make the comparative judgment. Let M. de P., then, acknowledge his error, and learn not to decide on matters that he does not know.

Among the proofs on which Count de Buffon wishes to support his system of the recent organization of matter in the New World, he says that the organs of the Americans were coarse, and their language barbarous. “Let the list of their animals be seen,” he adds, “their names are so difficult to pronounce that it is a wonder that there have been Europeans who took the trouble to write them.” But I do not wonder so much at their trouble in writing them as at their carelessness in copying them. Among so many European authors who have written the civil or natural history of Mexico in Europe, I have not found even one who has not altered and disfigured the names of the persons, the animals, and the Mexican cities, and some have done so to such a degree that it is not possible to guess what they meant to write. The history of the animals of Mexico passed from the hands of its author, Dr. Hernández, to those of Nardo Antonio Recchi, who knew nothing of Mexican; from the hands of Recchi it passed to those of the Lincean Academicians of Rome, who published it with notes and dissertations; and of this edition Count de Buffon made use. Among so many hands of Europeans ignorant of the Mexican language,

> tutt: fi son pubblicati trattati di religione, come faremo veder nel promesso Caralogo . Quegli Europei , che hanno imparato il messicano, tra i uali vi sono degl' Italia us , us, Francehì, de' Fiamminghi , de'Te. deschi, e degli Spagauoli, che hanno celebrata con pran lodi vella lingua, ed a tal segno vantata, che da alcuni è stara Îlimara superiore alla latina, e alla greca, come abbiam derto altrove. Il Cav. Boturini afferma, che nella urbanirà, nella pus litezza, e nella sublimità delle espressioni non v' è niuna lingua che possa paragonarsi colla messicana . Questo Autore noa era Spagnuolo, ma Milanese: non era uomo volgate , ma. erudito & critco: sapeva affai bene almeno il Latino, l'Italiano, il Francese, e lo Spagnuolo, e del Messicano seppe quanto bastava per poter farne il giudizio comparativo. Riconosca dunque il Sig. de P. il suo errore, ed impari a non decidere in quelle materie , che ignora. Tra le prove alle quali vuole il C. de Buffon appoggiare il suo fistema della recente organizzazione della materia nel nuo» vo Mondo, dice, che gli organi degli Americani erano. rozzi , e la lor lingua barbara. ,, Vedasi, soggiunge, la lista de’ loro 3» animali, i loro nomi son tanto difficili da pronunziare , che n è da maravigliare , che vi fieno starti degli Europei , i quali » fiensi presa la fatica di scriverli . ,, Ma io non mi maraviglio tanto della lor fatica nello fcriverli, quanto della lor trascuraggine nel copiarli . Tra tanti Autori europei , che hanno scritto la Storia civile o naturale del Messico in Europa , non ne ho trovato nemmen uno, che non abbia alterati, e sfigura» ti i nomi delle persone, degli animali, e delle Città messicane, e alcuni lo hanno fatto a tal segno, che non è poslibile indo- Vinare ciò , che vollero scrivere. La Storia degli animali del Melslico passò dalle mani del suo Autore il Dot, Hernan, dez a quelle di Nardo Antonio Recchi, il quale non sapeva . niente del Messicano: dalle mani di Recchi passò a quelle degli Accademici Lincei di Roma, i quali la pubblicarono con note e difserrazioni: e di questa edizione fi servì il C. de Bufs fon, Fra tante mani d' Europei, ignoranti della liogua messica- , FS [p. 247] ma, non poteano a meno di non essere alterati i nomi degli animali . Per rendersì certo chi volesse dell'alterazione, che eli sofsiirono nelle mani del C. de Buffon , basta confrontare i no» mi messicani , che fi leggono nella Storia naturale di quel Fi. lolofo, con quelli dell'edizione romana dell’ Hernandez, Del resto egli è certo , che quella difficoltà, chie troviamo, nel pro. nuaziare una lingua, alla quale non fiamo asluefartri , e maslimamente fe l'articolazione d' ella è troppo diversa da quella della nostra propria lingua , non convince, che quella sia barbara. Quella medesima difficoltà , che sente il C. de Buffon nel pronuaziare i nomi melslicani, seorirebbonla i Meisicani nel pronunziare i nomi francesi . Coloro, che sono avvezzi alla lin» gua \pagouola , seotono gran difficoltà nel pronunziarc la liogua tedesca , e la pollaca, e pajono loro le più aspre e più dure di tutte, La lingua messicana non è stara quella dei mici Genitori, nè io la imparai da fanciullo: eppac tutti i nomi mesficani d'animali dal C. de Buffon prodotti , come argomento della barbarie di quella liogua, mi sembrano più facili senza paragone da pronunziare, che molti altri presi da alcune lingue curopee , i quali egli adopra (N) nella sua Storia Natura» le: e forse parrà così a quegli Europei, che non sono afsue» fairi alle une, nè alle altre lingue; e non vi mancherà, chi fi maravigli, che il C. de Buffon fiafi presa la fatica di \cri« vere quei nomi capaci di far paura ai più coraggiosi scrittori , Finalmente 10 ciò, che riguarda le lingue americane, deeli stare al giudizio di quegli Europei , che le seppero anzichè all’ a+ pinuone di coloro, che non ne fanno puila.

[p. 247] could not but have the names of the animals altered. To satisfy himself of the alteration which they suffered in the hands of Count de Buffon, whoever wishes need only compare the Mexican names that are read in the Natural History of that philosopher with those of the Roman edition of Hernández. For the rest, it is certain that the difficulty we find in pronouncing a language to which we are not accustomed, and especially if its articulation is too different from that of our own language, does not prove that it is barbarous. That same difficulty which Count de Buffon feels in pronouncing Mexican names, the Mexicans would feel in pronouncing French names. Those who are accustomed to the Spanish language feel great difficulty in pronouncing German and Polish, and these seem to them the harshest and roughest of all. The Mexican language was not that of my parents, nor did I learn it as a child; and yet all the Mexican names of animals produced by Count de Buffon as an argument for the barbarity of that language seem to me incomparably easier to pronounce than many others taken from certain European languages, which he employs (N) in his Natural History: and perhaps it will seem so to those Europeans who are accustomed neither to the one nor to the other languages; nor will there be wanting someone to wonder that Count de Buffon took the trouble to write those names, capable of frightening the most courageous writers. Finally, as to what concerns the American languages, one must abide by the judgment of those Europeans who knew them rather than by the opinion of those who know nothing of them.

## § VII

> 48 DISSERTAZIONE VE & VII.

On the Laws of the Mexicans.

> Su le leggi dei Messicani , {

Wishing to impugn that antiquity which Gemelli attributes by mistake to the court of the Mexicans, M. de Pauw alleges the anarchy of their government and the scantiness of their laws; and treating of the government of the Peruvians he says “that there cannot be laws in a despotic state; and in case there once were, it is not possible at present to analyze them, because we do not know them; nor can we know them, because they were never written, and their memory must have failed with the death of those who knew them.”

> Volendo il Sig. de Paw impugnar quell'antichità, che ac: tribuì Gemelli per skbaglio alla corte dei Messicani, allega l' narchìa del loro governo , e la scarsezza delle loro leggi: è trartando del governo dei Peruani dice,, che non possono eflere del- 4 le leggi in uno Stato dispotico: e caso che vi sieno un tem- » po state, non è possibile presentemente di farne l'analisi , per- » chè non le conosciamo : nè possiamo conoscerle , perchè noa » furono mai scritte, e la loro memoria dovea mancare nella » morte di coloro, che le fapeano. ,, h

No one had made mention of the anarchy of the kingdom of Mexico before M. de P. came into the world, whose brain seems to have a particular organization for understanding things contrary to all other men. There is no one so ignorant of the history of Mexico as not to know that those peoples were subject to particular lords, and the whole state to one supreme head, who was the king of Mexico. All the historians extol the great authority of that sovereign, and the supreme respect which his vassals bore him: if this is anarchy, all the states of the world will doubtless be anarchic.

> Nessuno avea fatto menzione dell'anarchia del regno di Messico; prima che venifse al Mondo il Sig. de P. , il cui cervello aver sembra una particolar organizzazione per intender le cose al contrario di tutti gli altri uomini, Non vi è alcuno sì ignorante della Storia del Messico, che non sappia, che quei Popoli erano sottoposti a particolari Signori ye tutto lo Stato ad un supremo Capo, che era il Re di Messico. Tutti gli Storici vantano la grande autorità di quel Soyrano , € il fommo rispetto che pli portavano i suoi vassalli : Se questo è anarcha, saranno senza dubbio anarchici tutti gli Stati del Mondo.

Despotism was not introduced in Mexico until the last years of the monarchy. In earlier times the monarchs had always respected the laws promulgated by their predecessors, and had zealously watched over their observance. Even in the times of Moctezuma II, who was the only truly despotic king, the magistrates judged according to the laws of the kingdom, and Moctezuma himself severely punished transgressors, abusing his power only in what could serve to increase his opulence and his authority.

> Il disporismo non fu introdotto in Messico fino” agli ulcimi anni della Monarchia. Nel tempo addietro aveano sempre i Monarchi rispettato le leggi promulgare dai loro Anrecesso» ri, ed aveano zelata la lor oflervanza. Anche ai tempi di Motezuma IL,, il quale fu l'unico Re veramente disporico , 1 Ma» gistrati giudicavano secondo le leggi del regno, e lo stelo Motezuma puniva severamente i trasgressori, non abusando del suo Potere, fe non in quello , che potea servire all' accrescimento della sua opulenza, e della sua autorità . .

These laws were not written; but they were perpetuated in the memory of men no less by tradition than by paintings. There was no subject who did not know them; for fathers of families did not cease to instruct their children in them, so that

> Queste leggi non erano scritte ; ma fi perpetuavano nella memoria degli uomini non meno per la tradizione , che per ’ le pitture , Non v' era suddito, che noa le sapesse; perchè i Padri di famiglia non cefllavano d' istruirne i loro figliuoli , ac: [p. 249] ciocchè evitando la trasgressione, schivassero il pgastigo . Le co» pie delle pitture delle leggi erano senza dubbio infinite ; poi» chè quantunque elle foflero sì furiosamente persepuitate dagli Spagnuoli , nondimeno io ne ho vedute molte, L'intelligenza di tali pitture non è tanto difficile a chi ha cognizione della maniera, colla quale rappresentavano i Messicani le cose, dei caratteri da loro usati, e della loro lingua , ma pel Sig. de P. saranno tanto inintelligibili , quanto le leggi dei Chinefsi , espresse nei caratteri propri di quella Nazione . Oitracciò dopo la conquista molti Messicani bene intendenti scriflero nei nostri ca» rauteri le leggi di Messico , d' Acolhuacan , di Tlascalla, di Michuacan ec.- Tra gli altri D. Ferdinando de Alba Ixililxochiti scrifse in lingua Spagnuola le ottanta leggi pubbiicate già dal suo famoso arcavolo il Re Nezabualcojoti, siccome abbiam derro nella Storia. Gli Spagnuoli poi ricercarono le leggi ed i costumi antichi di quelle Nazioni con maggior diligeoza , che qualunque altro articolo della Storia; perchè la loro cognizione importava allui al governo criltiano, tanto civile , quanto Ecclehastico , massimamente in riguardo dei maritaggi, delle prerogative della Nobiltà, della qualità del Vasfallaggio, e della condizione degli schiavi, S'informarono a bocca dagl' Indiani meglio iltruiu , è studiarono le loro pitture. Oltre ai primi Misionarj, i quali faticarono fruttuosamente in questa imprefa, D. Alfonso Zurita, uno dei principali Giudici di Messico , dotto in materia di Legge , e pratico di quei paesi, ne fece diligenti ricerche per ordine del Re Cactolico , e compose» quell’ utilislima opera, di cui abbiam fatto menzione nel Caraloga degli Scrittori della Storia antica del Mellico. Ecco come po» terono saperlì le leggi antiche dei Messicani senza eslere da lo- IO scritre .

[p. 249] by avoiding transgression, they might shun the punishment. The copies of the paintings of the laws were without doubt infinite; for although they were so furiously persecuted by the Spaniards, I have nevertheless seen many of them. The understanding of such paintings is not so difficult for one who has knowledge of the manner in which the Mexicans represented things, of the characters they used, and of their language; but for M. de P. they will be as unintelligible as the laws of the Chinese, expressed in the characters proper to that nation. Moreover, after the conquest many well-informed Mexicans wrote down in our characters the laws of Mexico, of Acolhuacan, of Tlaxcala, of Michoacán, etc. Among others Don Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl wrote in the Spanish language the eighty laws promulgated long ago by his famous great-great-great-grandfather King Nezahualcoyotl, as we have said in the History. The Spaniards, besides, sought out the ancient laws and customs of those nations with greater diligence than any other point of their history; because a knowledge of them was of great importance to Christian government, both civil and ecclesiastical, especially with regard to marriages, the prerogatives of the nobility, the quality of vassalage, and the condition of slaves. They informed themselves by word of mouth from the best-instructed Indians, and studied their paintings. Besides the first missionaries, who labored fruitfully in this enterprise, Don Alonso de Zorita, one of the principal judges of Mexico, learned in matters of law and familiar with those countries, made diligent researches into them by order of the Catholic King, and composed that most useful work of which we have made mention in the Catalogue of the writers on the ancient history of Mexico. Here is how the ancient laws of the Mexicans could be known without having been written by them.

> Ma che Leggi? degne molre di esse, dice l' Acosta, delle nostra ammirazione, e secondo le quali doweano quei Popoli reg- Bersi anche nel loro cristianesimo. Imprima la coltituzione del loco [tato in ciò , che riguarda la successione alla Corona, non poteva eflere meglio intesa, come quella, nella quale del pari sfuggivansi gl' inconvenienti della successione ereditaria, e quel-

But what laws! Many of them worthy, says Acosta, of our admiration, and according to which those peoples ought to be governed even in their Christianity. First, the constitution of their state, in what concerns the succession to the crown, could not have been better conceived, as one in which the inconveniences of hereditary succession were avoided alike, and those

> Stroria Antica del Messico Tomo 1V. Ii li [p. 250] li dell’ elettiva. Dovea eleggerlì un individuo della famiglia Reale per conservar così lo splendore della corona, e impedire, che il trono fofle giammai occupato da un uomo di bassa nascita. Non succedendovi il figliuolo , ma il fratello nono v'era pericolo, che un sì eminente, e sì importante impiego fol fe esposto all' indiscrezione d'’ un giovane ‘inesperto, o alla ma» ligoità d’ un Reggente ambizioso.

Ancient History of Mexico, Vol. IV.         Ii [p. 250] of the elective. One individual of the royal family had to be elected, so as thus to preserve the splendor of the crown, and to prevent the throne from ever being occupied by a man of low birth. Since it was not the son who succeeded, but the brother, there was no danger that so eminent and so important an office would be exposed to the indiscretion of an inexperienced youth, or to the malignity of an ambitious regent.

> Se i fratelli poi avessero dovuto succedere secondo l'ordine della lor nascita, sarebbe neceflariamente talvolta toccata la corona ad un uomo inetto al governo , ed avrebbe altresì patuto accadere, che l' Erede presuntivo macchinasse contra la vita del Sovrano per anticiparsi la successione. All’uno e all’alrro inconveniente fi ovviava coll' elezione. Gli Electori sceglievano tra i fratelli del Re morto , e mancando essi, tra i figli dei- Re anteriori , il più idoneo a comandar la Nazione. Se folle stato di balha del Re il nomionar gli Elettori, avrebbe egli potuto scegliere coloro, che foflero più favorevoli ai suoi difleni, e procacciarli i loro suffragj in favor di quel fratello, che ofle a lui più caro, e forse anche in favor del figliuolo, non curando le leggi fondamentali dello Stato: ma non era così; poichè i medesimi Elettori erano eletti dal corpo della Nobiltà, la quale in loro comprometteva i suffrag} di tutta la Nî3zione. Se Î' impiego degli Elettori fosse staro perpetuo, avrebbono potuto costoro, abusando della lor autorità , divenir padroni della monarchia ; ma siccome finiva nella prima elezione a lor voce elettorale , e fi eleggevano allora puovi Elettori per la sepuente , così non era tanto agevole all' ambizione l' usurpar l'autorità , Finalmente per ischivare altri inconvenienti,i verì Elettori non erano più di quattro , uomini della prima nobiltà, di gran prudenza , € di notoria probità. E' vero, che nè anche dopo tante precapzioni poteausi impedire ruti I disordini; ma qual governo fu mai tra gli uomini , che nona folle esposto a maggiori mali?

Had the brothers, moreover, been bound to succeed according to the order of their birth, the crown would necessarily have fallen at times to a man unfit for government, and it might also have happened that the presumptive heir would plot against the life of the sovereign in order to anticipate the succession. Both inconveniences were obviated by election. The electors chose, from among the brothers of the dead king, and failing them from among the sons of former kings, the one most fit to command the nation. Had it been in the king’s power to name the electors, he could have chosen those who were most favorable to his designs, and procured their votes in favor of that brother who was dearest to him, and perhaps even in favor of his son, heedless of the fundamental laws of the state; but it was not so; for the electors themselves were elected by the body of the nobility, which entrusted to them the votes of the whole nation. If the office of the electors had been perpetual, they might, abusing their authority, have become masters of the monarchy; but since their electoral voice ended with the first election, and new electors were then chosen for the next, it was not so easy for ambition to usurp authority. Finally, to avoid other inconveniences, the true electors were no more than four, men of the first nobility, of great prudence and of notorious probity. It is true that not even after so many precautions could all disorders be prevented; but what government was ever among men that was not exposed to greater evils?

The Mexican nation was warlike, and therefore needed a head who was knowledgeable and expert in the trade of war: now what counsel could be taken more suited to this end than

> La Nazion Messicana era guerriera, © però abbisogaava d'un capo intendente, ed esperto nel mestier della guerra : of qual consiglio potea prendersi più confacente a tal fine, che [p. 251] DISSERTAZIONE VI. age quello di non eleggere Re colui, che non avesse per li suoi meriti ottenuta la carica di General d' esercito, e di non coropar colui, che dopo la sua elezione nona fì foffe nella guerra procacciate le vittime, che fecondo il loro sistema di religione doveano sacrificarsi nelle feste dell' Incoronazione ?

[p. 251] that of not electing as king one who had not by his merits obtained the post of general of the army, and of not crowning one who, after his election, had not procured in war the victims which, according to their system of religion, had to be sacrificed at the festivals of the coronation?

> Quella prontezza , colla quale i Messicani scossero il giogo de' Tepanechi, e quella gloria, che fi guadagnarono le loro armi nella conquista d' Azcapozalco , doveano naturalmente eccitare la. rivalità, e la diffidenza de' loro vicini, e spezialmente uella del Re d’ Acolhuacan , il qual era stato, ed era anche allora il maggior Re di quella terra, ed essendo peraltro ancor vacillante il trono di Meslico ,abbisognava d' un forte appoggio, che lo sostenefse . IL Re d' Acolhuacan , il qual avea di fresco ricuperata coll' ajuto de' Messicani la corona , usurpatagli già dal Tiranno Tezozomoc , dovea temere, che qualche suddito poderoso, seguendo l'orme di quel Tiranno, non eccitasfse alla ribellione una parte del suo regno, e lo privasse , come suo Padre, della corona, e della vita, Il Re di Tlacopan, il qual occupava un trono nuovamente stabilito, e poco considerabile , avea più da temere. Ciascun di questi Re era per se solo poco ficuro, e davea diffidarsi degli altri due; ma uniti tutti e rre insieme poreano formare una potenza invincibile . Or che fanpo? Formano una triplice alleanza, la qual renda ciascun ficura rispetto agli altn due, e tutti e tre rispetto a'lor sudditi. Questa fu quell*alleanza, che raflodò i troni d' Acolhuacan; e di Tlacopan, e che agevolò a' Messicani la loro conquista : alleanza ranto ferma , e così ben ordinata, che non fi sconcertò giammai fino all’ arrivo degli Spagnuoli . Questo sol colpo di politica basta a dimostrare il discernimento, e la (agacità di quelle Nazioni ; ma ve ne furono tanti altri simili, che se vo» lessimo rapportarli tutti, farebbe d'uopo- di copiare una buona parte della Storia.

That readiness with which the Mexicans shook off the yoke of the Tepanecs, and that glory which their arms won in the conquest of Azcapotzalco, were naturally bound to excite the rivalry and the distrust of their neighbors, and especially that of the king of Acolhuacan, who had been, and was even then, the greatest king of that land, and who, the throne of Mexico being moreover still unsteady, needed a strong support to sustain it. The king of Acolhuacan, who had recently recovered, with the help of the Mexicans, the crown formerly usurped from him by the tyrant Tezozomoc, had to fear that some powerful subject, following the footsteps of that tyrant, might incite to rebellion a part of his kingdom, and deprive him, as his father had been, of the crown and of life. The king of Tlacopan, who occupied a newly established and not very considerable throne, had more to fear. Each of these kings was by himself little secure, and had to distrust the other two; but united all three together they could form an invincible power. Now what do they do? They form a triple alliance, which makes each secure with regard to the other two, and all three with regard to their subjects. This was the alliance that strengthened the thrones of Acolhuacan and of Tlacopan, and that made their conquests easier for the Mexicans: an alliance so firm and so well ordered that it never fell apart until the arrival of the Spaniards. This single stroke of policy suffices to demonstrate the discernment and sagacity of those nations; but there were so many others like it that if we wished to relate them all, it would be necessary to copy a good part of the History.

The judicial system of the Mexicans and of the Texcocans furnishes us with several useful lessons of politics. That diversity of grades among the magistrates served good order; their assiduity in the tribunals from the break of day until evening shortened the course

> La forma giudiziale de’ Messicani , e de' Tezcucanì ci somministra parecchie lezioni utilì di Politica . Quella diversità di gradi ne' Magistrati serviva al buon ordine : la lor assiduità ne’ tribunali dallo spyutar del dì fino alla sera abbreviava iù poro [p. 252] az DISSERTAZIONE Yi.

Ii2 [p. 252] of the causes, and turned them away from many clandestine practices which could have swayed them in favor of one of the parties. The capital penalties prescribed against those who perverted justice, the promptness of their execution, and the vigilance of the sovereigns kept the magistrates in check, and the care taken to supply them at the king’s expense with everything necessary made them inexcusable. Those assemblies that were held every twenty days before the sovereign, and particularly that general assembly of all the magistrates every eighty days to conclude the pending causes, besides avoiding those great evils which the slowness of judgments occasions, brought it about that the magistrates communicated their lights to one another reciprocally; that the king came to know better those whom he had appointed depositaries of his authority; that innocence had more recourse; and that the apparatus of judgment rendered justice more respectable. That law which permitted appeal from the tribunal of the Tlacatecatl to that of the Cihuacoatl in criminal causes, and not in civil ones, shows that the Mexicans, respecting the laws of humanity, recognized that more was required to believe a man guilty than to declare him a debtor. In the trials of the Mexicans no other proof against the accused was admitted than that of witnesses. Torture was never seen employed among them to make the innocent guilty by force of torments, nor did they avail themselves of those barbarous proofs of the duel, of fire, of boiling water, and the like, which were once so frequent in Europe and are now read by us with astonishment in the histories. “There will be no one who does not marvel,” says Montesquieu on this subject, (O) “that our forefathers made the honor, the fortune, and the property of citizens depend on certain things which belonged less to the jurisdiction of reason than to that of chance; and that they constantly employed those proofs which proved nothing, and were connected neither with innocence nor with crime.” What we now say of those proofs, our posterity will say in time to come of torture, and

> delle cause, e gli distoglieva da molte pratiche clandestine , le quali avrebbono poturo prevenirli in favor d' alcuna delle parti. Le pene capitali prescritte contro i prevaricatori della piu. {tizia , la puntualità della loro esecuzione, e la vigilanza de’ Sovrani tenevano in freno i Magistrati, e quella cura, che fì avea di somministrar loro a conto del Re tutto il bisoznevole, gli readava inescutabili, Quelle radunanze , che fi tenevano 0% gni venti giorni innanzi al Sovrano, e particolarmente quell’ affemblea generale di tutti i Magistrati ogni ottanta ‘giorni per terminar. le cause pendenti, oltre allo schivare que’ gran malî, che cagiona la lentezza de' giudizj, faceano, che i Magistrati fi comunicaflero reciprocamente i loro lumi: ‘ che it Re conoscesls meglio coloro, i quali egli avea costituiti depositarj della fua autorità: che l'innocenza avesle più ricorlì, e che Î appa» zato del giudizio rendefle più rispettabile la ‘giustizia . Quella legge , che permetteva l’ appellazione dal tribunale del Teca tzecar! a quello del Cibuacoatl nelle causé criminali, e non nelle civili dà a divedere, che i Messicani, rispertando le leggi dell' umanità, riconoscevano, che i richiedeva più per credere un uomo delinquente, che per dichiararlo debitore. Ne' giudizj de' Messicani non fi ammetteva altra pruova contro il Reo , che quella de' testimonj. Non fu mai veduto appo loro adoprar la tortura per far colpevole per forza de’ tormenti l’ innocente, nè prevalersì di quelle barbare pruove del duello , dell fuoco, dell acqua bogliente, e fimili, che furono già sì frequenti in Euro» pa, ed oggi sono da noi lette con istupore nelle storie, ,, Noa » vi farà chi non fì maravigli,, dice sopra, questo: argomento. » il Montesquiea , (0) che i nostri Maggiori facessero dipender » l'onore, la fortuna, ed i beni de’ Cittadini da certe cose, le » quali erano meno della giurisdizione della ragione, che dî » quella” della sorte: e che adoperaffero inceflanzemente quelle »> pruove, che nulla provavano, e non eraco connesse nè coll >» innocenza, nè col delitto. », Ciù che ora diciamo di quelle pruove, dirà nell'avvenire la nostra posterità della ‘tortura, e non

will

> (0) L' Esprit des laix, lib. z#. cap. 17. [p. 253] non cefseranno mai di maraviglia:si, che sì fatta pruova sia (tzra generalmente in uso per tanti secoli nella parte più illumiî» nata del Mondo, Il giuramento era prova di gran momento ne'giudiz) de' Messicani, ficcome abbiam detto altrove; imperocchè siccome erano persuasi de' ternbili gastighi, che doveano infallibilmente eseguire gli Dei ne’ pergiuri, così credevano, che nesiuno olerebbe Fpergiurare; ma non sappiamo ,che fi permettefle tal prova agli Attori contra il Reo, ma solamente al Reo per purgarsiì dal delitto. i Punivino severamente i Messicani tutti que’ delitti, che sono pacticolarmente ripugnanti alla ragione, 0 pregiudiziali allo Stato, ik crimentese, l'omicidio, il furto, l adulterio, l' incelto , e gli altri eccessi in questa materia contra natura : il sacrilegio, l’ ubbriachezza, e la bugìa . Sì conduflero faviamente, non lasciando impuniti rali misfatti; ma peccarono nella quantità della pena , la quale in alcuni delitti era eccessiva, e crudele . Io non pretendo di scusare i falli di quella Nazione ; ma nemmen posso dislimulare, che di quanto è riprensibile nella loro legislazione wuoveranki elempj ne' più famoli Popoli dell’ antico Continente, e tali da far comparire affai miti le leggi de’ Messicani, e più conformi alla ragione . Le celebri leggi delle dodici tavole son piene, dice il Montesquieu , (P) di disposizioni crudelifsime. . . vedesi in esse il supplizio del fuoco , e le ene sempre capirali . Eppur quelta è quella lodatiflima compi- Lea: che fecero i Romani del meglio da lor trovato presso i Popoli Greci . (O) The Spirit of the Laws, bk. 28, ch. 17. [p. 253] will never cease to marvel that such a proof was generally in use for so many centuries in the most enlightened part of the world. The oath was a proof of great weight in the trials of the Mexicans, as we have said elsewhere; for just as they were persuaded of the terrible punishments that the gods would infallibly inflict on the perjured, so they believed that no one would dare to perjure himself; but we do not know that such a proof was permitted to the plaintiffs against the accused, but only to the accused, to clear himself of the crime.

The Mexicans severely punished all those crimes that are particularly repugnant to reason or prejudicial to the state: lese-majesty, homicide, theft, adultery, incest, and the other excesses of this kind against nature; sacrilege, drunkenness, and lying. They acted wisely in not leaving such misdeeds unpunished; but they erred in the measure of the penalty, which in some crimes was excessive and cruel. I do not claim to excuse the faults of that nation; but neither can I conceal that whatever is reprehensible in their legislation will find its examples among the most famous peoples of the old continent, and such as to make the laws of the Mexicans appear very mild and more conformable to reason. “The celebrated laws of the twelve tables,” says Montesquieu, (P) “are full of most cruel provisions… one sees in them the punishment of fire, and penalties always capital.” Yet this is that most praised compilation which the Romans made of the best that they found among the Greek peoples. Now if the best of the most civilized Greece was such, what must that have been which was not so good? What must have been the legislation of those peoples whom they called barbarians? What law more inhuman and cruel than that of the twelve tables, which permitted creditors to tear apart (Q) the debtor who did not pay, and for each to carry off his

share

(P) The Spirit of the Laws, bk. 14, ch. 15.

(Q) “If there were several to whom the accused had been adjudged, they permitted them, if they wished, to cut up and equally divide the body of the man handed over to them.” Aul. Gell., Noct. Att., bk. 20, ch. 1. I know well what several jurists say to justify this law, but I also know that they have not succeeded. [p. 254] share in satisfaction of his claim? And this law was not promulgated in Rome in the rude beginnings of that so renowned city, but three hundred years after its foundation. What law, on the contrary, is more iniquitous than that of the famous legislator Lycurgus, which permitted theft to the Lacedaemonians? The Mexicans punished this crime, so pernicious to society; but they did not proceed to capital punishment unless the thief was not in a condition to make satisfaction and to pay for the offense with his liberty and his goods. It was not so with regard to theft committed in sown fields; for these, being by their situation more exposed to plunder, had greater need of the protection of the laws; but that same law which prescribed capital punishment against him who stole there a certain number of fruits or plants permitted travelers in need to eat there as much as they required, to remedy their present necessity. How much more reasonable was this law than that of the twelve tables, which condemned to be hanged, without distinction, whoever took anything from the sown fields of others? (*)

> La bugia, quel peccato tanto pernicioso alla Società, fì lascia per lo più impunita in molrislimi paesi dell’antico Con» tinente, e nel Giappone fi castiga sp:flo con pena capitale. Lying, that sin so pernicious to society, is for the most part left unpunished in very many countries of the old continent, and in Japan is often punished with death. The Mexicans kept equally far from the one extreme and the other. Their legislators, well aware of the genius and inclinations of the nation, perceived that if they did not prescribe grave penalties against lying and drunkenness, men would lack the judgment to satisfy their respective obligations, truth would be lacking in trials, and good faith in contracts. Experience has shown how harmful to those nations the impunity of these two sins is.

Their laws concerning marriages were without doubt more honest and more decorous than those of the Romans, the Greeks, the Persians, the Egyptians, and other peoples of the old continent. The Tartars marry their daughters; the ancient Persians and the Assyrians took their own mothers; the Athenians and the Egyptians their sisters. In Mexico every marriage was strictly forbidden between persons related in the first degree of consanguinity and of affinity, except between brothers- and sisters-in-law, when the brother on dying left any child. That prohibition shows that the Mexicans judged better of matrimony than all the aforesaid nations. That exception demonstrates their sentiments of humanity. If a widow passes to second nuptials, she often has the displeasure of seeing her children little loved by a father who did not give them life; her new husband little respected by those same children, who regard him as a stranger; and the children of the one marriage and of the other so disunited and discordant among themselves as if they had been born of different mothers. Now what better counsel (I speak according to the rules of human politics, by which those nations were guided that had no knowledge of the holy laws of Christianity), what better counsel, I say, could the Mexicans take to remedy
