(R) The Spirit of the Laws, bk. 14, ch. 15. [p. 256] those evils all too common than that of marrying the widow to her brother-in-law? Many ancient nations of Europe, imitated by not a few modern peoples of Asia and of Africa, bought their wives, and therefore exercised over them an authority far greater than that which the author of Nature granted them, and treated them more as slaves than as companions. The Mexicans acquired their wives only by means of lawful and decorous suits; and although they presented gifts to the parents, these were not on account of a price for the daughter, which they did not claim, but only a token of respect to win their goodwill and to bend their will to the contract. The Romans, though they had no scruple about lending their wives, (S) nevertheless had the right by law to take their lives whenever they were caught in adultery. This iniquitous law, which made the husband judge in his own cause, and even executor of his own sentence, instead of preventing adulteries increased parricides. Among the Mexicans that infamous traffic in their wives was not permitted to husbands, nor did they have any authority over their lives. He was punished with capital punishment who took the life of his wife, even though he caught her in adultery. This, they said, is to usurp the authority of the magistrates, to whom it belongs to take cognizance of crimes and to punish them according to the tenor of the laws. Before the Julian law De Adulteriis was made by Augustus, we do not know, says Vives, (*) that any trial for adultery was ever held in Rome: that is to say, that that celebrated nation lacked justice on a point so grave and so important for more than seven centuries.

> Il tributo, che fi pagava a' Re d' Anahuac éra eccessivo, ed erano altresì tiranniche le leggi, che il prefcrivevano; ma queste leggi furono conseguenze del dispotismo , guar ri ( " gli

As for the laws of war, it is difficult for them to be just among a warlike people: the great esteem that it has for valor and military glory makes it regard as enemies those who are not, and the ambition to conquer drives it to overstep the bounds prescribed by justice. Nevertheless in the laws of the Mexicans such traits of equity are seen as would do honor to the most civilized nations. War could not be declared without having first examined its reasons in full council, and without their having been approved by the High priest. Moreover, embassies, often repeated, had to be sent beforehand to those against whom war was being resolved, in order to obtain peacefully, by way of some accommodation, what was wanted, before coming to a rupture. Such delays gave their enemies time to prepare for defense; but besides serving as their justification, they contributed likewise to their glory, since among them it was reckoned cowardice to make war on unprepared enemies, and without having first solemnly challenged them, so that the victory could never be ascribed to anything but their bravery. It is true that these laws were not always observed; but they were not for that reason less just: and if there was injustice in the conquests of the Mexicans, it was certainly no less in those of the Romans, the Greeks, the Persians, the Goths, and other celebrated nations. One of the great evils that war usually brings with it is that of famine, on account of the hostilities that are carried on in the fields. It is not possible to prevent this evil altogether; but if there was ever anything capable of moderating it, it was without doubt that custom of the Mexicans and of the other peoples of Anahuac of having in every province a place assigned as a field of battle. No less conformable to reason and humanity was that other custom of theirs of having in time of war, every five days, a whole day of truce and rest.

Ancient History of Mexico, Vol. IV.         Kk [p. 258] Those nations had formed a kind of Jus Gentium, by virtue of which, if the lord, the nobility, and the commons rejected the proposals made to them by another people or nation, and referred the decision to arms, and were defeated, the lord lost his sovereign right, the nobility the supreme dominion that it had over its possessions, the commons were subjected to personal service, and all those who had been taken prisoner in the heat of the fray were deprived, quasi ex delicto, of liberty and of the right to life. This is assuredly opposed to those ideas of humanity that we hold; but the general convention of those peoples made that inhumanity less blameworthy, and the far more atrocious examples of the most civilized nations of the old continent dispel that horror which the cruelty of those American peoples at first sight causes in us. “Among the Greeks,” says Montesquieu, (T) “the inhabitants of a city taken by force of arms lost their liberty, and were sold as slaves.” Certainly the inhumanity that the Mexicans exercised toward their enemy prisoners is not to be compared with that which the Athenians used toward their own citizens. “A law of Athens,” says the aforesaid author, “ordained that when the city was besieged, all the useless people should be put to death.” Neither among the Mexicans, nor among any other nation of the New World at all polished, will a law be found as barbarous as that of the most civilized people of ancient Europe; indeed the greatest concern of the Mexicans, and of all those nations of Anahuac, when some city of theirs was about to be besieged, was to place their children, women, and invalids in safety, either by sending them to other cities or else to the mountains. Thus they withdrew that weak folk from the fury of the enemies, and otherwise prevented the excessive consumption of provisions.

The tribute that was paid to the kings of Anahuac was excessive, and the laws that prescribed it were likewise tyrannical; but these laws were consequences of despotism, introduced there in the

> Ma se cenfuriamo nelle leggi su i tributi la tirannica ambizione di quea' Monarchi , non possiamo a meno di non lodare ed ammirare nelle lor leggi sul commercio la coltura di quelle Nazioni, e la (aviezza de’ loro Legislatori. L' avere in ogni Città o Borgo una piazza , destinata pel commercio di tutte le cole, che poreano servire a' bisogni, ed alle delizie della vira , giavava a riunirvi tutti i Mercatanti pel più pronto spaccio delle merci, e gli metteva sotto gli occhi degli Istrori , @ Commessarj, acciocchè fi evitafle ogni frode, e diordine ne’ contratti. L'avere ogni merce il suo luogo determinaro contribuiva al buon ordine, e al comodo di coloro, che volevano provvedersene. Il Tribunal di Commercio, stabilito nella medesima piazza del mercaro per aggiustar le differenze insorte tra i negozianti, & per punir prontamente qualunque ecceflo vi fosse , confervava inviolabili i dritti della giustizia, ed assicurava la pubblica tranquillità . A quelte savie disposizioni fi davette quell’ ordine maraviglioso, che in mezzo ad un sì eccessivo numero di negozianti vi ammirarono i primi Spagnouoli.

But if we censure in the laws on tributes the tyrannical ambition of those monarchs, we cannot help praising and admiring in their laws on commerce the civilization of those nations and the wisdom of their legislators. To have in every city or town a square destined for the trade in all the things that could serve the needs and the delights of life was useful for bringing all the merchants together there for the readiest sale of wares, and put them under the eyes of inspectors or commissaries, so that all fraud and disorder in contracts might be avoided. That every ware had its determined place contributed to good order and to the convenience of those who wished to provide themselves with it. The Tribunal of Commerce, established in the same square of the market to settle the differences that arose among the traders and to punish promptly any excess that might occur there, kept the rights of justice inviolable and ensured public tranquillity. To these wise provisions was owed that marvelous order which the first Spaniards admired there, in the midst of so excessive a number of traders.

Finally, in the laws on slaves the Mexicans were superior to the most civilized nations of ancient Europe. If one wishes to make a comparison of the laws of the Mexicans with those of the Romans, the Lacedaemonians, and other celebrated peoples, one will soon see in the latter such barbarity and cruelty as causes horror, and in the former great humanity and great respect for the law of Nature (I do not speak now of prisoners of war, of whom I shall treat later). What law is more humane than that which made free at birth

> Finalmente nelle lepgî su gli (schiavi furono i Messicani fuperiocri alle più colte Nazioni dell’ antica Europa . Se vuol farsi il paragone delle leggi de’ Messicani , con quelle de’ Romapì, de’ Lacedemonj, e d' altri celebri Popoli, tosto fi vedrà in queste una tal barbarie e crudeltà, che fa ribrezzo, e in quelle una grande umanità, è un gran rispetto alla legge della Natura ( pon parlo ora de’ prigionieri di guerra, di cui poi ragionerò « ) Qual legge più umana di quella, che faceva TA” aNa [p. 260] 269 DISSERTAZIONE Vi.

Kk2 [p. 260] all men, even of slave parents; which left to the slave the ownership of his goods and of what he acquired by his own industry or labor; which obliged the master to treat the slave as a man and not as a beast; did not allow him any authority over his life, and even deprived him of the power to sell him in the market, unless after having had his unruliness legally established? Now how different from these were the laws of the Romans! Those people, by the supreme authority granted them by the laws, were masters not only of all that their slaves acquired by their labor, but even of their lives, (V) of which they deprived them according to their caprice; they treated them with the greatest inhumanity, and made them endure the most atrocious torments: and, that the inhuman character of this nation may be seen, while they so extended the authority of masters against slaves, they restricted it likewise in what was in favor of these. The Fufia Caninia law forbade masters to manumit by testament beyond a certain number of slaves. In the Silanian law, and in others, it was prescribed that whenever a master was killed, all those slaves of his who lived within the same house, or in a place near it from which his voice could be heard, should likewise be put to death. If he was killed on some journey, all those slaves who had remained with him had to die, and likewise all those who had fled from him, however manifest their innocence might be. The Aquilian law included under one and the same action the wound inflicted on a slave and that inflicted on another man’s beast. To such an excess did the barbarity of the most civilized Romans go. Nor indeed were the laws of the Lacedaemonians more humane, which granted slaves no action at law against those who insulted or injured them.

> beri tutti gli uomini anche da genitori schiavi: che lasciava allo schiavo il dominio della roba sua, e di quello che acquistava colla propria industria o fatica: che obbligava il padrone a trattar lo (schiavo come uomo, e non come bestia ;non gli permetteva verun'autorità su la vita di lui, e anche lo privava della facoltà di poter venderlo nel mercato, se non dopo, avar fatto constar giuridicamente dell’ indocilità d' esso lui? Or quanto diverse-da queste erano le leggi de' Romani? Costoro per la somma autorità loro accordata dalle leggi erano padromi non che di tutto ciò, che gli schiavi acquistavano colla loro fatica, ma eziand)o della lor vita, (V) della quale gli privavano giu. ta il lor capriccio, gli trattavano colla maggior inumanità , e lor faceano tollerare i più atroci tormenti: ed acciocchè fi veda l' indole inumana di questa Nazione, mentre tanto ampliavano l'autorità de' Padroni contro gli schiavi, la ristrignevano pure in ciò, che era in favor di costoro. La legge Fusia Caninia vietava a' Padroni il maromettere per testamento oltre ad un certo numero di schiavi. Nella legge Silaniana , è in altre era prescritto, che ogni volta, che fofle ucciso un Padrone fi faceflero parimente morire tutti que’ suoi schiavi, che abitafsero dentro la medesima, casa, o in luogo ad effa vicino, donde sentir fi potesse la sua voce. Se egli era ucciso in qualche viaggio , doveano morire rutti quegli schiavi , che foflero con lui restati, e similmente rutti quelli, che fe ne fossero fuggiti, quantunque manifesta fosse la loro innocenza. La legge Aquilia comprese fotto una medesima azione la ferita fatta ad uno schiavo, e quella fatta a una bestia altrui . A coral ecceslo giunse la barbarie de’ coltisslimi Romani. Non furono in vero più umane le leggi de' Lacedemon}, le quali non concedevano agli schiavi verun' azione in giudizio contra coloro, che gl' insultavano, “a ingiuriavano . Se

(V) What wonder that the Romans granted that barbarous authority to masters over slaves, when they had granted it also to fathers of families over their lawful children? “Let the father have over his lawful children the power of life, of death, and of sale.” This single law, published in Rome by the first kings, and afterwards inserted by the Decemvirs in the twelve Tables, suffices to show that the legislation of the Mexicans was more humane.

> (V) Che maraviglia che i Romani accordasiero quella barbara auterità a' Padront su gli Schiavi , avendola concessa anche a' Padri di famiglia sopra i lor figli legittimi è Endo liberis fustîs jus vite, necii, venumdandique poteffai Patri . Questa fola legge pubblicata in Roma da'primi Re,e inserita poi da' D8cem=viri nelle dodici Tavole basta per dare a divedere, che la legislazione de' Mefficani fu più umana.

[p. 261]

> Se oltre il detto fin quì fi vuol paragonare il fistema di educazione , che v'era preflo i Messicani con quello de' Gréci, riconoscerassi, che non era sì grande l'istruzione de' Greci a’ lor figliuoli nelle arti e nelle (cienze , come que!la, che aveano i fanciulli, ed i giovani Messicani ne' costumi da” lor genitori . I Greci s' adoperavano più ad illustrare la mente, i Messicani a rettificare il cuore. Gli Ateniesi gere i lor giovani alla più esecranda oscenità in quelle medesime scuole, che erano destinate ad istruirli nelle arti . [ Lacedemon} ammaestravano i lor figliuoli, secondo il prescritto di Licurgo, nel rubare per rendergli scaltri e svelti, e gli sferzavano fortemente, quando gli còglievano in qualche furto, castigando in loro non ‘quel peccato; ma la poca industria nel farlo sì, che vi foflero colti. Ma i Messicani insegnavano a' lor figliuoli infieme colle arti la religione, la modestia , l'onestà, la sobrietà, la vita laboriosa, l’ amor della verità , e il rispetto a' maggiori .

If, beyond what has been said so far, one wishes to compare the system of education that existed among the Mexicans with that of the Greeks, it will be recognized that the instruction which the Greeks gave their children in the arts and in the sciences was not so great as that which Mexican children and young people received in manners from their parents. The Greeks applied themselves more to enlightening the mind, the Mexicans to rectifying the heart. The Athenians prostituted their young men to the most execrable obscenity in those very schools that were destined to instruct them in the arts. The Lacedaemonians trained their children, according to the precept of Lycurgus, in stealing, to make them cunning and nimble, and whipped them severely when they caught them in some theft, punishing in them not that sin, but the little skill in committing it, whereby they were caught. But the Mexicans taught their children, together with the arts, religion, modesty, honesty, sobriety, the laborious life, the love of truth, and respect for their elders.

> Questo è un breve, ma vero fapgio della coltura de'Mesficani preso dalla loro Storia antica , dalle lor pitture, da' rag» guagli de' più esarti Storici Spagnuoli . Così si reggevano que’ Popoli , i quali il Sig. de Paw crede i più selvaggi del mondo. Così fi reggevano que” Popoli inferiori quanto alla industria , ed alla sagacità a più rozzi Popoli dell'antico Continente . Così si reggevano que’ Popoli , della cui razionalità vollero dubitare alcuni Européi ,

This is a brief but true sample of the civilization of the Mexicans, drawn from their ancient history, from their paintings, and from the accounts of the most exact Spanish historians. Thus were governed those peoples whom M. de Pauw believes the most savage in the world. Thus were governed those peoples inferior in industry and sagacity to the rudest peoples of the old continent. Thus were governed those peoples whose rationality some Europeans have wished to doubt.

## D I S S E RTAT I O N V I I 

> ' 2655 ‘DISSERTAZIONE VII.

O N T H E B O U N DA R I E S A N D P O P U L AT I O N O F

## T H E K I N G D O M S O F A N A H UAC 

> SOPRA I CONFINI, E LA POPOLAZIONE DEI REGNI DI ANAHUAC.

The mistakes of many Spanish writers concerning the boundaries of the Mexican empire, and the absurdities of M. de Pauw and of other foreign authors concerning the population of those countries, have obliged me to write this Dissertation in order to set the truth in a clear light: which I shall try to do with all possible brevity.

> Li sbaglj di molti Scrittori Spagnuoli intorno ai confini dell’ Imperio Melslicano , e gli spropofiti del Sig. de Paw A e d'altri Autori Stranieri intorno alla popolazione di quei pae si , mi hanno coltretto a far questa Difsertazione per mettere in chiaro il vero: lo che procurerò di fare con tutta la bre. vità possibile, SE

§ I.

> Sopra i confini Dei Regni di Anabuac .

On the Boundaries of the Kingdoms of Anahuac.

> Il Sohs, tenendo dietro a parecchi Scrittori Spagnuoli mal informati, aflerma, che l’imperio Messicano fi (tendeva dall’ 1tmo di Panamà fino al Capo Mendocino nella California, Il P. Touron , Domenicano Francese », volendo nella sua Storia General d' America ampliare ancor più quei termini, dice, che turti i paesi scoperti nell’ America Settentrionale erano fortoposti al Re di Messico: che l'estensione di quell' [mperio da levante a ponente era di leghe cinquecento, e da tramontana a mezzogiorno di leghe dugento , © dugento cinquanra: che i suoi termini erano’ a tramontana l' Oceano Atlantico, a ponente il Fri d'Anian, a mezzogiorno il mar Pacifico, éd a levante 'Istmo di Panamà ; ma oltre agli errori geografici, che hav- Vi in questa descrizione , v'è ancora della contraddizione; poichè se mai fosse vero, che quell' Imperio fi stendeva dall’ l\tmo di Panamà fino al golfo , o piuttosto stretto d' Anian, la sua estensione non sarebbe slata di sole cinquecento leghe , ma ancor di mille , mentre non vi sarebbono (tati compresi meno di cinquanta gradi, 4

Solís, following several ill-informed Spanish writers, asserts that the Mexican empire extended from the Isthmus of Panama to Cape Mendocino in California. Father Touron, a French Dominican, wishing in his General History of America to extend those limits still further, says that all the countries discovered in North America were subject to the king of Mexico; that the extent of that empire from east to west was five hundred leagues, and from north to south two hundred or two hundred and fifty; that its limits were on the north the Atlantic Ocean, on the west the gulf of Anian, on the south the Pacific sea, and on the east the Isthmus of Panama; but besides the geographical errors in this description, there is also a contradiction; for if it were ever true that that empire extended from the Isthmus of Panama to the gulf, or rather strait, of Anian, its extent would not have been only five hundred leagues, but even a thousand, since no fewer than fifty degrees would have been included in it.

> Storia Anrica del Messico Tom, IP. L l La [p. 266] 268 DISSERTAZIONE Yll,

Ancient History of Mexico, Vol. IV.          Ll [p. 266] The cause of such errors is that these authors were persuaded that in Anahuac there was no other sovereign than that of Mexico; that the kings of Acolhuacan and of Tlacopan were his subjects, and that the Michoacans and the Tlaxcalans, who also belonged to that Crown, afterwards rebelled. But it is not so: for none of the aforesaid states ever belonged to the kingdom of Mexico, as appears from the testimony of all the Indian historians and of all those Spanish writers who obtained information from them, such as Motolinía, Sahagún, and Torquemada. The king of Acolhuacan had always been an ally of the king of Mexico since the year 1424, but was never his subject. It is true that when the Spaniards arrived there, King Cacamatzin seemed to depend on Moctezuma his uncle; because, on account of the overbearing power of his brother Ixtlilxochitl, he needed the help of the Mexicans. The Spaniards afterwards saw Cacamatzin come to meet them as ambassador of the king of Mexico, and even serve this man as an arm-bearer. They saw also that he was taken prisoner to Mexico by order of Moctezuma. All this makes the error of the Spaniards excusable on many counts; but it is certain that those demonstrations made by Cacamatzin to Moctezuma were not services of a vassal toward his king, but courtesies of a nephew toward his uncle; and that Moctezuma, in having him seized to please the Spaniards, arrogated to himself an authority that did not belong to him, and did that king a most grievous wrong, for which he afterwards had cause to repent. As for the king of Tlacopan, it is true that he was created king by the king of Mexico; but there was granted to him perfect dominion and full sovereignty in his states, on the sole condition of being the perpetual ally of the Mexicans and of giving them aid with his troops whenever they should need it. The king of Michoacán and the republic of Tlaxcala were always rivals and capital enemies of the Mexicans, and there is no record that either state was ever subject to the Crown of Mexico.

> La cagion di tali errori fi è, perchè erano persuafi questi Autori, che in Anahuac non v' era altro Sovrano che quello di Messico; che i Re di Acolhuacan , e di Tlacopan Lira sudditi di lui, e che i Michuacaneli, ed i Tiascalle(i apparte» nenti anch' eslli a quella Corona, fi fossero poi ribellai. Ma non è così : poichè niuno de' sopraddetti Stati apparteone ma al regno di Messico , ficcome consta dalla deposizione di curti gli Storici Indiani, e di tutti quegli Scrittori - Spagnuoli , che da eflo loro presero informazione, come Motolinìa , Sahagun , e Torquemada, Il Re d' Acolhuacan era [tato sempre allearo di teri di Messico infin dall’ anno 1424; ma non ne fu mai uddito. E' vero, che quando vi giunlero gli Spagnuoli , il Re Cacamatzin pareva dipendere da Motezuma suo zio; perchè a cagione della prepotenza del suo fratello Ixtlilxochicl ab» bisognava dell'ajuto de' Messicani. Gli Spagnuoli poi videro Cacamatzin venir loro incontro, come Ambasciatore del Re di Messico, e servire anche a costui da bracciere . Videro altresì condurlo prigione a Messico per ordine di Motezuma . Tutto ciò rende scusabile per molti capi l' errore degli Spagnuoli ;ma egli è certo, che quelle dimostrazioni fatte da Cacamarzin a Motezuma noa erano servizj di vaffallo verso il suo Re, ma oflequj di Nipote verso il suo Zio: e che Motezuma nel farlo pigliare per compiacere agli Spagnuoli s' arrogàò quell' autorità , che non gli conveniva, e fece a quel Re ua gravissimo torto, del qual. ebbe poi a pentirsi, Quanto al Re di Tlacopan è vero, che egli fu creato Re dal Re di Messico; ma gli fu accordato un perfetto dominio e piena sovranicà ne’ suoi Seacri colla sola condizione d' eslere perperno alleato de' Messicani , e di dar loro ajuto colle sue truppe, ogni volta che bilognafie, Il Re di Michuacan, e la Repubblica di Tlascalla furono mai sempre rivali, e nemici capitali de' Messicani , e non v' è m& moria, che nè l'uno, nè l'altro Stato fosle mai forcoposto al la Corona di Messico,

We must say the same of many other countries which were believed by the Spanish historians to be provinces of the Mexican empire. How was it possible that a nation which had been reduced to

> Lo stesso dobbiamo dire di molri altri paesi , che dagli Storici Spagnuoli furoa creduti provincie dell' lmperio meslicano, Come era possibile, che una Nazione, che era ridotta ad [p. 267] una sola Città sotto il dominio de’ Tepanechi , soggiogafse in meno d’ un secolo tanti Popoli, quanti ve n'erano dall' Istmo di Panamà fino alla California? Tutto ciò, che in realtà fecero i Meslicani, quantunque aflai meno di quello, che dicono i suddetti Autori, fu una cosa in vero sorprendente, e non sarebbe credibile la rapidità delle loro conquiste, se non- venisse confermata con tanti innegabili documenti. Del resto nè dalla narrazione degli Storici Indiani , nè dall’ enumerazione degli Stati conquistati da' Re di Messico, che trovasi nella Raccolta di Mendoza, nè dalla matricola delle Città tributarie, esposta nella medesima Raccolta , fi può aver niun fondamento da confermare quell’ arbitraria ampliazione de’ Dominj messicani ; anzi consta tutto il contrario dal ragguaglio di Bernal Diaz . Questi nel cap. 93. della sua Storia dice cos): ,, Avea il gran Mo- » tezuma molci presidj, è gente di guerra nelle frontiere de’ » suoi Stati, Uno ne avea in Soconusco per difendersi da Gua- » timala, e da Chiapa: un altro per difendersi da' Pauuchesi tra » Tuzapan e quel luogo, che noi appelliamo Almerta: un altro » in Coarzacualco , e un altro in Michuacao. ,, (a)

a [p. 267] single city under the dominion of the Tepanecs should subjugate in less than a century as many peoples as there were from the Isthmus of Panama to California? All that the Mexicans actually did, although far less than what the aforesaid authors say, was a truly astonishing thing, and the rapidity of their conquests would not be credible if it were not confirmed by so many undeniable documents. For the rest, neither from the narrative of the Indian historians, nor from the enumeration of the states conquered by the kings of Mexico that is found in the Collection of Mendoza, nor from the register of the tributary cities set out in the same Collection, can any foundation be had for confirming that arbitrary enlargement of the Mexican dominions; on the contrary, the very opposite is established by the account of Bernal Díaz. He says thus in ch. 93 of his History: “The great Moctezuma had many garrisons and men of war on the frontiers of his states. He had one in Soconusco to defend himself against Guatemala and Chiapas; another to defend himself against the people of Pánuco, between Tuzapan and that place which we call Almería; another in Coatzacoalcos, and another in Michoacán.” (a)

> Siam dunque ficuri imprima, che i Dominj messicani non si stendevano verso Sgrocco di la da Xoconochco , e che niuna di tutte quelle Provincie, che oggidì son comprese nelle tre Dioceh di Guatimala, di Nicarazua, e di Honduras apparreneva all' Imperio Meslicano., Nel libro 4. della Storia abbiam detto , che Tlilrororl, celebre General Meslicano, negli ultimi anni del Re Ahuitzorl portò le sue armi vittoriose fino a Quauhtemallan : ma quivi ancora aggiugniamo, chs non fi sa, che restasle allora quel paese sortomefslo alla Corona di Messico: ans zi dalla Storia appare rutro l'opposto. We are certain, then, in the first place, that the Mexican dominions did not extend toward the southeast beyond Soconusco, and that none of all those provinces which are today included in the three dioceses of Guatemala, Nicaragua, and Honduras belonged to the Mexican empire. In the fourth book of our History we said that Tliltototl, a celebrated Mexican general, in the last years of King Ahuitzotl carried his victorious arms as far as Cuauhtemallan; but here too we add that it is not known that that country then remained subject to the Crown of Mexico: on the contrary, history shows quite the opposite. Torquemada, in bk. 2, ch. 81, makes mention of the Conquest of Nicaragua by the Mexicans; but the very same writer who in the cited place affirms it of a Mexican army in the time of Moctezuma II attributes it, in bk. 3, ch. 10, to a colony that went out many years earlier by order of the

The same Bernal Díaz, both in the place cited and in ch. 166, affirms expressly that the Chiapanecs were never subjugated by the Mexicans; but this cannot be understood of the whole country of the Chiapanecs, but only of one part of it; for we know from Remesal, the chronicler of that province, that the Mexicans had a garrison in Tzinacantlan, and it is established by the Register of the tributes that Tochtlan, (*) and other cities of that country, were tributary to the Mexicans.

> Lo stesso Bernal Diaz tanto nel luogo citato, quanto nel cap. 166. afferma espreflamente , che i Chiapanesi non furono mai soggiogati da' Messicani; ma ciò non può intendersi di rutto il paele de' Chiapaneh , ma d' una sola parte; poichè sappiamo dal Remezal, Cronichista di quella Provincia, che i Messicani avtano presidio in Tzinacantla , e ci consta dalla Marricola de’ rributi, che Tochelan, (*) ed altre Città di quel pacse erano tri» butarie de' Messicani .

On the northeast the Mexicans did not advance beyond Tuzapan, as is established by the cited passage of Bernal Díaz; and we know for certain that the Panucans were never subjected to the Mexicans. On the east we have fixed the boundaries at the river Coatzacoalcos. Bernal Díaz says that the country of Coatzacoalcos was not a province of Mexico; on the other hand we find among the tributary cities of that Crown Tochtlan, Michapan, and other places of the aforesaid province. We are therefore persuaded that the Mexicans possessed all that lay to the west of the river Coatzacoalcos, but not what lay to the east, and that that river was on that side the limit of their empire. Toward the north it was bounded by the country of the Huastecs, never subjugated by the Mexicans. Toward the northeast the empire did not extend beyond the province of Tula: all that great tract of land which lay beyond that province was occupied by the barbarous Otomis and Chichimecs, who had no settled population and obeyed no sovereign. On the west it is known that the empire ended at Tlaximaloyan, the frontier of the kingdom of Michoacán; but on the coastal lowlands it reached as far as the western extremity of the province of Colima, and no farther. In the Catalogue of the tributary cities are seen Colima and other places of that province, and none of those which are

[p. 269] beyond it; nor is any mention of them made in the history of Mexico. The Mexicans had nothing to do with California, nor could they expect any advantage from the conquest of a country so distant, the most depopulated and the most wretched in the world. If that arid and rocky peninsula had ever been a province of the Mexican empire, some settlements would have been found there; but it is certain that not even a single house was found there, nor any remnant or trace of one. Finally, on the south the Mexicans had taken possession of all those great states that lay from the Valley of Mexico to the Pacific sea. Now, the Mexican coastal lowlands stretching from Soconusco to Colima, there precisely was the greatest length of their dominions.

Dr. Robertson says that “the territories belonging to the chiefs of Tezeuco and Tacuba, were hardly inferior in extent to those of the Mexican monarch.” (b) But this is too far from the truth, and contrary also to what all the historians of Mexico say about it. The kingdom of Texcoco, or rather of Acolhuacan, was bounded on the west partly by the lake of Texcoco and partly by Zumpango and other Mexican states, and on the east by the dominions of Tlaxcala; so that it could not have more than sixty miles from west to east; on the south it was bounded by the state of Chalco, which also belonged to Mexico, and on the north by the independent country of the Huastecs. Now from the frontier of this country to that of Chalco there are about two hundred miles. Here is the whole extent of the kingdom of Acolhuacan, which does not make even the eighth part of that of the Mexican dominions. The states of the petty king of Tlacopan, or Tacuba, were so small that they did not deserve the name of kingdom; for from the Mexican lake on the east to the frontier of Michoacán on the west there were not more than eighty miles, nor more than fifty from the Valley of Toluca on the south to the country of the Otomis on the north. Therefore the comparison

> La Repubblica di Tlascalla, circondata dai Dominj messicani e tezcucani, e dagli Stati d' Huexorzinco, e di Cholulla , era sì ristretta, che da levante a ponente appena avea miglia cioquanta, e da mezzogiorno a tramontana trenta in cicca . Non ho trovato verun Autore, che dia maggior estensione a quello Stato, se non Cortés, il qual dice, che i Domioj di Tlascalla aveano leghe novanta di circuito; ma questo è un manifesto sbaglio.

The republic of Tlaxcala, surrounded by the Mexican and Texcocan dominions, and by the states of Huexotzinco and of Cholula, was so confined that from east to west it had scarcely fifty miles, and from south to north about thirty. I have found no author who gives greater extension to that state, except Cortés, who says that the dominions of Tlaxcala had ninety leagues of circuit; but this is a manifest mistake.

> Intorno al regno di Michuacan nefsuno, che io sappia, ne ha accennati tutti gli antichi confini, fuorchè il Cav. Botrurini . Questo Autore dice, che l'estensione di quel regno, dalla Valle d' Ixilahuacan preflo a -Toloccao fino al mar paci. fico, era di leghe cencinquanta, e da Zacatollan fino a Xichù di leghe centoseffanta: è che nei Domin} Michuacanesi erano comprese le Provincie di Zacarollan, di Coliman, e quella , che gli Spagnuoli appellarono Provincia d'’ Avalos , fituata a maestro di quella di Coliman, Ma in tutto ciò s& ingannò il citato Cavaliere; poichè si sa Gicuramente, che il regno di Michuacan non aveva i suoi confini in Ixtilahuacan, -ma in Tlaximalojan, fin dove arrivavano i Dominj messicani . Si fa dal- Ia matricola dei tributi, che. le provincie marittime di Zacatollan, e di Coliman appartenevano a Messico. Finalmente non poteano i Michuacanesi ampliare i suoi Dominj fino a Xichù senza soggiogar prima i barbari Cicimechi , che occupavano quella contrada; ma di questi sappiamo, che non furono soggiogati, che dagli Spagnuoli molti anni dopo la conquista di Melsico, Non era dunque tanto grand@ il regno di Michuacan , quanto credette il Cav. Boturini . La sua estensione non comprendeva, che tre gradi in circa di longitudine, e poco più di due di latitudine .

Concerning the kingdom of Michoacán, none, so far as I know, has indicated all the ancient boundaries, except the Chevalier Boturini. This author says that the extent of that kingdom, from the Valley of Ixtlahuacan near Toluca to the Pacific sea, was a hundred and fifty leagues, and from Zacatollan to Xichú a hundred and sixty; and that in the Michoacán dominions were included the provinces of Zacatollan and of Colima, and that which the Spaniards called the Province of Ávalos, situated to the northwest of that of Colima. But in all this the cited Chevalier was mistaken; for it is known for certain that the kingdom of Michoacán had its boundaries not in Ixtlahuacan but in Tlaximaloyan, which was as far as the Mexican dominions reached. It is known from the register of the tributes that the maritime provinces of Zacatollan and of Colima belonged to Mexico. Finally, the Michoacans could not extend their dominions as far as Xichú without first subjugating the barbarous Chichimecs who occupied that country; but of these we know that they were not subjugated until many years after the conquest of Mexico, and then only by the Spaniards. The kingdom of Michoacán was not, therefore, as great as the Chevalier Boturini believed. Its extent comprised only about three degrees of longitude, and a little more than two of latitude.

> Quanto finora abbiam detto giova a dimostrare l' esattezza della nostra descrizione, e delle nostre carte geografiche intorno ai confini di quei regni, fondata su la stessa Storia, su la matricola dei criburi, .e- su la testimonianza degli Storici an-

All that we have said so far serves to demonstrate the accuracy of our description, and of our geographical maps, concerning the boundaries of those kingdoms, founded on the history itself, on the register of the tributes, and on the testimony of the ancient historians.

> Sopra la Popolazione di Anabuac.

§ II.

> Non' pretendo di ragionar quì della popolazione di tutta l'America; perchè ral argomento farebbe troppo vasto, ed alieno altresì dal mio proposito, ma solamente di quella del Mesfico che appartiene alla mia Storia, Nell' America vi erano, e vi sono dei paesi molto popolati, e vi sono ancora dei vaiti deserti: e non meno s'allontanano dal vero coloro, che s'im+ maginano i paesi del nuovo Mondo tanto popolari , quanto quelli della China, che quegli alcri che gli credono taoto spo. polati, quanto quelli dell’ Africa . Tanto incerto è il calcolo del P. Riccioli, quanto quelli di Susmilch, e del Sig. de Paw. Il P. Riccioti conta nell’ America trecento milioni d' abitatori, Gli Aritmetrtici politici non ve ne contano, dice il Sig. de Paw, più di cenato : Susmilch in un luogo della sua opera vi com» puta cento, e in un altro cencinquanta milioni. Il Sig. de P., 1l qual rapporta rutti questi calcoli , dice, che non vi sono di veri Americani, che da trenta in quaranta milioni, Ma rutti questi calcoli sono, torno a dire, incertisflimi, e non lì appoggiano a verun fondamento; imperocchè se non fi sa finora, neppure a un diprefso la popolazione di quei paesi , nei quali s\onofi stabiliti gli Europei, come quelli del Messico, di Guatimala , del Perù, del Quito , di Terraferma , del Chile ec. chi sarà capace d' indovinare il numero degli abitatori delle Immense contrade niente o poco conosciute dagli Europei, co» me quelle che sono a tramontana e a maestro della Coahuila , del nuovo Metflico, della California , e del fiume Colorado , o sia roflo nell’ America Settentrionale ? Chi porrà numerar gli abitatori del nuovo Monda ,. mentre non lì sa, nè fi può sapere neppur il numero delle provincie, e delle Nazioni, che vi fi contengono? Lasciando dunque fiffatri calcoli, i quali non pofono intraprendersi senza temerità, ci contenteremo d' esaminare ciò , che dicono il Sig. de law, e il Dou. Robertson su la popolazione del Melslico,

On the Population of Anahuac.

I do not intend to discuss here the population of all America, because such a subject would be too vast and moreover foreign to my purpose, but only that of Mexico, which belongs to my History. In America there were, and are, very populous countries, and there are also vast deserts; and those who imagine the countries of the New World to be as populous as those of China stray no less from the truth than those others who believe them to be as depopulated as those of Africa. The calculation of Father Riccioli is as uncertain as those of Süssmilch and of M. de Pauw. Father Riccioli counts three hundred millions of inhabitants in America. The political arithmeticians, says M. de Pauw, count no more than a hundred there; Süssmilch in one place of his work reckons a hundred millions, and in another a hundred and fifty. M. de P., who reports all these calculations, says that there are no more than thirty to forty millions of true Americans. But all these calculations are, I repeat, extremely uncertain, and rest on no foundation; for if the population is not known even approximately in those countries in which the Europeans have established themselves, such as Mexico, Guatemala, Peru, Quito, Tierra Firme, Chile, etc., who will be capable of guessing the number of the inhabitants of the immense regions little or not at all known to the Europeans, such as those to the north and northwest of Coahuila, of New Mexico, of California, and of the river Colorado, or Red River, in North America? Who can count the inhabitants of the New World, when it is not known, nor can it be known, even how many provinces and nations are contained in it? Leaving aside, then, such calculations, which cannot be undertaken without rashness, we shall content ourselves with examining what M. de Pauw and Dr. Robertson say on the population of Mexico.

The

[p. 272]

> ai DISSERTAZIONE VI.

“The population of Mexico and of Peru,” says M. de Pauw, “has undoubtedly been exaggerated by the Spanish writers, accustomed to paint objects in immoderate proportions. Three years after the conquest of Mexico the Spaniards had need to bring people there from the Lucayan islands, and afterward from the coasts of Africa, in order to people the kingdom of Mexico. If this monarchy contained thirty millions of inhabitants in 1518, why was it depopulated in 1521?” I shall never deny that among the Spanish writers there have been some exaggerators, just as there have been among the Prussians, the French, the English, and the other peoples; for the immoderate desire to magnify the things one describes is a passion quite common to all the nations of the world, and M. de P. has certainly not been preserved from it, as he makes plain throughout his work; but to charge all the Spaniards indiscriminately with it is to do a very grave wrong to that nation, which has, like all the others, both good and bad. For my part, at least, after reading the best historians of the civilized nations of Europe, I have not found two who seem to me comparable in truthfulness (c) with the two Spaniards Mariana and Acosta, who are therefore held in the highest esteem, and justly praised even by the enemies of their nation and of their religion. Among the early historians of Mexico there have been some, such as Acosta, Bernal Díaz, and Cortés himself, whose truthfulness cannot be doubted. But even if none of those authors had been endowed with the qualities required to merit our belief, the uniformity of their testimonies would nevertheless form a most effective argument in favor of the truth of their account. Authors who are little truthful never agree with one another, except when they copy one from another; but this did not happen with our historians, who, intent solely on writing what they had seen with their own eyes, or had found true through their inquiries, did not trouble themselves about what

Let us see, then, what the early Spanish writers say of the population of Mexico. They all agree in affirming that those countries were very populous, that there were very many great cities and countless towns and villages; that to the markets of the populous cities many thousands of merchants flocked; that they put numerous armies into the field, etc. Cortés in his letters to Charles V, the Anonymous Conqueror in his Relation, Alonso de Ojeda and Alonso de Mata in their memoirs, Monsignor de las Casas in the work that bears the title On the Destruction of the Indies, Bernal Díaz in his History, Motolinía, Sahagún, and Mendieta in their writings, all eyewitnesses of the ancient population of Mexico; Herrera, Gómara, Acosta, Torquemada, and Martínez, all are agreed concerning the great population of those countries. M. de Pauw cannot allege to me a single early author who does not confirm it with his testimony, whereas I can cite to him several writers who make no mention of that superstitious rite of the Mexicans, such as Cortés, Bernal Díaz, and the Anonymous Conqueror, the three oldest Spanish historians of Mexico. Nevertheless M. de Pauw affirms that one cannot doubt that rite by reason of the unanimous testimony of the other Spaniards: why, then, will he wish to doubt the great population

But if the population of Mexico was so great in 1518, why in 1521 was it necessary to bring people there from the Lucayan Islands, and afterward from the coasts of Africa, to people it? I confess candidly that I cannot read this objection of M. de P. without indignation, seeing such boldness in affirming what is absolutely false and wholly contrary to the account of the authors. Where has M. de P. ever read that in order to people Mexico it was necessary to transport people there from the Lucayas? I challenge him to produce me a single author who says so; on the contrary, from many writers we know quite the opposite. We know from the chronicler Herrera and from other writers that from 1493, the year in which the Spaniards established themselves on the island of Santo Domingo, until 1496, a third of the inhabitants of that great island perished through the war and through other very grave hardships. (e) In 1507 there remained no more than a tenth part of the Indians who had been there in 1493, as Monsignor de las Casas, an eyewitness, attests; (f) and from then on the population of that island diminished to such a degree that in 1540 scarcely two hundred Indians were left there. For this reason, from the beginning of the sixteenth century the Spaniards began to draw thousands of Indians from the Lucayas to replenish the population of Hispaniola; but as these too perished, they began, before the conquest of Mexico, to bring settlers there from Tierra Firme and from other countries of the American continent, as these were discovered. We know from a letter written to the Council of the Indies by the first bishop of Mexico, and cited to the Emperor Charles V by Monsignor de las Casas, that the cruel Nuño de Guzmán, governor of Pánuco, sent from there twenty-eight ships laden with enslaved Indians to be sold in the islands; so that it is so far from the truth that the Spaniards

All that we say here is established no less by the testimony of the same Monsignor de las Casas in the work entitled The Suppliant Indian Slave, and in others, than by that of the chronicler Herrera in his Decades. [p. 275] brought people from the islands to people the continent of North America that, on the contrary, they drew people from the latter to people the islands, as the two authors cited say expressly, and others as well. It is true indeed that after the conquest of Mexico slaves were transported there from Africa; not, however, because there was need of settlers, but because the Spaniards wished to employ them in the making of sugar and in the labor of the mines, to which they could not compel the Americans, on account of the laws then recently published. It is therefore false, and contrary to the deposition of the aforesaid authors, that Mexico was so depopulated three years after the conquest that it was necessary to bring people there from the Lucayas and from Africa to people it again; on the contrary, we are certain that from the countries subject to the king of Mexico and to the republic of Tlaxcala colonies were sent, some years after the conquest, to people other countries, such as Zacatecas, San Luis Potosí, Saltillo, etc.

But let us see what those early writers say in particular of the population of Mexico. I do not know that any of them has had the boldness to state the number of the inhabitants of the Mexican empire: whether it contained thirty millions or not could be known only to the kings of Mexico and to their ministers; and although the Spaniards could have informed themselves of it from them, none, so far as I know, did so. What several of those authors affirmed is that among the feudatories of the crown of Mexico there were thirty, each of whom had about a hundred thousand subjects, and three thousand other lords who had a smaller number of vassals. (g) Laurentius Surius affirms (h) that this is established by documents which were in the royal archive of Charles V. Cortés, in his first letter to the same emperor, says to him thus: “So great is the multitude of inhabitants in these countries that there is not even a palm of

The Valley of Mexico, although the lakes occupied a great part of it, was at least as populous as the most populous country of Europe. There were forty considerable cities, named by us elsewhere and mentioned also by the early writers; the other inhabited places in it were innumerable, and their names would be set down here by us, if we did not fear to weary our readers. The most truthful Bernal Díaz, describing in ch. 88 of his History what they saw on their way through the Valley of Mexico toward the capital, says thus: “When we saw things so marvelous, we did not know what to say to ourselves, nor whether what we had before our eyes was real; for we saw so many great cities standing on dry land, and many others in the lake, and everything full of boats.” He says, besides, that some of his fellow soldiers, exceedingly amazed at seeing so many and such fine settlements, doubted whether what they saw was dreams, or things of enchantment. This and many other candid confessions of Bernal Díaz suffice to answer Dr. Robertson, who made use of certain words of that author, misunderstood by him, to make his readers believe that the population of Mexico was not as great as is claimed.

Concerning the population of the ancient capital there is a great variety of opinions; nor can it be otherwise, whenever one wishes to judge by eye the population of a great city; but

> Intorno alla. popolazione dell’antica Capitale v’ è una gram varìetà. di pareri : nè può avvenire altrimenti, qualora f vuol giudicare ad. occhio della popolazione d° una grau città. ; ma [p. 277] tutti gli Scrittori, che la videro, o furono informati da testi monj oculari , son d'acordo nel dire, che efla era affai grande. Il Cronichista Herrera dice (5), che era grande al doppio di Mihno: Cortès afferma, che era tanto grande come Siviglia , e Cordova : (&) Lorenzo Surio (1) citando certi documenti, che erano nell’ Archivio Reale di Carlo V.,, dice, che la popolazione di Messico fi componeva di 130, mila cale : Torquemada , tenendo dietro a Sahagun , è ad alcuni Storici Indiani, vì numera 120. mila case, (m) è soggiugne, che in ciascheduna cala v' erano da quattro in dieci abitatori . Il Conquistatore Anonimo ne parla così: ,, Può avere questa Città di Temistican » più di due leghe e mezza, 0 preslo a tre, poco più o me- » no di circuito : la maggior parte di coloro, che l'hanno ve- » duta , giudica , che vi fieno più di feflanta mila fuochi, e » piuttosto più, che meno. ,, Questo calcolo adottato da Gomara, e da Herrera mi par quello, che più s' accosta al vero, atteso la estensione della città, e la maniera d'abitar di quelle penti.

[p. 277] all the writers who saw it, or were informed by eyewitnesses, are agreed in saying that it was very large. The chronicler Herrera says (i) that it was twice as large as Milan; Cortés affirms that it was as large as Seville and Córdoba; (k) Laurentius Surius (l), citing certain documents that were in the royal archive of Charles V, says that the population of Mexico City was made up of 130,000 houses; Torquemada, following Sahagún and some Indian historians, counts 120,000 houses there, (m) and adds that in each house there were from four to ten inhabitants. The Anonymous Conqueror speaks of it thus: “This city of Tenochtitlan may have more than two leagues and a half, or nearly three, more or less, of circuit; most of those who have seen it judge that there are more than sixty thousand hearths in it, and rather more than less.” This calculation, adopted by Gómara and by Herrera, seems to me the one that comes nearest to the truth, considering the extent of the city and the manner in which those people lived.

But all this is contradicted by M. de Pauw. He calls “excessive and extravagant the description given us of this American city, which contained, according to some authors, seventy thousand houses in the time of Moctezuma II; so that it would then have had three hundred and fifty thousand inhabitants, whereas it is notorious that the city of Mexico, considerably enlarged under the dominion of the Spaniards, has at present no more than sixty thousand inhabitants, including twenty thousand Blacks and Mulattoes.” (n) Here is another passage of the Recherches philosophiques that will make the Mexicans laugh. Let him know, then, that Mexico is the most populous city of all those that the Catholic King has in his vast dominions. From the list of births and deaths in Madrid and in Mexico, published in the journals of each of the two cities, it appears that the number of the inhabitants of Madrid is more than a quarter less than that of Mexico: (o) that is, if Madrid, for example, has 160,000 inhabitants, Mexico without doubt has more than 200,000. There has been a great diversity of opinions concerning the number of souls of the modern city of Mexico, as there was concerning the ancient one, and as there likewise is concerning other cities of the first rank; (p) but the count having been made in these last years with greater diligence, both by the parish priests and by the magistrates, it has been found that the inhabitants of that capital exceed two hundred thousand, although the exact amount of the excess cannot be known. One can form some idea of the population

(o) It is certain that in proportion to the excess of one city over another in the number of births and deaths, there will also be the excess in the number of inhabitants; and there is no surer means of finding approximately the number of inhabitants of a very large city than that of knowing the number of births and deaths in it, provided that the precautions required for this are employed.

(p) It is enough to know the diversity of opinions among modern writers concerning the population of Paris: one counts five hundred thousand inhabitants there, another seven hundred thousand, another a million. In the same way the opinions concerning modern Mexico have been diverse. Lionel Wafer, a celebrated English traveler of the last century, believed that there were three hundred thousand inhabitants there; to the traveler Gemelli there seemed to be a hundred thousand, and to the missionary Tallandier sixty thousand; a very recent European traveler, who went to Mexico after traveling through Europe and the principal countries of Asia, was of the opinion that there were no fewer than a million and a half inhabitants. The latter erred by excess, and Tallandier by defect. [p. 279] of that city from the quantity of pulque (q) and of tobacco that is consumed there daily. (r) Every day more than six thousand arrobas of pulque enter it, that is, a hundred and ninety thousand Roman pounds; in the year 1774 there entered 2,214,294½ arrobas, that is, more than seventy-three millions of Roman pounds; but this computation does not include what is introduced by contraband, nor what the exempt Indians sell in the principal square of the city. This so great a quantity of pulque is consumed almost entirely by the Indians alone and the Mulattoes, whose number is exceeded by that of the white Europeans and Creoles, among whom there are not many who habitually use that drink. The duty on it amounts annually, in the capital alone, to about two hundred and eighty thousand scudi (pesos fuertes). The consumption of smoking tobacco in that capital amounts every day to about 1250 scudi, which in a year makes the sum of four hundred and fifty thousand scudi and more. But it must be known that among the Indians those who use tobacco are rare; among the Creoles and the Europeans there are very many who do not use it, and among the Mulattoes some. Now who will wish to give more credit to the calculation of M. de Pauw than to the very registers of that capital, and to esteem more highly the judgment of a modern Prussian so extravagant concerning the ancient population of that court than that of so many early writers who saw it with their own eyes?

Torquemada, following Sahagún and the accounts of the Indians, affirms that the population of those four cities comprised a hundred and forty thousand houses; and if we wished to take half from that number, a very large population would nonetheless remain. No historian has told us how great the population of the court of Tlacopan was, although all affirm that it was considerable. Of that of Xochimilco we know that it was the largest of all after the courts. Of Iztapalapa Cortés affirms that it had from twelve to fifteen thousand hearths; of Mixcoac he says that it had about six thousand, of Huitzilopochco from four to five thousand, of Acolman and of Otompan four thousand each, and of Mexicaltzinco three thousand. Chalco, Azcapotzalco, Coyoacan, and Cuauhtitlan were incomparably larger than these last cities. All these, and very many other settlements, were comprised within the Valley of Mexico alone; the sight of them caused no less admiration than fear in the conquerors when they first beheld that delightful valley from the summits of the mountains. The same befell them when they saw the population of Tlaxcala. Cortés in his letter to Charles V speaks thus of that city: “It is so large and marvelous that, although I pass over much of what I could say of it, the little that I shall say, I believe, will be incredible; for it is much larger and more populous than Granada was when it was taken from the Moors, much stronger, with such good buildings, and much better supplied with everything.”

The Anonymous Conqueror speaks of it likewise: “There are,” he says, “great cities, and among others that of Tlaxcala, which in some respects resembles Granada, and in others Segovia; but it is more populous than any of them.” Of Tzompantzinco, a city of that republic, Cortés affirms, (s) that a count having been made there by his order, more than twenty thousand houses were counted in it. Of Huejotlipan, a place likewise of the same republic, he says that it had from three to four thousand

The great population of those countries can no less be shown by the innumerable gatherings that were seen in the markets, by the very numerous armies that were raised whenever there was need, and by the astonishing number of baptisms that took place after the conquest. Concerning the gatherings in the markets and the armies we have said enough in the History, on the authority of many eyewitnesses. It might be suspected that the conquerors had exaggerated the number of the Indian troops in order to make their conquests more glorious, but this could be done by them in speaking of the enemy troops, not however in counting the troops confederated with them; for the more the number of these was increased, the less difficult and the less glorious their conquests must have appeared. Yet the conqueror Ojeda counted a hundred and fifty thousand men of allied troops from Tlaxcala, Cholula, Tepeyacac, and Huexotzinco in the review that was held at Tlaxcala in order to go and lay siege to Mexico. Cortés himself affirms that the allied troops who accompanied him to the war of Cuauhquechollan exceeded a hundred thousand, and that those who aided him in the siege of the capital exceeded two hundred thousand by far. On the other hand the besieged were so many that, although more than a hundred and fifty thousand of them died during the siege, as we have said in the History, nevertheless when that capital was taken by the Spaniards and all the Mexicans were ordered to leave it, the three streets were seen full for three days and three nights continuously of the people who were leaving it to take refuge in other places, as Bernal Díaz, an eyewitness, attests. As for the number of baptisms, we are sure

Nn [p. 282] by the testimony of those same apostolic religious who employed themselves in the conversion of those peoples, that the children and adults baptized there by the Franciscan Fathers alone (t) from the year 1524 until 1540 were more than six millions; most of whom were inhabitants of the Valley of Mexico and of the surrounding provinces. Now in this number are not included those who were baptized by the priests, by the Dominicans, and by the Augustinians, among whom and the Franciscans that most abundant harvest was then divided; and besides, it is certain that those Indians were innumerable who remained obstinate in their heathenism, or did not receive the Christian faith until many years afterward. We know, moreover, from the noisy controversies stirred up there by some religious and referred to the Supreme Pontiff Paul III, that on account of the extraordinary and never before seen multitude of catechumens the missionaries were compelled to omit certain ceremonies of baptism, and among others that of the saliva, since from so much spitting their mouths, tongues, and throats became dry.

Since the discovery of Mexico the number of the Indians has been continually diminishing. Besides the countless thousands who perished in the first contagion of smallpox brought there in 1520, and in the war of the Spaniards, in the epidemic of 1545 eight hundred thousand died, and in that of 1576 more than two millions in the dioceses of Mexico, Puebla, Michoacán, and Oaxaca alone; which was learned from the list of the dead of every parish presented to the viceroy. Nevertheless the chronicler Herrera, who wrote toward the end of the sixteenth century, reports on the authority of authentic documents sent to him by the viceroy of Mexico that in the dioceses of Puebla and of Oaxaca alone, and in those provinces of the diocese of Mexico that were adjacent to the capital, 655 principal places of Indians were then counted, and innumerable other smaller ones dependent on them:

(u) But it must be known that among the tributaries are not included the nobles, nor the Tlaxcalans, nor other Indians of those who aided the Spaniards in the Conquest; for, in regard to their birth or to the services rendered to the conquerors, they were exempt from tribute. Herrera himself, very well instructed on this subject, affirms that at that time there were counted in the capital four thousand families of Spaniards and thirty thousand houses of Indians. From then on the number of the Indians went on continually diminishing, and that of the Spaniards, or Whites, increasing.

M. de P. will reply, according to his style, that all the documents we have adduced to demonstrate the great population of Mexico are worth less than nothing, because they were taken from rude and wicked soldiers, or from ignorant and superstitious religious; but even if all the writers we have cited were such, which is altogether false, their testimony would nevertheless be of great weight on account of their uniformity. Who, moreover, can be persuaded that Cortés and the royal officers who subscribed his letters with him dared to deceive their kings, when they could so easily be contradicted by so many hundreds of witnesses and by not a few enemies? Would it ever be possible that so many writers, Spaniards as well as Indians, should all agree in exaggerating the population of those countries, and that among them there should not be a single one who respected posterity? Of the truthfulness of the first missionaries one cannot doubt. They were men of exemplary life and of great learning, chosen from among many to plant the Gospel in that New World: some of them had been lecturers in the most celebrated universities of Europe, had obtained the first offices in their Order, and had deserved the favor and confidence of the Emperor Charles V. Those honors which they renounced in Europe, and those which they did not accept in America (x), clearly show

(x) Among the first fifteen Franciscan missionaries there were six who, having been named bishops by Charles V, did not accept that dignity. [p. 284] their disinterested zeal; their voluntary and austere poverty, their continual converse with God, their unspeakable labors in so many journeys, so long and so difficult, made on foot and without provisions, and in so many such toilsome ministries, and above all their exceptional charity toward those afflicted nations, full of compassion and gentleness, will render their memory forever venerable in that kingdom, in spite of M. de P. and of any other malicious writer for whom it suffices to recognize in an author the quality of religious in order to despise and insult him. In the writings of those immortal men there is seen such a character of truthfulness as to permit no suspicion against the truth of their accounts. It is true that, in the judgment of M. de P., they committed a great sin in burning, as superstitious, the greater part of the historical paintings of the Mexicans. I prize those paintings more than M. de P. does, and their loss grieves me far more; but I do not for that reason despise the authors of that deplorable fire, nor blame their memory; because the evil to which they were then led by a zeal too ardent and not well informed is not to be compared with the great good that they did there besides; and moreover they themselves sought to repair that loss by their works, especially Motolinía, Sahagún, Olmos, and Torquemada.

[p. 285] lived in society, that they had settlements many, large, and well ordered, and they name the cities seen by them (y); and those who have traveled through those regions two centuries and a half after the conquest have seen with their own eyes the aforesaid settlements in the very places indicated by those authors: so that either M. de P. persuades himself that those writers announced prophetically the future settlements, or he must confess that even then they were where they are at present. It is true that the Spaniards founded many settlements there, such as the cities of Puebla, Guadalajara, Valladolid, Veracruz, Celaya, Potosí, Córdoba, León, etc.; but the settlements founded by them within the bounds of the Mexican empire, in relation to those founded by the Indians, are not even in the proportion of one to a thousand. The Mexican names given to the settlements, which are preserved to this day, show clearly that it was not the Spaniards but the Indians who were their founders. Now that those places of which we make frequent mention in the History were not for the most part miserable villages, but cities and settlements large and well formed, like those of Europe, is established by the deposition of all those writers who saw them.

What we have adduced against M. de P. serves equally to refute Dr. Robertson, who, seeing so many witnesses contrary to his opinion, has recourse to a subterfuge entirely similar to that of the heat of imagination, of which he availed himself to deny credit to the Spanish writers concerning what they say of the excellence of the Mexican cast-metal work. Reasoning, then, on that wonder which the sight of the cities of Mexico caused the Spaniards, he says thus in bk. 7 of his History: “In the first fervour of their admiration, they compared Zempoalla, though a town only of the second or third size, to the cities of greatest note in their own country. When, afterwards, they visited in succession Tlascala, Cholula, Tacuba, Tezeuco, and Mexico itself, their amazement increased so much, that it led them to convey ideas of their magnitude and populousness bordering on what is incredible… For this reason, some considerable abatement ought to be made from their calculation of the number of inhabitants in the Mexican cities, and we may fix the standard of their population much lower than they have done.” So commands Robertson; but I am not disposed to obey him. If the Spaniards had written their histories, letters, and relations in the first fervor of their wonder, it might well then be suspected that astonishment had led them to exaggerate; but it did not happen so: Cortés, the oldest of those writers, did not write his first letter to Charles V until a year and a half after he had arrived in that country; the Anonymous Conqueror wrote some years after the conquest; Bernal Díaz after more than forty years of continual residence in those regions, and so the others. Is it possible that that first fervor of wonder should last one, twenty, and even forty years? But whence did their wonder arise? Let us hear it

[p. 287] from Dr. Robertson himself: “The Spaniards,” he says, “accustomed to this mode of habitation (of isolated huts) among all the savage tribes with which they were then acquainted, were astonished, on entering New Spain, to find the natives residing in towns of such extent as resembled those of Europe.” But Cortés and his companions, before going to Mexico, already knew that those peoples were not savage tribes and that their houses were not huts: having already heard from all those who a year earlier had made that voyage with Grijalva that there were fine settlements, furnished with houses well built of stone and lime, and with lofty towers, as Bernal Díaz, an eyewitness, attests. That was not, then, the cause of their wonder; but rather the real greatness and multitude of the cities which they saw there. “It is not surprising, then,” adds Robertson, “that Cortes and his companions, powerfully tempted to magnify, in order to exalt the merit of their own discoveries and conquests, should have been betrayed into this common error, and have raised their descriptions considerably above truth.” But Cortés was no fool, and saw well that to exaggerate the number of his allies, so far from exalting the merit, served to diminish the glory of his conquests. Yet he often confesses that he was aided in his conquests now by eighty, now by a hundred thousand, now by more than two hundred thousand men: and as these candid confessions make plain his truthfulness, so those so numerous armies demonstrate the great population of that country. Moreover Dr. Robertson supposes that whatever the Spanish authors wrote concerning the number of the houses of the Mexican cities was expressed by them only by conjecture and according to the judgment they formed by eye; but it did not happen so: for Cortés himself testifies in his first letter to the Emperor Charles V that he had caused a count to be made of the houses that were in the district of the republic of Tlaxcala, and had found more than a hundred and fifty thousand, and in the city of Tzompantzinco alone more than twenty thousand.

## Dissertation

[p. 288]

## D I S S E RTAT I O N V I I I 

## ON THE RELIGION OF THE MEXICANS

## I    have nothing to do in this dissertation, as in the others, with M.

> SU LA RELIGIONE DEI MESSICANI,

de Pauw; for he candidly acknowledges the resemblance that there is between the delusions of the Americans and those of other nations of the old continent in matters of religion. “Since the religious superstitions of the peoples of America,” he says, (a) “have had a sensible resemblance to those which the nations of the old continent have practiced, these absurdities have been spoken of only in order to make the comparison, and to show that, in spite of the diversity of climes, the weakness of the human mind has been constant and invariable.” If he had reasoned with the same judgment on other points, he would have spared us several disputes, and would have preserved his work from those grave and strong censures that some wise men of Europe itself have made of it. I, however, address this dissertation to those who, from ignorance of what has passed and is passing at present in the world, or from want of reflection, have made such an outcry in reading in the History of Mexico of the cruelty and superstition of those peoples, as if they were things never heard of among mortals. I shall therefore make their error plain, and shall demonstrate that the religion of the Mexicans was less superstitious, less indecent, less puerile, and less irrational than that of the most civilized nations of ancient Europe, and that examples of cruelty like theirs have been seen, and perhaps even more atrocious ones, among almost all the peoples of the world.

> On ho che fare in questa dissertazione , come nelle altre, col Sig. de PawW ; poichè egli ingenuamente riconosce la fomiglianza , che v'è tra i deliri degli Americani, e quelli d' altre Nazioni dell'antico Continente in materia di Religio- De + » Siccome le superstizioni religiose dei Popoli d’ America, » dice egli, («) hanno avuto una somiglianza sensibile con quel» » le, che hanno usato le Nazioni dell'antico Continente, 009 » 5'è parlato di questi sproposici, che per farne il paragone , € ” per dare a divedere, che malgrado della diversità dei climi, » la debolezza dello spirito umano è stara costante. ed Jovaria- » bile. ,, Se collo steslo giudizio avelle discorso in altri puati, ci avrebbe risparmiate parecchie cootese , ed avrebbs® preserva» ca la sua opera da quelle gravi e forti censure, che ne hanno fatte alcuni uomini faggi della medesima Europa . lo però indirizzo questa differtazione a coloro, che per ignoranza di quanro è passato, e passa presentemente al Mondo, o per mancanza di riflessione, hanno tanto schiamazzato in leggendo pella Storia del Messico la crudeltà , e la superstizione di quei Popoli, come se fossero cole non mai sentite tra i morrali . The system of natural religion depends principally on that idea which one has of the Deity. If the Supreme Being is conceived

(a) In the preface to the Recherches philosophiques. [p. 289] as a father full of goodness, whose providence watches over his creatures, love and respect will be seen in the religious practices. If, on the contrary, he is imagined as an inexorable tyrant, the worship will be bloodthirsty. If he is believed omnipotent, veneration will be directed to one alone; but if his power is judged to be restricted, the objects of worship cannot but be multiplied. If the holiness and perfection of his being are recognized, his protection will be sought with a pure and holy worship; but if he is reputed subject to the imperfections and vices of men, the religion itself will consecrate crimes.

Let us compare, then, the idea that the Mexicans had of their gods with that which the Greeks, the Romans, and other nations, from whom the latter learned religion, had of their deities, and we shall soon recognize the advantages of the Mexicans in this matter over those ancient nations. It is true that the Mexicans divided the power among various gods, imagining the jurisdiction of each to be restricted within certain limits. “I do not doubt,” said King Moctezuma to the conqueror Cortés in a conference on religion, “I do not doubt the goodness of the God whom you adore; but if he is good for Spain, our gods are likewise good for Mexico.”

“Our god Camaxtli,” the Tlaxcalans said to the same Cortés, “grants us victory over our enemies; our goddess Matlalcueye sends the rain necessary to our fields, and defends us from the inundations of the Zahuapan. To each of our gods we are indebted for a part of the happiness of our life;” but they never believed their gods so impotent as the Greeks and Romans did theirs. The Mexicans had no more than one deity, under the name of Centeotl, for the care of the countryside and of the sown fields, and although they were so fond of their children, they were content with a single god for their protection. The Romans, besides the goddess Ceres, employed in grain alone a great crowd of gods, (b) and in the care and

Thus, exclaims Saint Augustine here, (d) thus Forculus could not guard at once the doors, and the hinge, and the threshold. So paltry, in the judgment of the Romans, was the power of their gods! Romans show better the opinion they had of their gods than in those vices which they attributed to them. Their whole mythology is a long series of crimes; the whole life of their gods came down to grudges, vengeances, incests, adulteries, and other base passions, capable of disgracing even the vilest of men. Jove, that omnipotent father, that source of all things, that king of men and of gods, as the poets call him, shows himself at times disguised as a man to deal with Alcmena, at times as a satyr to enjoy Antiope, at times as a bull to carry off Europa, at times as a swan to abuse Leda, and at times as a shower of gold to corrupt Danae; at times he takes other forms to accomplish his guilty desires. Meanwhile the great goddess Juno, enraged with jealousy, knows nothing to do but to take vengeance on her faithless husband. Of this same stamp were the other immortal gods, especially the greater gods, or chosen, as they were called by them. Chosen, says St. Augustine, (f) for the superiority of their vices, not for the excellence of their virtues. And to tell the truth, what good examples could those nations find among their gods, who, while they boasted of teaching men virtue, consecrated nothing in their gods but vices? What merits had Leaena among the Greeks, and Lupa, Faula, and Flora among the Romans, to obtain apotheosis, if not that of having been famous courtesans? Hence it came about that various gods were put in charge of the most infamous and shameful offices. (g)

> Assai diversa da questa era l'idea, che aveano del lor Numi i Messicani. I Messicani onoravano le virtù, non i vizj, nelle loro Divinità: in Huirzilopochili la prodezza, in Cenreorl , in Tzaporlatenan , in Opochili, e 10 altri la beneficenza , è in Querzalcoarl la castità , la giustizia, e la prudenza. Benchè fingeflero Numi d' ambidue & fe{si, non gli muaritarono, nè gli credettero capaci di quei piaceri osceni , che sono stari tanto comuni negli Dzi Greci, e‘ Ro» mani . Very different from this was the idea that the Mexicans had of their gods. There is not to be found in all their mythology a single trace of those stupendous wickednesses with which those other nations defamed their gods. The Mexicans honored virtues, not vices, in their divinities: in Huitzilopochtli, prowess; in Centeotl, in Tzapotlatenan, in Opochtli, and in others, beneficence; and in Quetzalcoatl, chastity, justice, and prudence. Although they imagined gods of both sexes, they did not marry them off, nor did they think them capable of those obscene pleasures that have been so common among the Greek and Roman gods. The Mexicans supposed in them a supreme aversion to every sort of crime; hence their worship was directed to appeasing the wrath of the gods, provoked by the sins of men, and to winning their protection by repentance and by religious observances.

Wholly conformable to the idea of the gods were the rites used by those nations. Superstition was common to all; but that of the Mexicans was less, and less childish; one need only compare their auguries. The Mexican astrologers observed the signs or characters of the days for their marriages, for their journeys, etc., just as the European astrologers observed the position of the stars in order to foretell from it the fortunes of men. Both alike feared eclipses and comets, as forerunners of great calamity; for this superstition has been common to all the peoples of the world. All likewise were frightened on hearing the voice of the owl, or of some other such bird. These and other similar superstitions have been general, and are even today only too common among the common people of both continents, even in the heart of the most civilized Europe; but all that we know of those American nations in this matter is certainly not to be compared with what is told us of the ancient Romans by their own historians
