[p. 293] and poets. The works of Livy, of Pliny, of Virgil, of Suetonius, of Valerius Maximus, and of other judicious authors (which cannot be read without compassion) show to what excess the childish superstition of the Romans went in their auguries. There was no animal, whether among the quadrupeds, or among the reptiles, or among the birds, from which they did not take an augury of the future. If the bird flew toward the left hand, if the raven croaked, if the voice of the crow was heard, if the mouse tasted the honey, if the hare crossed the road, all this was held to be a presage of some great misfortune. The expiation, or lustration, of all Rome has been seen performed for no other reason than that an owl had entered the Capitol. (i) And not only animals, but even the most trivial and contemptible things were enough to cause them a superstitious fear, as for example if, while at table, the wine or the salt was spilled, or some particle of the food fell to the ground. Who would not have marveled on contemplating those gentlemen Haruspices, persons of such authority, seriously occupied in observing all the movements of the victims, the state of their entrails, and the color of their blood, in order to foretell from such signs the principal events of that famous republic? I wonder, said the great Cicero, (k) that a haruspex does not laugh on seeing another of the same profession. What in truth is more ridiculous than that kind of augury which they called Tripudium? Who could be persuaded that a nation on the one hand so enlightened, and on the other so warlike, should carry with it in its armies, as the thing most important for the success of its arms, a cage of chickens, and that without first consulting them it should not dare to give battle? If the chickens did not taste the mash that was set before them, it was a bad sign; if besides not eating it they escaped from the cage, worse; if on the contrary they ate it greedily, this was held the happiest augury. So that

> A fsiffarti eccessi è facilmente portato lo spirito umano, qualora fi abbandona a' proprj suoi lumi , La sperienzz di que’ groflolani errori , di quella ridicola puerilità, e di quelle mo- Îtruole abbominazioni, nelle quali son incorse le più colte Na» Zioni del Gentilelimo, dà a divedere, che non dobbiamo asperttar la vera e fanra Religione, se non da quel medesimo Dio, che adoriamo. Iddio volesse che quegli itessi Fi» losofi del nostro illuminato secolo, che tanto vantano le forze della ragione, non ci dessero nelle medesime lor opere tante € sì chiare prove della loro imbecillicà!

To such excesses the human mind is easily carried, when it abandons itself to its own lights. The experience of those crude errors, of that ridiculous childishness, and of those monstrous abominations into which the most civilized nations of gentilism have fallen, shows that we must not expect the true and holy religion from any other than that same God whom we adore. It is for him to reveal the truths that we must believe, and to prescribe the worship with which we must revere him. If the most weighty business of religion is entrusted to human reason, of whose weakness we have so much experience, the greatest absurdities will be presented to our mind as true dogmas; and the worship due to the Supreme Being will be defective through impiety, or excessive through superstition. Would to God that those very philosophers of our enlightened age, who so vaunt the powers of reason, did not give us in their own works so many and such clear proofs of their weakness of mind!

But in the end Americans, Greeks, Romans, and Egyptians were all superstitious and childish in the practice of their religion; not so, however, in the obscenity of their rites; for in the rites of the Mexicans there is not found the slightest vestige of those abominations so common among the Romans and other civilized nations of antiquity. What is more indecent than the Eleusinian festivals that the Greeks held, than those that the Romans celebrated in honor of Venus on the Kalends of April, and above all those most obscene games that were held in honor of Cybele, of Flora, of Bacchus, and of other such wicked gods, against which several Fathers of the Church, and even some of the Romans themselves, inveighed most strongly? What rite is more obscene than that which was performed upon the statue of Priapus amid the nuptial ceremonies? (l) How could they celebrate the festivals of those incestuous and adulterous gods, if not

It is true that although no obscenity entered into the rites of the Mexicans, there were nevertheless some which, supposing the divinity of their gods, would have been indecent, such as that of smearing the lips of the idols with the blood of the victims; but would it not have been far more indecent to slap them, as the Romans did to the goddess Matuta at the Matralia? Granting the error of the one and the other, the Mexicans were certainly less unreasonable in giving their gods to taste a liquor which, according to the principles of their religion, was pleasing to them, than the Romans in performing toward their goddess an action which is held to be gravely insulting among all the peoples of the world.

What we have said thus far, although sufficient to show that the religion of the Mexicans was less blameworthy than that of the Romans, the Greeks, and the Egyptians, may be called almost nothing if compared with what we omit so as not to weary the readers. But otherwise I see well that the comparison should not be made only in the aforesaid articles, but rather in that which concerns the quality of the sacrifices. I confess that the religion of the Mexicans was too bloody, that their sacrifices were most cruel, and their austerities exceedingly barbarous; but whenever I set myself to consider what the other nations of the world have done, I am confounded on recognizing the weakness of the human mind, and the deplorable errors into which it plunges when it is not guided by the light of the true religion; and I render infinite thanks to the Most High for having preserved me from so many evils.

There has been scarcely any nation in the world that has not at some time sacrificed human victims to the god it worshipped. We know from the holy books that the Ammonites burned some of their children in honor of their god Moloch, and that other peoples of the land of Canaan did the same, whose example was at times imitated by the Israelites. It is established from bk. 4 of Kings that Ahaz and Manasseh, kings of Judah, practiced that pagan

> Non v'è tara quasi alcuna Nazione al Mondo, la quale pon abbia talvolta sacrificare vittime uinane a quel Dio, che adorava. Sappiamo da' libri santi, che gli Ammoniri bruciava» po alcuni de’ lor figliuoli ad onore del loro Dio M>loch, e che lo [teffo faceano altri Popoli del pacse di Canaam, il cui esempio. fu talora imitaro dagl' Israeliti, Consta dal lib. 4. de' Re, che Achaz , è Manafle Re di Giuda usarono quel rito gen E [p. 296] as DISSERTAZIONE Vili;

[p. 296] rite of passing their children through the fire. The expression of the sacred text seems to signify rather a mere lustration, or consecration, than a holocaust; but Psalm 105 does not allow us to doubt that the Israelites truly sacrificed their sons to the gods of the Canaanites, (m) the stupendous and evident miracles wrought by the almighty arm of the true God not sufficing to turn them from that barbarous superstition. Of the Egyptians we know, from the testimony of Manetho, a priest and celebrated historian of that nation, cited by Eusebius of Caesarea, that every day three men were sacrificed at Heliopolis to the goddess Juno alone. Now just as the Ammonites sacrificed human victims to their Moloch, and the Canaanites to their Beelphegor, so the Persians sacrificed them to their Mithras, or the Sun, the Phoenicians and Carthaginians to their Baal, or Saturn, the Cretans to Jupiter, the Lacedaemonians to Mars, the Phocians to Diana, the Lesbians to Bacchus, the Thessalians to the Centaur Chiron and to Peleus, the Gauls to Esus and to Teutates, (n) the Bards of Germany to Tuisto, and other nations likewise to their tutelary gods. Philo says that the Phoenicians in their public calamities

(n) A certain French author, driven by a blind love of his country, boldly denies that human victims were ever sacrificed by the Gauls; but he offers no reason by which to refute the testimonies of Caesar, of Pliny, of Suetonius, of Diodorus, of Strabo, of Lactantius, of St. Augustine, and of other weighty authors. The testimony of Caesar is enough to confound him, who, as one who had the most acquaintance with the Gauls, knew them better: The whole nation of the Gauls, he says, is greatly given to religious observances; and on that account those who are afflicted with graver diseases, and those who are engaged in battle and in dangers, either sacrifice human beings for victims, or vow that they will sacrifice them, employing the Druids as ministers of those sacrifices; because they judge that unless a man’s life be given for a man’s life, the divine will of the immortal gods cannot otherwise be appeased; and they have sacrifices of the same kind instituted publicly. Others have images of immense size, whose limbs, woven of wicker, they fill with living men; these being set on fire, the men, surrounded by the flames, perish. They hold that the punishment of those who have been taken in theft, or robbery, or some other offense, is more acceptable to the immortal gods; but when a supply of that kind fails, they descend even to the punishment of the innocent. Bk. 6 of the Gallic War, ch. 5. From which it is seen that the Gauls were still more cruel than the Mexicans. [p. 297] offered in sacrifice to their inhuman Baal the dearest of their children, and Curtius affirms that this sacrifice was in use among the Tyrians until the destruction of their famous city. The Carthaginians, their countrymen, did the same in honor of Saturn the cruel: so rightly named by them. We know that when they had been defeated by Agathocles, King of Syracuse, in order to appease their god, whom they believed to be angered, they sacrificed to him two hundred noble boys, besides three hundred young men who of their own accord offered themselves for the sacrifice to show their bravery, their piety toward the gods, and their love of country; and according to what Tertullian affirms, who, as an African, and not long after the epoch of which he spoke, must have known it well, those sacrifices were in use in Africa until the times of the Emperor Tiberius, as in Gaul until the times of Claudius, as Suetonius attests.

The Pelasgians, ancient inhabitants of Italy, sacrificed, in obedience to an oracle, the tenth part of their children, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus relates. The Romans, who were as bloodthirsty as they were superstitious, did not reject such sacrifices. All the time that they were under their kings they were accustomed to sacrifice boys to the goddess Mania, Mother of the Lares, for the happiness of their houses, induced, as Macrobius says, by a certain oracle of Apollo; and we know from Pliny (o) that it was not forbidden to sacrifice human victims until the year 657 of Rome; but it was not by this prohibition that the examples of that barbarous superstition altogether ceased, for Augustus, according to what some writers cited by Suetonius affirm, after the capture of Perugia, where the consul L. Antonius had fortified himself, sacrificed in honor of his uncle Julius Caesar, already deified by the Romans, three hundred men, part senators and part Roman knights, chosen from among Antonius’s people, on an altar erected to that new god. Lactantius Firmianus, a man very well instructed in the affairs of the Romans, who flourished in the fourth century of the Church, says expressly that even in his own times those sacrifices to Jupiter Latialis were still made in Italy. (q) Nor did the Spaniards preserve themselves from that barbarous superstition. Strabo relates in bk. 3 that the Lusitanians sacrificed their prisoners, cutting off their right hands to consecrate them to their gods, observed their entrails, and watched them for their auguries; that all the inhabitants of the mountains were accustomed to sacrifice prisoners together with horses, offering such victims to the god Mars by the hundred; and speaking in general he says that it was characteristic of the Spaniards to sacrifice themselves for their friends. Not alien to this way of thinking is what Silius Italicus relates of the Baeticans, his ancestors: that after passing the age of youth, grown weary of life, they gave themselves death; which he praises as a heroic action. (r) Who would have believed that this ancient fashion of Baetica should in our own days be renewed in England and in France? Coming then to later times, Father Mariana, speaking of the Goths who occupied Spain, says as follows: (s) “Because they were persuaded that the war would not go well for them unless they offered human blood for the army, they sacrificed prisoners of war to the god Mars, to whom they were chiefly devoted; and they were accustomed also to offer him the first fruits of the spoils, and to hang from the trunks of trees the skins of those whom they killed.” If those Spaniards who wrote the history of Mexico had not forgotten what had happened earlier in their own peninsula, they would not have been so astonished at the sacrifices of the Mexicans.

[p. 299] detailed account of the nations among whom those barbarous sacrifices have been in use; for what we have indicated suffices us to show that the Mexicans did nothing but follow in the footsteps of the most celebrated nations of the old continent, and that their rites were no more cruel, nor more unreasonable. Is it not a greater inhumanity to sacrifice one’s own citizens, one’s own children, and oneself, as for the most part those nations did, than prisoners of war, as was the custom among the Mexicans? The Mexicans were never seen to sacrifice their own countrymen, except those who by their crimes were guilty of death, and at times the wives of the lords, so that they might accompany them also into the other world. That answer which Moctezuma gave to Cortés, who reproached him with the cruelty of their sacrifices, shows that although their sentiments were not just, they were still less unreasonable than those of other nations that had fallen into the same superstition. We, he said, have the right to take the life of our enemies: we could kill them in the heat of battle, as you do your enemies. Now what injustice is there in putting to death, in honor of our gods, those who are guilty of death?

The frequency of such sacrifices was certainly no less in Egypt, in Italy, in Spain, and in Gaul, than in Mexico. If in the single city of Heliopolis there were sacrificed annually, according to Manetho, more than a thousand human victims to the goddess Juno alone, how many must have been those that were sacrificed in the other cities of Egypt to the famous goddess Isis, and to the other innumerable gods worshipped by that so superstitious nation? How great must the frequency have been among the Pelasgians, who sacrificed to their gods the tenth part of their children? What number of men must have been consumed in those hecatombs, and centenary sacrifices of the ancient Spaniards? And what shall we say of the Gauls, who, after sacrificing prisoners of war and malefactors, made even innocent citizens die in sacrifice, as Caesar says? The number of the Mexican sacrifices, moreover, has certainly been exaggerated by the greater part of the historians of Mexico, as we have said elsewhere.

The most humane Romans, who had scruples about looking upon human entrails, (t) although at the end of six centuries and a half after the founding of their famous metropolis they finally forbade the sacrificing of men, nevertheless permitted with all too great frequency the gladiatorial sacrifice. I so call those barbarous combats which, while serving for the amusement of that ferocious people, were moreover prescribed by their religion. Besides the great quantity of human blood that was shed in the Circus games and at banquets, there was in truth no little shed at the funerals of the well-to-do, either by gladiators fighting among themselves, or by the putting to death of some prisoners to appease the Manes of the dead; and they were so persuaded of the necessity of human blood for such an end, that when for lack of means the expenses of gladiators or of prisoners could not be borne, mourning women were paid, so that they might draw blood from their cheeks with their nails. How many, then, must have been the victims put to death by the superstition of the Romans at so many funerals, especially as there was emulation among them, each seeking to surpass the others in the number of gladiators and prisoners that were to serve for his funeral pomp? This sanguinary spirit of the Romans was what wrought such slaughters among the peoples of Europe, Asia, and Africa, and it likewise often flooded Rome with the blood of her own citizens, especially during those horrible proscriptions which darkened the glory of that famous republic.

Not only were the Mexicans inhuman toward their prisoners, but also toward themselves, with those barbarous austerities which we have set forth in the History. But drawing blood from the tongue, the arms, and the legs with the thorns of the maghei, as all did, and piercing the tongue with bits of cane, as some of the more austere were wont to do, will seem slight mortifications beside those frightful and unheard-of austerities performed by the penitents of the East Indies and of Japan, which cannot be read without horror. Finally, the Mexicans, not content with sacrificing human victims, also ate their flesh. I confess that in this they were more inhuman than those other nations; but examples of such inhumanity have not been so rare in the old continent, even among civilized nations, that the Mexicans must on that account be numbered among the absolutely barbarous peoples. “That horrible custom,” says the historian Solís, “of men eating one another, was seen earlier among other barbarians of our hemisphere, as Galicia confesses in its Annals.” Besides the ancient Africans, whose descendants are even today in part cannibals, it is certain that many of those nations that were once known by the common name of Scythians were likewise so, and also the ancient settlers of Sicily and of the mainland of Italy, as Pliny and other authors say. Of the Jews who lived in the times of Antiochus the Illustrious, Apion, an Egyptian historian (not a Greek, as M. de Pauw says), wrote that they kept a Greek prisoner to eat him at the end of a year. Of the famous Hannibal Livy says that he had human flesh eaten by his soldiers in order to hearten

(u) The priests of the Great Goddess, who were called Galli, cut off their own virile parts, and, driven by frenzy, whirled their heads, and with knives lacerated their faces and the muscles of their whole body; they also attacked themselves with their teeth. Augustine, City of God, bk. 2, ch. 7. One cuts off his virile parts, another slashes his arms. Where do they fear angry gods, who thus earn propitious ones? … So great is the frenzy of a mind disordered and driven from its seat, that the gods are appeased in a manner in which not even the most savage men rage; the tyrants handed down in fables for their cruelty have mangled the limbs of some, but have ordered no one to mangle his own. For the pleasure of a king’s lust some have been castrated; but no one, at his master’s bidding, laid hands on himself so as not to be a man. These men cut themselves to pieces in the temples, they supplicate with their wounds and their blood. If anyone has leisure to look at what they do and what they suffer, he will find things so unbecoming to honorable men, so unworthy of free men, so unlike sane men, that no one would doubt that they were mad, if they were mad in company with fewer; as it is, the multitude of the insane is the defense of their sanity. Seneca, On Superstition. [p. 302] them for war. Pliny severely reproaches the Greeks for the custom of eating all the parts of the human body to cure various diseases. (x) Now what wonder that the Mexicans performed as a maxim of religion what the Greeks practiced for medicine? But no, I do not pretend to make an apology for the Mexicans on this point. Their religion in what concerns anthropophagy was without doubt more barbarous than that of the Romans, the Egyptians, and those other civilized nations; but for the rest it cannot be doubted, given what we have said, that it was less superstitious, less ridiculous, and less indecent.

## D I S S E RTAT I O N I X 

## ON THE ORIGIN OF THE FRENCH DISEASE

## I   n the present Dissertation we have to dispute not only with M. de

> 3953 DISSERTAZIONE IX.

Pauw, but also with nearly all Europeans, who are already generally persuaded that the French disease had its origin in America: for after various nations of Europe had for more than thirty years laid the blame on one another for the origin of so shameful a disease, they finally agreed to blame the New World. We should without doubt be charged with rashness in wishing to combat so universal an opinion, if the arguments that we are about to oppose to it, and the example of two modern Europeans, did not render our boldness excusable. (a) Since among the supporters of the common opinion the principal one, the most renowned, and he who has written about it most copiously and most learnedly is M. Astruc, a learned French physician, it is he who will be chiefly attacked by us, availing ourselves for this purpose in large part of those very materials which he furnishes us in his work. (b)

§ I.

> Nei primi trenta anni , dappoi che cominciò a sentir in Italia il Malfrancele, non vi fu verun Autore , che accribuisse la sua origine all’ America, come poi diremo . Tutti ‘ gli Au» tori, che ne scriflero prima del 1525.,. ed alcuni anche dî quelh, che scriflero dopo, lo attribuirono a diverse cagioni, la cui notizia recherà ai Lettori e compaslione e piacere. ì

Opinions of the Early Physicians on the Origin of the French Disease.

> Alcuni dei primi Medici allor viventi, come Corradino Gillini, e Gaspare Torella , fi persuasero secondo le idee di quei tempi, che. il Malfrancese era itato cagionato dalla gran cons giunzione del Sole con Giove , Saturno , € Mercurio nel segno di Libra accaduta nel 148z, è Altri, dietro al celebre Niccolò Leoniceno (-), l’accribuirono alle abbondantissime pioggie, e alle inondazioni avvepute in Italia «quell'anno, in cui cominciò il contagio.

In the first thirty years after the French disease began to be felt in Italy, there was no author who attributed its origin to America, as we shall say later. All the authors who wrote about it before 1525, and some even of those who wrote afterward, attributed it to various causes, the knowledge of which will bring the readers both compassion and pleasure.

> Giovanni Manardi , dotto Profeflore dell’ Università di Ferrara, ascrifle l'origine di tal male al commercio impuro d' un Cavalier Valenzano infetto dalla lebbra con una mgretrice; e Paracelso al commercio d'un Lebbroso francese con ‘una prostituta. Antonio Musa Brasfavola, dotto Ferrarese , afferma, che il malfrancese ebbe principio da una meretrice, che trovavasi nell'esercito dei France in Napoli, la quale avea un alsceflo nella bocca dell’ utero.

Some of the earliest physicians then living, such as Corradino Gillini and Gaspar Torrella, were persuaded, according to the ideas of those times, that the French disease had been caused by the great conjunction of the Sun with Jupiter, Saturn, and Mercury in the sign of Libra, which occurred in 1483.

> Gabrielle Fallopio , celebre medico Modonese , afferma, che gli Spagnuoli essendo pochi nella guerra di Napoli, ed i Francesi infiniti, avvelenarono una . notte l’acqua dei pozzi, della quale doveano bere i lor nemici, e che quindi ebbe ori: gine il contagio.

Others, following the celebrated Niccolò Leoniceno, (c) attributed it to the most abundant rains and to the inundations that occurred in Italy in that year in which the contagion began.

> L'A dimmi —— _ (ec) Itaque dicimu:, malum hoc, quod Morbum Gallicum wulgo appellant 11 ter. epidemias debere connumerari. .. Giovanni Manardi, a learned professor of the University of Ferrara, ascribed the origin of this disease to the impure intercourse of a Valencian knight infected with leprosy with a harlot; and Paracelsus to the intercourse of a French leper with a prostitute. Antonio Musa Brasavola, a learned Ferrarese, affirms that the French disease had its beginning from a harlot who was to be found in the army of the French at Naples, who had an abscess in the mouth of the womb.

Gabriele Falloppio, a celebrated Modenese physician, affirms that the Spaniards being few in the war of Naples, and the French countless, poisoned one night the water of the wells, from which their enemies were to drink, and that from this the contagion had its origin.

(c) Therefore we say that this ailment, which they commonly call the Gallic disease, ought to be reckoned among the epidemics … This is sufficiently established, that in that year there was a great overflowing of waters throughout all Italy … and that the summer, moreover, came on to that [season] with an intemperance, namely a hot and humid one, etc. Opusc., On the Gallic Disease.

> Andrea Cesalpino, Medico di Clemente VIII, dice , ave» re egli saputo da quelli, che intervennero alla guerra di Na» poli, -che allorchè era affediata dai Francesi Somma, luogo nel vesuvio , dove è una grande abbondanza d' eccellepte vino greco, gli Spagnuoli scapparono segretamente una notte, lasciandovi: una gran quantità di quel vino, meschiato con sangue degli ammalati di San Lazzaro, € che entrandovi immediatamente i Francesi bevvero di quel vino, e tosto cominciarono a sentir, gli efferti del mal venereo.

Andrea Cesalpino, physician to Clement VIII, says that he had learned from those who took part in the war of Naples that when Somma, a place on Vesuvius where there is a great abundance of excellent Greek wine, was besieged by the French, the Spaniards slipped away secretly one night, leaving there a great quantity of that wine, mixed with the blood of the sick of Saint Lazarus, and that the French, entering immediately, drank of that wine, and soon began to feel the effects of the venereal disease.

> Leonardo Fioravanti douo Medico Bolognese , dice nella sua opera intitolata: Capricci Medicinali, avere egli saputo dal figliuolo di colui , che era stato vivandiere dell’ esercito d' Alfonso Re di Napoli verso l’ anno 1456. , che venendo a mancare i viveri per la luoghezza della guerra tanto nell’ esercito di quel Re, quanto in quello de' Francelì, i vivandieri somminiltravano agli uni, e agli altri della carne umana condita, e che da ciò prese origine il Malfrancese, Il celebre Cancelliers Bacone di Verulamio soggiugne, (4) che la carne lor ministrara era d' uomini ammazzati in Barberìa, la quale concia» vano , come il Tonno.

Leonardo Fioravanti, a learned physician of Bologna, says in his work entitled Capricci medicinali that he had learned from the son of the man who had been sutler to the army of Alfonso, king of Naples, around the year 1456, that when provisions began to fail through the length of the war, both in the army of that king and in that of the French, the sutlers furnished both with seasoned human flesh, and that from this the French disease took its origin. The celebrated Chancellor Bacon of Verulam adds (d) that the flesh furnished them was that of men killed in Barbary, which they prepared like tuna.

> Siccome nefluno seppe, nè porè sapere , chi fu in Euro il primo a patir quel gran male, così nemmeno se ne può laper la cagione; ma vediamo ciò, che porè avvenire.

Since no one knew, nor could know, who in Europe was the first to suffer that great disease, so neither can its cause be known; but let us see what could have happened.

To show that the French disease could have been communicated by contagion to Europe from other countries of the same continent, it is necessary, and sufficient, to prove that the aforesaid disease was already suffered in some of those countries, and that they had commerce with Europe before the New World was discovered. The one and the other will here be fully demonstrated.

Vatable, Father Pineda, Father Calmet, and other authors maintained that among the diseases with which holy Job was afflicted, one was that of the French disease. This opinion is so ancient that as soon as that disease appeared in Italy, some called it Job’s disease, as Battista Fregoso, an author living at the time, attests. (e) Father Calmet strives (f) to prove his view with great erudition; but since we know nothing of Job’s infirmity except what is indicated in the sacred book, which can easily be understood of other known diseases, or of some wholly unknown to us, no account is to be made of this opinion.

Jacob Bontius, physician to the Dutch in the East Indies, testifies (l) that that disease was endemic in Amboina and in the Moluccas, and that to contract it no previous carnal intercourse was needed. Father Foureau, a French Jesuit, learned, exact, and experienced in the affairs of China, being asked by M. Astruc (n) whether the physicians of China reputed the venereal disease to be native to their country, or else brought there from elsewhere, replied that the Chinese physicians consulted by him were of the opinion that this disease had been suffered in that empire from the most remote antiquity, and that in fact the books of medicine written in Chinese characters, which are esteemed by them as ancient, said nothing about the beginning of that malady, but rather made mention of it as of a most ancient evil even at the time in which the aforesaid books were written: that therefore it was not known, nor even probable, that this disease had been brought there from other countries.

> Finalmeme lo steflo Sig. Astruc dice, (o) a lui parere, dopo) avere elaminate e ponderate le testimonianze degli Autori, che il mal venereo non era proprio solamente dell' [sola Haitì o Spagnuola, ma comune eziandio a molte regioni dell’ antico Continente, e forse a tutti i paesi equinoziali del Mon» do, ne' quali regaava eflo ab antico. Questa ingenua ‘confessione d' un uomo, ranro istruito in questa materia, e peraltro tanto impegnato contra l' America, oltre a' testimoni sopraccenonati , vale affai a dimostrare, - che ancorchè supponghiamo il Malfrancefe anticamente efiltente in quel nuovo Mondo, nulla però può allegarsi in questa matecia dagli Europei contra l' America , che non possa dir dagli Americani contra parecchj paesi del Mondo antico, e che fe era puasto, come vuole il Sig. de P., il sangue degli Americani non era più sano quello di tanti Afiatici ed Africani.

Finally, M. Astruc himself says (o) that in his opinion, after having examined and weighed the testimonies of the authors, the venereal disease was not peculiar only to the island of Haiti or Hispaniola, but common also to many regions of the old continent, and perhaps to all the equatorial countries of the world, in which it had reigned from of old. This candid confession of a man so well instructed in this matter, and moreover so committed against America, goes far, besides the testimonies mentioned above, to show that even if we suppose the French disease to have anciently existed in that New World, nothing can however be alleged in this matter by the Europeans against America that cannot be said by the Americans against several countries of the Old World; and that if the blood of the Americans was spoiled, as M. de P. will have it, the blood of so many Asiatics and Africans was no healthier.

(o) De morbis venereis, bk. 1, ch. 11. [p. 308] great commerce which Egypt had for so many centuries, on the one hand with the equatorial countries of Asia, and on the other with Italy? Now why might not the Asiatic merchants have carried the venereal disease from India together with the drugs to Egypt, and thence the Venetians, the Genoese, and the Pisans, who had for a long time had continual commerce with the city of Alexandria, have carried it to Italy, just as other Europeans carried leprosy to Italy from Syria, and smallpox from Arabia? Moreover, among those many Europeans who from the twelfth century onward undertook the journey into the southern countries of Asia, such as Benjamin of Tudela, Carpini, Marco Polo, and Mandeville, among whom some, like Marco Polo, penetrated as far as China, could not someone of them have brought back with him on his return to Europe the contagion taken in those Asiatic countries? Here we are not discoursing of what in fact happened, but only of what might have happened.

> gran commercio, che ebbe per tanti secoli l'Egitto da una parte co' paesi equinoziali dell’ Asia, e da un' altra coll' Italia ? Oc perchè o0n avranno potuto i Negozianti afiatici portar dall’India insieme colle droghe il mal venereo in Egitto, e quindi fonia in Italia i Veneziani, i Genovesì, ed i Pisani, 1 qua- 1 aveano da gran tempo un continuo commercio colla Cui d' Alefiindria, ficcome altri Europ:i pertarono in Italia dalla Sora la lebbra, e dall' Arabia il vajuolo? Oltraccid tra que’ molti Europei , che dal secolo XI, innanzi intrapresero il viaggio ne paeli meridionali dell’ Asia, come Benjamino di Tudela, Carpini , Marco Polo, e Mandeville , tra i quali alcuni, come Marco Polo, s' innoltrarono fin nella China, non potè qualcun di loro portar nel suo ritorno in Europa il contagio preso in que' paesi asiatici ? Quì non discorriamo di quello , che in’ fatti avvenne, ma di ciò folamente , che poteva avvenire. —

Not only from Asia, but also from Africa could the French disease have passed into Europe before America was discovered; for the Portuguese, thirty years before the glorious expedition of Columbus, had already discovered a great part of the equatorial countries of Africa, and had opened commerce there. Now could not some Portuguese, there infected with the French disease, have infected in turn his countrymen, and subsequently other nations of Europe, as perhaps in fact happened, according to what we shall say below? Let M. Astruc see, then, in how many ways the French disease could have been communicated to Europe without the intervention of America, although the torrid zone was believed by the ancients to be inaccessible.

This poison, communicated to a healthy man, must not be considered, says the aforesaid author, as a new humor added to the natural humors, but rather as a mere dyscrasia, or vicious quality of the natural humors, which, degenerating from their natural state, change into acido-salty ones.

Now nearly all physicians are persuaded that this evil cannot arise otherwise than by way of contagion, communicated through the seminal fluid, or the milk, or the saliva, or the sweat, or the contact of venereal ulcers, etc. But I, with the good leave of these gentlemen, maintain that the French disease can absolutely be generated in a man without any contagion or communication with the infected; because it can absolutely be generated in that same manner in which it was generated in the first man who suffered from it: now this man did not have it by contagion, for then he would not have been the first to suffer from it, but from another, quite different cause: therefore from a similar cause, whatever it was, that same cachexy could be produced without contagion in other individuals of the human species. This is true, says M. Astruc, in America, or in some other similar country, but not in Europe. And why is Europe so privileged? Because, replies the aforesaid author, those causes do not concur there which in the beginning could have caused that evil in America. And what are these causes? Let us examine them.

(q) The air, indeed, seems to be struck from the number of causes: in Hispaniola it could perhaps bring on other diseases, but by no means the venereal pox. It is certainly established that the Europeans who have inhabited that island for 200 years (indeed, nearly 300) never contracted the venereal pox there except by contagion. Yet the Europeans there breathe the same air that the natives formerly breathed, and without doubt tempered and constituted in the same way. Astruc, De morbis venereis, bk. 1, ch. 12. [p. 310] maladies in Hispaniola, but not the venereal disease, because the Europeans who for two hundred years and more have lived on that island have never contracted that malady there except by way of contagion; and yet the air is not at present different from what it was three hundred years ago: and even supposing it is different at present, at least it was not so at the beginning of the fifteenth century. The air, therefore, is not to be taken into account where the question is to discover the first origin of the venereal disease. Nevertheless the same M. Astruc, after having excluded the air from the number of the causes of the French disease, has recourse to it, openly contradicting himself, as we shall see below.

Only two causes are indicated by M. Astruc: food and heat. As to food, he says that the inhabitants of Hispaniola, when they lacked maize, cassava, etc., fed on spiders, worms, bats, and other such small creatures. As to heat, he affirms that women in hot countries are apt to be troubled by menstrual discharges that are too acrid and almost virulent, especially if they eat unwholesome foods. This being supposed, the author in question reasons thus: “Therefore the natives of the island of Haiti must once have been afflicted with many and most grievous diseases, where no one kept away from menstruating women; where men, impotent through lust, were driven to venery after the manner of beasts; where the women, who were most shameless, admitted men promiscuously, as Gonzalo de Oviedo attests, Hist. Indiar., bk. 5, ch. 3; nay, more shamelessly provoked these same men, and more of them, at the time of menstruation, when, the womb then growing warm, they raged more madly with lust after the manner of cattle. What wonder, then, if the various, heterogeneous, acrid semen of many men, mixed together in one, blended with the most acrid and virulent menstrual blood, shut up within the seething and foul womb of most filthy women, putrefied in a short time through delay, heterogeneity, and the heat of the place, and formed the first seeds of the venereal disease, which spread to others, if any perhaps were more continent?”

Here is the whole argument of M. Astruc on the first origin of the venereal disease, full from head to foot of falsehood, as we shall show below; but supposing now that all were true,

I affirm that this same thing which, by his account, happened in Hispaniola could likewise happen in Europe; for just as those Americans, lacking maize and other customary foods, fed on spiders, worms, etc., so the Europeans, lacking wheat and other good provisions, have at times been seen to eat mice, lizards, and other such small creatures, the excrement of several animals, and even bread made of the flour of human bones, bringing upon themselves the gravest illness. It is enough to recall the dreadful famines suffered in Europe in the past, caused partly by the weather and partly by war. Then there have always been men who, like beasts, have let themselves be carried by an unbridled lust to the most execrable excesses. There have always been shameless and most filthy women, and one could say of them what Plautus says: There are more harlots there than flies at the very time when it is hottest. For the rest, there has never been a lack of excessively acrid seminal fluids, nor of seething wombs, nor of virulent menses. Such causes, then, could produce the French disease in Europe, as they produced it in America, according to M. Astruc.

I am willing to concede many things to M. Astruc that surely no one else would concede to him. I concede to him that there never were in Europe either that abuse of menstruating women, or that acrimony, or that virulence in the fluids of the human body, or that fervor in the womb, which he supposes on the island of Hispaniola, although from the books of medicine published these two thousand years the exact opposite is established. I concede to him that no examples of the most unbridled lust were ever seen there; for it seems to him too much to confess such examples in Europe, (r) and I concede to him besides that all the women and men of Europe have been most healthy and most chaste. All this I concede to him, although it is contradicted by history and by the common opinion of the Europeans themselves. Nevertheless I affirm that the French disease could absolutely be generated in Europe without contagion; because all those disorders which M. Astruc supposes on the island of Hispaniola could also have occurred in Europe, even though in reality they never did. Those most chaste women, led on by those evil passions which are common to all the children of Adam, could become as incontinent and shameless as that author believes the American women of Hispaniola to have been. Those men, so healthy, could feed on foods as harmful as were those of the Haitians. Human sperm, which is by itself very acrid, as the same M. Astruc says, could, by reason of unwholesome foods, become more and more acrid, until it took on that degree of acrimony which the venereal disease requires. The menses could become virulent either from their previous suppression, or from plethora, or from many other morbid causes, in the fluids as well as in the vessels.

Because in Europe, he says, the air is more temperate.

Perchè in Europa, dice egli, l aria è più temperata,

This is the only subterfuge that remains to M. Astruc; but it avails him nothing; for it is certain that in many countries of Europe, as in Italy, and particularly in the southern part of it, the air is hotter in summer than in Hispaniola, and there is moreover no reason to believe that the heat of the whole year is necessary, and that that of some months does not suffice to cause that depravation of the humors. But who ever thought that the external heat of the air is needed to cause that extraordinary acrimony and virulence in the humors? Scurvy is a cachexy very similar to that of the venereal disease, but more terrible, which brings with it a stupendous acrimony and corruption in the blood: now this kind of malady arises as much in the hot regions as in the northern countries and seas, and is more often caused by traveling in the temperate or cold zones than in the torrid: therefore hot air is not necessary for a stupendous acrimony and corruption to be generated in the humors.

Thus far we have reasoned on the supposition that what M. Astruc reports in his discourse was true; but besides some errors in matters of physics, on which it is not fitting to discourse, there are also facts arbitrarily supposed and contrary to the truth. He supposes 1. that the Indians of Hispaniola fed on worms, spiders, etc.; but this perhaps happened some years after the discovery of that island, when the Americans, fleeing the fury of the European conquerors, went wandering lost through the woods, and, lacking maize and cassava, because they had not sown them, out of hatred for their enemies, as Peter Martyr d’Anghiera bears witness (u), ate whatever they found there; but no ancient author affirms that they used such foods before the Spaniards landed there; and to show that the aforesaid foods had some influence on the French disease, it would have to be proved that the use of them was at least as ancient on that island as that infirmity was in the judgment of M. Astruc: which he has not done, nor could do. 2. He affirms that on the island of Hispaniola no one kept away from menstruating women; but I should have wished that to confirm this he had cited the testimony of some ancient author; for I do not find anyone who says it; on the contrary, I see that among the singular things noted by European writers in the Americans, even in the barbarous tribes, is that of not having intercourse with

M. Astruc represents the men and women of Hispaniola as exceedingly heated and agitated by a violent and raging lust; Count de Buffon and M. de Pauw (x) represent, on the contrary, all the Americans as most cold and insensible to the stimuli of love. What does such a contradiction mean, if not that these systematic authors paint the Americans in whatever colors turn out to suit them? When they want to bring out the apathy or insensibility of those men, they say that they are most cold; but when they claim to discredit their customs, or to blame them for the French disease, then they affirm that they are beyond measure libidinous. M. Astruc cites the testimony of Gonzalo de Oviedo in bk. 5, ch. 3 of his History to convince us that the Haitian women were too shameless, and that they prostituted themselves indiscriminately to all men; but besides that the testimony of this author against the Americans is worth less than nothing, as we shall show below, he does not say what M. Astruc would have us believe. Here is what Oviedo says in the cited place: The women of this island were continent with their own men; but with the Christians they willingly made free of themselves. Here is what Herrera says of it: (y) The women were continent with their fellow natives, and dishonest with the Castilians. If they were continent with their fellow natives, their incontinence could not cause the French disease before the Spaniards landed there. If they were dishonest only with the Christians, it must be believed

We have indicated above that in the first thirty years after America was discovered, no one ascribed the origin of the French disease to that New World. I, at least, after consulting a great many authors, physicians as well as historians, who wrote at that early time of such a disease and of its origin, have not found a single one who was of that opinion; nor could M. Astruc find one, although he looked among all the Italian, French, English, Spanish, and German writers for someone who would support his opinion. Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, who in the Sumario of the History of the West Indies, presented to Charles V in 1525, asserted that the Spaniards infected on the island of Hispaniola, who afterward returned to Spain with Admiral Columbus and then passed into Italy with the Great Captain, communicated that evil to the Neapolitan women, and these to the French, etc. As this author was a man of letters, and lived some years in America, holding an honorable office, his authority drew after it almost all the writers; for on the one hand everyone believed him well informed, and on the other it suited everyone that he should be believed, so that each might free his own nation from the imputation of so shameful a disease. But before examining his account, it is necessary to make this writer known, whose authority has been the chief, or rather the sole, support of the common opinion.

Monsignor Bartolomé de las Casas, who lived in America at the same time as Oviedo and knew him quite well, in his refutation of Dr. Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda, who alleged the authority of Oviedo against the Indians, says thus: “What most prejudices the person of the Reverend Doctor among prudent and God-fearing men who have eyewitness knowledge of the Indies is the allegation he makes of Oviedo as an irrefragable author in his most false and execrable History, he having been one of the tyrants, robbers, and destroyers of the Indies, as he himself confesses in the preface to the first part and in bk. 6, ch. 8, and for that reason a capital enemy of the Indians. Let wise persons judge whether such a writer is a fit witness against the Indians. And yet this man is called a grave and diligent chronicler by the Doctor, because he found him suited to his purpose; but it is certain that that History has little more leaves than lies, as we amply prove in other writings and in the Apologia.” In fact the chronicler Herrera, a judicious and impartial man, says that Monsignor de las Casas had reason to complain of Oviedo, and that this man was not too exact in some reports. He, moreover, promoted some extravagant opinions, induced by the spirit of flattery, or

It is enough to read the second book of his History, in which, besides saying that the Trojans descended from the Spaniards, he affirms that the Antilles are the Hesperides of the ancients, and that they were so called from Hesperus, twelfth king of Spain, who was lord of them 1658 years before the Christian era. “In this manner,” he adds, “with so ancient a claim, and by the aforesaid route, this dominion returned to Spain after so many centuries: and as its own possession, it seems, Divine Justice was pleased to restore it to her, that she might possess it through the good fortune of the two happy and Catholic Kings Don Ferdinand and Doña Isabella.” (A) Such is the author of the common opinion; let us now examine his account.

> Egli parla con qualche varierà nel Sommario della Sto. ria , e nella Storia medesima; ma siccome questa è l’ opera sua principale, la più stesa , pubblicata alcuni anni dopo 1l Sommario, @ lavorata con maggiore studio, così dobbiamo piuttosto stare a ciò, che dice in essa, dovunque fia qualche divario. Egli dunque dice nel lib. 2. cap. 14. della Storia Gene. rale delle Indie, che gli Spagnuoli ritornari con Colombo in Ispagna nel 1496. dal seconda lor viaggio in America, vi ri.

He speaks with some variation in the Sumario of the History and in the History itself; but since the latter is his principal work, the more extensive, published some years after the Sumario, and composed with greater study, we ought rather to stand by what he says in it, wherever there is any divergence. He says, then, in bk. 2, ch. 14 of the General History of the Indies, that the Spaniards who returned with Columbus to Spain in 1496 from their second voyage to America brought back from the island of Hispaniola the French disease together with samples of the gold of the famous mines of Cibao: and that some of them, already infected, who passed into Italy with the Great Captain Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, infected through the Italian women the French who had come with King Charles VIII to take possession of the kingdom of Naples: But this account is wholly untenable, and full of anachronisms; for Columbus returned to Spain from his second voyage on June 3, 1496, and we know from countless eyewitnesses that Europe was already infected with the French disease at least as early as 1495: therefore such infection could not have come from those Spaniards who then returned with Columbus. VIII, could not have been infected by the Spanish troops who came with the Great Captain into Italy, it suffices simply to set out the dates, as we find them in Guicciardini, Mariana, Mézeray, and other Italian, Spanish, and French historians. King Charles VIII marched with his army toward Italy in August 1494: he arrived at Asti, a city on the Tanaro, on September 9: entered Rome on December 31, and Naples on February 22, 1495. In this city he stayed no more than three months; for, aware of the great confederation formed against him, he hastened to return to France. He left Naples on May 20, as is attested by Guicciardini, Bembo, Mariana, etc., and having won on July 6 the famous battle of Fornovo against the Venetians, he withdrew precipitately to his court, leading his army infected with the venereal disease, as all the historians of those times testify. The Great Captain, held back at Majorca and in Sardinia by contrary winds, could not arrive with his fleet at Messina before May 24, 1495, that is, four days after King Charles had departed from Naples with his infected army: therefore this army was not, nor could it have been, infected by those Spanish troops, unless one is willing to say that those same contrary winds which prevented the Great Captain’s fleet from approaching Italy carried the contagion there. I wonder that the authors of the common opinion did not notice so manifest an anachronism. Someone might say that that contagion was not brought by the troops of the Great Captain, but by other Spanish troops that came earlier into Italy; but besides that both Oviedo, the inventor of the common opinion, and the other writers who follow him generally ascribe the contagion of Naples to the troops of the Great Captain, I have not been able to find, though I have made diligent researches, that from the discovery of America until the arrival of the Great Captain any other Spanish troops came to the mainland of Italy; on the contrary, from Mariana’s account the very opposite appears: it was not, therefore, the Spanish troops that caused the contagion of Naples.

From what we have said above it must not be thought [p. 320] that the French disease was only a few days earlier in Italy than the arrival of the Spanish troops; for we know from the deposition of the ablest physicians of that time that this malady began there at least some months before the Spanish fleet landed. Gaspar Torrella, a Valencian, physician to Pope Alexander VI, then reigning, (B) Wendelin Hock, a learned German, and professor of medicine in those times in this University of Bologna, (C) Giacomo Cattaneo of Lagomarsino, a learned Genoese physician, (D) Giovanni de Vigo, a Genoese, physician and surgeon to Pope Julius II (E): these four authors, besides others of much authority, because learned and well versed in diseases, and because they were eyewitnesses of it, testify that the French disease began to be felt in Italy as early as 1494. There is, moreover, no reason to wonder that there is some divergence among the authors about the beginning of that evil; since by some it was observed sooner than by others, because it was not felt at the same time in all the states of this peninsula.

(E) In the year 1494, in the month of December, in which year that most serene Charles, King of the French, with a great retinue set out toward the parts of Italy to recover the kingdom of Naples, there appeared that same year a certain kind of disease, of a nature almost unknown throughout all Italy, which the different nations called by various and diverse names. In Praxis chirurgiae, printed in 1514, bk. 5, ch. 1. [p. 321] published some years earlier, in which he gives clearly to understand that even among those who had returned to Spain with the same Columbus in 1493 some came infected; but neither is this true, nor probable. It is established by the letters of Christopher Columbus himself, adduced by his learned son Don Ferdinand, that he first set foot on land on the island of Hispaniola on December 24, 1492, because a caravel of his wretched fleet was wrecked on a shoal for him: that all those days that he stayed there, from December 24 until January 4, were employed by his few people in extracting from the shoal the timber of the caravel in order to make of it a small fortress, in which, having left forty men, he embarked that same day with the rest of his people to return to Spain to carry the news of the discovery of that New World. All the circumstances of their arrival on that island do not permit us to suspect that the Spaniards had leisure to advance to such familiarity with the American women as was required to remain infected by the French disease. The reciprocal wonder caused in both parties by the sight of so many new objects, and the very brief stay of only eleven days, occupied in the great labor of extracting the timbers of the caravel and of building that fortress in such haste, after the hardships of a voyage the longest and most perilous that had been made until then, render this conjecture wholly improbable. No less improbable is it rendered by the silence of Columbus himself, of his son Don Ferdinand, and of Peter Martyr d’Anghiera, who, describing the great hardships of that navigation, say nothing of such a disease.

Not content with affirming that the French disease came from Hispaniola, Oviedo offers also to prove it. Here are his proofs: 1. With guaiacum (a wood abundant in Hispaniola) that dreadful infirmity of the pustules is cured better than with any other medicine: and the Divine Clemency, where it permits the evil for our sins, there in its mercy provides remedies. If this argument were good, it should be concluded that Europe, rather than the island of Hispaniola, is the native country of the French disease; for all know that the most efficacious remedy against such an evil is mercury, which, being common in Europe, was not found in Hispaniola, and was not even known to the Indians: it is certain that as soon as the Gallic disease appeared in Europe, they began to employ mercury there, and that it was used by Giovanni Berengario da Carpi, Gaspar Torrella, Giovanni de Vigo, Wendelin Hock, and other famous physicians of that time, although, discredited afterward by the indiscretion of some empirics, it fell for some time into disuse. Guaiacum did not begin to be employed until 1517, that is, twenty-five years after the discovery of the French disease. Sarsaparilla began to be used in 1535, china root about the same time, and sassafras a little after.

M. de Pauw thinks he has won the case, (M) and has demonstrated the truth of the common opinion by the testimony of Rodrigo Díaz de Isla, physician of Seville, who is called by him a contemporary author, as his testimony is held to be decisive; but Díaz was not a contemporary author, for he did not write until sixty years after the discovery of the French disease, and his account merits no credence. He says that the first Spaniards, returned from Hispaniola with Columbus in 1493, brought the contagion to Barcelona, where the court then was: that this city was the first to be infected: that the evil wrought such havoc there that recourse was had to public prayers, to fasts, and to alms to placate the wrath of God: that, King Charles of France having passed into Italy the following year, certain Spaniards who were infected there, or many regiments, according to M. de P., sent from Spain to oppose the invasion of King Charles, infected the French. But from history we know that no regiment, whether infected or healthy, nor any other Spaniards were sent into Italy before King Charles left Naples with his army already infected to return to France. As for the contagion of Barcelona, we know that at the arrival there of Columbus,

It seems that the Sevillian physicians were at those times the worst informed about the origin of the French disease; for Nicolás Monardes, a physician too of that city, and a contemporary of Díaz, gives an account of it so full of fables that it cannot be read without indignation. He says, then, (N) that “in the year 1493, in the war that the Catholic King had at Naples with King Charles of France, there came Don Christopher Columbus from the first discovery that he made of the island of Santo Domingo, etc., and brought with him from that island a great multitude of Indian men and women, whom he took to Naples, where the Catholic King then was, the war being ended. And because there was peace between the two kings, and the armies mingled together, Columbus having arrived there with his Indian men and women, the Spaniards began to consort with the Indian women, and the Indians with the Spanish women, and in this way the Indian men and women infected the army of the Spaniards, Italians, and Germans,” etc. Who would be persuaded that a Spanish man of letters would disfigure to such a degree the public facts of his nation, which occurred not more than eighty years before, that there would not be in his account a single proposition that was not a gross error? But where it is a matter of discrediting America, no regard is had for truth. It is certain and notorious that there was no war between Spain and France in 1493: that the Catholic King was not then at Naples, but at Barcelona, not yet healed of the wounds that he received from a

madman

(N) On the Things That Are Brought from the West Indies Pertaining to the Use of Medicine. Pt. 1, ch. 9. [p. 326] madman: that Columbus did not bring with him a great multitude of Indian men and women, but only ten Indians: that Columbus never came to Italy after his glorious expedition: that the Indians led by him never saw Italy, etc.

> Qual è cunque la vera patria del Malfrancese ; poichè ef so non ebbe origine né dall' Europa, nè dall' America ? Io nol so; ma se in mezzo all' incertezza mi fi permette di servirmi di congetture, io sospetto, che quel contagio fia venuto dalla Guinea, 0 da altro paese equinoziale dell’ Africa , Di questo me desimo seatimento fa. il dortvillimo Medico Iaglese Tommaso Sydeoham (HD), e vien confermato da ciò , che afferma Battista Fulgosfio, reltimonio oculare del cominciameoto del Malfranc &

I, on the contrary, after having made the most diligent researches, am so far from believing that the French disease came to Europe from America that, rather, I am persuaded that it, no less than smallpox, was carried to America by Europeans. 1. For neither Don Christopher Columbus in his Diary, nor Don Ferdinand Columbus in the Life of his famous father, who saw those countries recently discovered and noted their particularities, make any mention of the French disease, although they relate minutely the hardships and sufferings of those first voyages. Nor did Peter Martyr d’Anghiera make mention of it in his history of those same countries, a contemporary author of Columbus and well informed, as one who was Protonotary of the Council of the Indies and Abbot of Jamaica. Oviedo, the first who attributed that evil to America, did not go there until twenty years after the island of Haiti was inhabited by the Spaniards. What we say of the silence of those authors concerning the Antilles we can say also of that of the first historians of other countries of America. 2. If America had been the true native country of the French disease, and if the Americans had been the first to suffer from it, it would be suffered more in America than elsewhere, and the Americans would be subject to such an evil more than any other nation; but it is not so. Of the Indians of the Antilles we cannot now speak, because it is now two centuries since they perished entirely: but among the present inhabitants of those islands the aforesaid contagion is far rarer than in Europe, and is not felt except in those places where there is a great frequency of European soldiers and sailors. In the capital of Mexico there are some whites and Indians infected with the venereal disease, but very few in proportion to the great number of the inhabitants. In other great cities of that vast kingdom the infected are very rare, and in others there is none at all; but in those places of Americans in which there is no great concourse of whites, such a disease has not

> (O) Viage è la America Merid. part. 1. Lib. 6. can. 6. Pare, che questa Scrittore abbia confuso, adottando l'opinione del volgo, il Malfrancese collo Scorbuco; poichè io so, che il Dutt. Giulio Rondoli Pesarese, Medico famo» so di Lima, aff:rmò ad una persona autorevole, che tra molti infermi cre» duti inferri dal Malfrancese, e da lui curati, quasi niuno avea trovato, che fosse travagliato da quel male; ma quasi tutti erano scorbutici, ed egli era riuscito nella lor curazione, adoprando i rimedj dello scorbuto. (P) Recb. Philo/. part. T. vydenham-atterma

[p. 327] been seen or heard of. Concerning South America I have been well informed by exact persons, truthful and very conversant with those countries, and have learned that in the provinces of Chile as well as in those of Paraguay that evil is very rare among the whites and never seen among the Americans. Some missionaries who have dwelt twenty or thirty years among different nations of Americans agree in affirming that they never saw anyone infected with that evil, nor even knew that it existed. As to the provinces of Peru and Quito, Señor Ulloa says, (O) that although in those countries the venereal disease is so common among the whites and among the other races of men, it is nevertheless a very rare thing to see an infected Indian there. America, therefore, is not the native country of that evil, as has commonly been believed, nor is that evil to be considered, as M. de P. would have it, (P) as an affection of the spoiled blood and of the bad temperament of the Americans.

> Sy Ain-um-delle-ine lettere (Enift:x7resp) che’ il Malfrancese è tanto forestiere în America, quanto in Europa ,e che vi su porta to da' Mori condotti schiavi dalla Guinea; ma non È vero, che gli fessi Mo-

What, then, is the true native country of the French disease, since it had its origin neither in Europe nor in America? I do not know; but if in the midst of uncertainty I am permitted to make use of conjectures, I suspect that that contagion came from Guinea, or from some other equatorial country of Africa. Of this same opinion was the most learned English physician Thomas Sydenham (Q), and it is confirmed by what Battista Fregoso affirms, an eyewitness of the beginning of the French disease

in

(O) Voyage to South America, pt. 1, bk. 6, ch. 6. It seems that this writer has confused the French disease with scurvy, adopting the opinion of the common people; for I know that Dr. Giulio Rondoli of Pesaro, a famous physician of Lima, affirmed to a person of authority that among many sick persons believed to be infected with the French disease, and treated by him, he had found almost none who was afflicted by that evil; but almost all were scorbutic, and he had succeeded in their cure by using the remedies for scurvy.

(P) Recherch. philosoph., pt. 1.

> Ti lo portalsero în America ; poichè prima che essi fossero condotii nella Spagnuola avea già questa isola cominciato ad infetrarsene, [p. 328] se in Europa. Costui dice nell’ opera già’ citarà (R), che il Malfrancese fu portato da Spagaa in Italia, e da Etiopia in Il, agna . Il Sig. Astruc precende, che Fulgofsio volle fignoificar l'America col nome d' Etiopia, Ecco un modo curioso di trarlì dalla difficoltà. Ma chi mai ha appellato Etiopia l Kmerica? Noi sappiamo per lo contrario, che èra comune preso gli Autori di quel Secolo il dare il nome d' Etiopia a qualunque paese abitato da uomini neri, è chiamare Etiopi rali uomini : ficchè il senso naturale delle parole del Fulgosio fi è, che il Malfraricese fu portato dai paesi equinoziali dell’ Africa nella Spagna Lusitanica, o fia Portogallo . Io pertanto sospetto, che il primo paese d' Europa a conragiarsi fa il Portogallo ; ma pon oserei affermarlo senza far nuove ricerche , e procacciarmai documenti migliori .

(Q) Sydenham affirms in one of his letters (Epist. 2, resp.) that the French disease is as foreign in America as in Europe, and that it was brought there by Blacks led as slaves from Guinea; but it is not true that these same Blacks carried it to America; for before they were brought to Hispaniola that island had already begun to be infected with it. [p. 328] in Europe. This man says in the work already cited (R) that the French disease was carried from Spain into Italy, and from Ethiopia into Spain. M. Astruc claims that Fregoso meant to signify America by the name of Ethiopia. Here is a curious way of getting out of the difficulty. But who ever called America Ethiopia? We know, on the contrary, that it was common among the authors of that century to give the name of Ethiopia to any country inhabited by black men, and to call such men Ethiopians: so that the natural sense of Fregoso’s words is that the French disease was carried from the equatorial countries of Africa into Lusitanian Spain, that is, Portugal. I therefore suspect that the first country of Europe to be infected was Portugal; but I should not dare to affirm it without making new researches and procuring better documents.
